<!-- Source: https://lgtmaybe.coles.codes/how-to/post-as-a-github-app/ -->

# Post as lgtmaybe[bot]

lgtmaybe is a GitHub Action. The Action runs the reviewer, and the provider,
model, and provider credentials stay in the workflow's `with:` block. A GitHub
App is optional: it only changes the author of lgtmaybe's GitHub comments from
`github-actions[bot]` to a branded bot.

You have three choices:

- **Do nothing:** the Action uses GitHub's workflow token and posts as
  `github-actions[bot]`.
- **Install the public lgtmaybe App:** the Action posts as `lgtmaybe[bot]`. You
  never receive or manage an App private key.
- **Use your own GitHub App:** an advanced, self-managed setup where you supply
  its App ID and private key.

## Install the public lgtmaybe App

1. [Install the lgtmaybe App](https://github.com/apps/lgtmaybe/installations/new)
   and select only the repositories where it should review pull requests.
2. Add `id-token: write` to the workflow permissions.
3. Set `github_identity: lgtmaybe` on the Action step.

Here is a complete OpenAI workflow. It gates reviews on trusted authors and
slash commands, as explained in
[Who can trigger a review](use-as-github-action.md#who-can-trigger-a-review):

```yaml
name: lgtmaybe

on:
  pull_request_target:
  issue_comment:
    types: [created]

permissions:
  contents: read
  id-token: write

jobs:
  review:
    if: >-
      (github.event_name == 'pull_request_target' &&
       contains(fromJson('["OWNER", "MEMBER", "COLLABORATOR"]'), github.event.pull_request.author_association)) ||
      (github.event.issue.pull_request &&
       contains(fromJson('["OWNER", "MEMBER", "COLLABORATOR"]'), github.event.comment.author_association) &&
       (contains(github.event.comment.body, '/review') ||
        contains(github.event.comment.body, '/improve') ||
        contains(github.event.comment.body, '/ask') ||
        contains(github.event.comment.body, '/describe') ||
        contains(github.event.comment.body, '/diagram')))
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7 # base repository only
      - uses: MattJColes/lgtmaybe@v2
        with:
          github_identity: lgtmaybe
          provider: openai
          model: gpt-5.5
          api_key: ${{ secrets.OPENAI_API_KEY }}
```

The provider configuration is unchanged: `github_identity` chooses who posts
on GitHub, not which model runs or where.

The public App has only:

- `contents: read`, to fetch repository and pull-request content
- `pull requests: write`, to post reviews, comments, and labels
- `issues: write`, to answer pull-request issue comments

The Action exchanges GitHub's signed workflow identity token for a short-lived
App token limited to the triggering repository and exactly those permissions.
The identity broker checks the repository, the event, and that the workflow
runs from the default branch. It never receives your diff, provider key,
prompt, model response, or review findings.

`github_identity: lgtmaybe` is an explicit choice. If `id-token: write` is
missing, the App is not installed on the repository, the workflow is not
trusted, or the identity service is unavailable, the job fails with setup
guidance. A misconfiguration is never papered over by quietly posting as
`github-actions[bot]`.

Reviews and the `/review`, `/improve`, `/ask`, `/describe`, and `/diagram`
commands arrive on `pull_request_target` or `issue_comment`, which run from the
default branch, so they post as `lgtmaybe[bot]`. Replies inside review threads
do not start a model run; the next review checks a pushed fix.

To remove access, uninstall the App or remove the repository from the
installation. To return to `github-actions[bot]`, remove
`github_identity: lgtmaybe` and `id-token: write` from the workflow (and add
back `pull-requests: write`). The Action revokes its temporary App token after
each run, once the review has stopped. A cancelled review gets up to 60 seconds
to post first. GitHub expires the token anyway if that cleanup cannot run.

The public App intentionally has no `Checks: write` permission, so
`github_identity: lgtmaybe` cannot be combined with `fail_on`. When lgtmaybe
must create a merge gate, keep the default `github_identity: actions` and grant
the workflow `checks: write`, or use a self-managed App with `Checks: write`.
The public App also cannot resolve fixed conversations: GitHub refuses
`resolveReviewThread` for it, so those threads stay open. See
[What the public App cannot do](use-as-github-action.md#what-the-public-app-cannot-do).

## Use your own GitHub App

Use this path only when your organisation already runs a GitHub App and wants
reviews attributed to it.

Give the App the repository permissions `contents: read`,
`pull requests: write`, and `issues: write`, plus `checks: write` if you use
`fail_on`. Install it on the repositories it may review. Store its ID as the
`LGTMAYBE_APP_ID` repository variable and its PEM private key as the
`LGTMAYBE_APP_PRIVATE_KEY` Actions secret:

```yaml
permissions:
  contents: read

steps:
  - uses: actions/checkout@v7
  - uses: MattJColes/lgtmaybe@v2
    with:
      provider: openai
      model: gpt-5.5
      api_key: ${{ secrets.OPENAI_API_KEY }}
      app_id: ${{ vars.LGTMAYBE_APP_ID }}
      app_private_key: ${{ secrets.LGTMAYBE_APP_PRIVATE_KEY }}
```

The Action mints a short-lived token for the current repository from these and
revokes it at the end of the job. To review across repositories, set
`app_owner` and `app_repositories` (see the
[Action inputs](use-as-github-action.md#github-identity-and-runtime)).

Do not combine `app_id` / `app_private_key` with
`github_identity: lgtmaybe`. The Action checks this before minting a token.

---

<!-- Source: https://lgtmaybe.coles.codes/how-to/review-stacked-pull-requests/ -->

# Review Stacked Pull Requests

A stack is a chain of small pull requests, each built on the one below it. You
review and merge them from the bottom up. GitHub supports stacks natively, and
tools such as Graphite, ghstack and git-town build them from ordinary branches.

lgtmaybe reviews each pull request in a stack on its own. It also knows where
that pull request sits, so its findings make sense for one layer of a bigger
change.

## Contents

- [What lgtmaybe Does](#what-lgtmaybe-does)
- [How It Finds the Stack](#how-it-finds-the-stack)
- [Set Up the Workflow](#set-up-the-workflow)
- [Review a Stacked Branch Locally](#review-a-stacked-branch-locally)
- [Other Code Hosts](#other-code-hosts)
- [See Also](#see-also)

## What lgtmaybe Does

Each pull request in a stack shows only its own changes: its layer. lgtmaybe
reviews that layer and nothing else. On GitHub it adds three things.

**It tells the model about the stack.** Every
[lens](../reference/glossary.md#lens) learns the layer's position, such as
"layer 2 of 3", and the branch the stack lands on. It also gets the number,
title and changed files of every other open layer. Code this layer uses may
come from a layer below, and a gap it leaves may be filled by a layer above.
Knowing that, the model hedges such claims instead of reporting them as bugs.
The review summary names the layer too.

The other layers' titles and paths are handled like the diff. They are
[redacted](../reference/glossary.md#redaction) before they leave, and the model
is told they are data, not instructions. lgtmaybe names at most eight layers on
each side.

**It skips a rebase that changes nothing.** When a lower pull request merges,
GitHub rebases every pull request above it. Each one gets a new commit, but its
diff is the same. lgtmaybe stamps a fingerprint of the whole diff next to its
[watermark](../reference/glossary.md#watermark). When a new commit's diff
matches it, the run stops without calling the model or posting anything.

The fingerprint ignores line numbers and blob ids, which a rebase moves. Any
change to an added, removed or surrounding line still counts, so that layer is
reviewed again. The skip is part of
[incremental review](../reference/glossary.md#incremental-review), which is on
by default for pushes.

**It reviews a retargeted pull request.** Tools that chain branches move a pull
request onto its parent's base when the parent merges. GitHub reports that as
an `edited` event that changes the base. The head commit stays the same, but
the diff changes. lgtmaybe runs a full review and refreshes the change
overview. Any other edit, such as a new title, runs nothing.

## How It Finds the Stack

GitHub's native stacks put a `stack` object on each pull request. lgtmaybe
reads it, then lists the layers through GitHub's stacks API.

Without that object, lgtmaybe follows branch names. When the pull request's base
is not the default branch, it looks for the open pull request whose head is that
base, and repeats downwards. It then looks for open pull requests based on this
one's head, and repeats upwards. A step with more than one match ends the walk
on that side. Only branches in the same repository count, so a pull request from
a fork is never walked.

When the walk stops early, at the eight-layer cap, an ambiguous step or a branch
it has already seen, lgtmaybe cannot know the layer's exact position. It then
tells the model, and the summary, only that the stack has at least that many
pull requests.

The lookup is best effort. If it fails, the review runs without stack context
and the failure is logged.

## Set Up the Workflow

The starter workflows in
[`examples/workflows/`](https://github.com/MattJColes/lgtmaybe/tree/main/examples/workflows)
already listen for the events a stack needs. If you wrote your own workflow,
add `edited` to the trigger:

```yaml
on:
  pull_request_target:
    types: [opened, synchronize, reopened, edited]
```

Then skip the edits that leave the base alone. Add the middle line below to the
`pull_request_target` arm of your job's `if:`, and keep the rest as it is:

```yaml
      (github.event_name == 'pull_request_target' &&
       (github.event.action != 'edited' || github.event.changes.base) &&
       contains(fromJson('["OWNER", "MEMBER", "COLLABORATOR"]'), github.event.pull_request.author_association)) ||
```

If your workflow sets `concurrency` at the top level, give those edits a group
of their own. Otherwise a title edit joins the review's group, and
`cancel-in-progress` cancels the running review. The starter workflows show how.

Every layer runs its own review, so a stack of five pull requests costs five
reviews. The rebase skip keeps the repeat cost down when lower layers merge.

## Review a Stacked Branch Locally

`lgtmaybe review` compares your branch with the repository's main branch. On a
stacked branch, that includes every layer below yours. Pass the parent branch
to review only your layer:

```bash
lgtmaybe review --base feature-a
```

The CLI does not find the parent branch for you.

## Other Code Hosts

Stack support is GitHub only. On GitLab, Gitea and Azure DevOps, each pull or
merge request is reviewed on its own, with no stack context.

## See Also

- [Use as a GitHub Action](use-as-github-action.md) - the workflow and its
  inputs.
- [Glossary: stacked pull requests](../reference/glossary.md#stacked-pull-requests).

---

<!-- Source: https://lgtmaybe.coles.codes/how-to/review-on-azure-devops/ -->

# Review Pull Requests on Azure DevOps

lgtmaybe posts reviews to Azure DevOps Repos as well as GitHub, GitLab and
Gitea. The review itself is identical, because none of it depends on the host.
It runs the same [lenses](../reference/glossary.md#lens), the same
[reflection](../reference/glossary.md#reflection) pass, and produces the same
findings. Only the adapter that reads the change and posts the comments differs.

Azure DevOps Services is supported: `dev.azure.com/{organisation}` and the
legacy `{organisation}.visualstudio.com`. Azure DevOps Server (on-premises) is
not supported yet.

## Set It Up

Azure Pipelines runs a pull request build from the YAML in the pull request
itself. So the job that holds the model key must not live in the repository
being reviewed. The setup below keeps it in a template in a separate, protected
repository, and the reviewed repository only extends it. Read
[Security: who can change the pipeline](#security-who-can-change-the-pipeline)
before choosing anything simpler.

1. **Create a protected template repository.** For example
   `Platform/pipeline-templates`. Add branch policies to its `main` branch, so
   nobody can change it without a review from someone trusted with the secrets.
   Commit
   [`examples/azure-devops/lgtmaybe-review.yml`](https://github.com/MattJColes/lgtmaybe/blob/main/examples/azure-devops/lgtmaybe-review.yml)
   to it.

2. **Store the model key in a variable group.** In *Pipelines → Library*,
   create a variable group named `lgtmaybe-secrets` holding the provider key as
   a secret, for example `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`. Use a key with a spend limit.

3. **Require the template.** On that variable group, open *Approvals and
   checks*, add a **Required template** check, and name the template
   repository, `refs/heads/main` and `lgtmaybe-review.yml`. A pipeline that does
   not extend exactly that template is refused the key, whatever its YAML says.

4. **Let the pipeline comment.** lgtmaybe posts with the job's own token,
   `System.AccessToken`. In *Project settings → Repositories → Security*,
   select the project's build service identity
   (`<Project> Build Service (<Organisation>)`) on the reviewed repository.
   Allow **Contribute to pull requests**, and nothing broader.

5. **Add the pipeline to the reviewed repository.** Copy
   [`examples/azure-devops/azure-pipelines.yml`](https://github.com/MattJColes/lgtmaybe/blob/main/examples/azure-devops/azure-pipelines.yml),
   and point its `resources.repositories` entry at your template repository.
   Create a pipeline from it. Approve its access to the template repository and
   the variable group on the first run.

6. **Run it on pull requests.** Azure Repos starts pull request builds from a
   branch policy, not from a `pr:` trigger. In *Project settings →
   Repositories → Policies*, open the target branch and add the pipeline under
   **Build validation**.

The reviewed repository's pipeline holds no steps and no secrets:

```yaml
trigger: none

resources:
  repositories:
    - repository: trusted
      type: git
      name: Platform/pipeline-templates
      ref: refs/heads/main

extends:
  template: lgtmaybe-review.yml@trusted
```

The template in the protected repository runs the GHCR image with the
`azure-pipelines` command:

```yaml
jobs:
  - job: lgtmaybe
    pool:
      vmImage: ubuntu-latest
    variables:
      - group: lgtmaybe-secrets
    steps:
      - checkout: none

      - script: |
          docker run --rm \
            -e SYSTEM_COLLECTIONURI -e SYSTEM_TEAMPROJECT \
            -e BUILD_REPOSITORY_NAME -e BUILD_REPOSITORY_PROVIDER \
            -e SYSTEM_PULLREQUEST_PULLREQUESTID \
            -e SYSTEM_ACCESSTOKEN -e ANTHROPIC_API_KEY \
            ghcr.io/mattjcoles/lgtmaybe:v2 \
            azure-pipelines --provider anthropic --model claude-sonnet-4-6
        displayName: lgtmaybe review
        env:
          SYSTEM_ACCESSTOKEN: $(System.AccessToken)
          ANTHROPIC_API_KEY: $(ANTHROPIC_API_KEY)
```

Secret variables, `System.AccessToken` included, reach a script only when they
are mapped under `env:`. That is why both are listed there. The template takes
no parameters on purpose: a parameter would let the pull request's YAML pass
steps into the job that holds the secrets.

`azure-pipelines` finds the pull request from these predefined variables:

- `SYSTEM_COLLECTIONURI`;
- `SYSTEM_TEAMPROJECT`;
- `BUILD_REPOSITORY_NAME`;
- `SYSTEM_PULLREQUEST_PULLREQUESTID`.

A build that is not validating a pull request has no id. There, lgtmaybe fails
with an error naming the missing variable rather than guessing.

A pipeline building a GitHub repository is refused too. Those pull requests
live on GitHub, so use the [GitHub Action](use-as-github-action.md).

Azure Pipelines always sets `BUILD_REPOSITORY_PROVIDER`. When it is unset
(running the command by hand), lgtmaybe treats the repository as Azure Repos.

Configure the review with the command's flags: `--provider`, `--model`,
`--fallback-model`, `--api-key`, `--api-base` and `--config`.

### Without Docker

On a self-hosted agent without Docker, install the CLI instead. These steps
replace the `steps:` of the protected template, never the reviewed
repository's pipeline:

```yaml
    steps:
      - checkout: none
      - task: UsePythonVersion@0
        inputs:
          versionSpec: "3.12"
      - script: |
          pip install lgtmaybe
          lgtmaybe azure-pipelines --provider anthropic --model claude-sonnet-4-6
        displayName: lgtmaybe review
        env:
          SYSTEM_ACCESSTOKEN: $(System.AccessToken)
          ANTHROPIC_API_KEY: $(ANTHROPIC_API_KEY)
```

## Tokens

lgtmaybe reads the Azure DevOps token from one of two variables:

| Variable | What it is | Sent as |
|---|---|---|
| `AZURE_DEVOPS_TOKEN` | A personal access token with **Code (Read & write)** scope | Basic auth, empty user name |
| `SYSTEM_ACCESSTOKEN` | The job's own token, mapped from `$(System.AccessToken)` | Bearer token |

When both are set, `AZURE_DEVOPS_TOKEN` wins. Use a personal access token when
the comments should come from a named account rather than the build service.
Either way, the token travels only in the `Authorization` header and is never
logged.

## Try It Locally First

Reviewing a pull request by URL happens in the pipeline, where the token and
the pull request live. Locally, `lgtmaybe review` reviews the branch you have
checked out against the remote primary branch. It prints the findings instead
of posting them:

```bash
git switch my-feature-branch
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=...
lgtmaybe review --provider anthropic --model claude-sonnet-4-6
```

## How It Differs from GitHub

Azure DevOps serves no unified diff (the standard text format for a change),
so lgtmaybe builds the diff itself:

1. It reads the pull request's latest iteration (Azure DevOps's name for one
   version of the pull request: one when it opens, then one per push).
2. It lists the files that iteration changes against the merge base.
3. It fetches each file's text before and after.
4. It builds the diff from the two.

Its limits and failure handling:

- Lockfiles, vendored and binary files are listed as changed but never fetched.
- A file side over 1 MB is treated like a binary.
- A pull request changing more than 300 files is not reviewed. lgtmaybe says so
  instead of reviewing part of it.
- When Azure DevOps reports no merge base for the pull request, the same
  applies: lgtmaybe says so and does not review it.
- lgtmaybe retries a file Azure DevOps keeps throttling or failing to return.
  If it still fails, lgtmaybe leaves that file out on its own and names it under
  **Files not reviewed** in the summary.
- A 401 or 403 fails the review, since that means the token is wrong.

Each finding is its own comment thread on the changed line. lgtmaybe leaves it
**active**, so a "resolve all comments" branch policy can hold the merge until
someone deals with it. The summary is a general thread that is edited in place on each run.
It is created **closed**, so it never holds a merge on its own. lgtmaybe does not
post a finding again when its thread is already open, or marked *Won't fix* or
*Closed*. It does post a finding again when its thread was marked *Resolved*
and the finding comes back.

On a later run, lgtmaybe marks a finding thread it opened *Resolved*, with a
`✅ Looks resolved.` reply. It does this when the finding is no longer reported
**and** the line it was posted on has changed since. Azure DevOps has no "this
code moved" flag. So lgtmaybe records the iteration each thread was posted at,
and compares the file then with the file now.

- Threads anyone else opened are never touched.
- Nothing is resolved after a run that failed or finished only partly.
- The token needs the same *Contribute to pull requests* permission it already
  uses to post.
- Set `resolve_fixed: false` in `.lgtmaybe.yml` to resolve threads by hand.
- A thread posted by an earlier lgtmaybe version may carry no iteration. One
  that doesn't stays open for a person to resolve.

These are not available yet:

| Not available | Why | What happens instead |
|---|---|---|
| Incremental review | Not built yet | Every run is a full review |
| Slash commands (`/review`, `/ask`, …) | `azure-pipelines` reviews the pull request; nothing routes comments to it | Queue the build again to review again |
| Change overview comment | `azure-pipelines` runs the review only | No description or diagram thread is posted |
| PR labels and the `fail_on` merge gate | Not built yet in the Azure DevOps adapter | No labels or pull request status are set |
| 👎 feedback (`learn_feedback`) | Not built yet | A downvoted finding can be posted again on a later run |
| Symbol resolution | No base-branch clone in the Azure DevOps adapter | Reflection judges cross-file findings without the symbol's definition |
| One-click suggestions | Azure DevOps has no suggestion blocks | A suggested fix shows as a code block |
| Azure DevOps Server | Only Azure DevOps Services URLs are recognised | The URL is refused with an error naming Azure DevOps Server |

Keyless model auth (Bedrock, Vertex, Azure OpenAI through GitHub OIDC) is built
into the GitHub composite action, not the `azure-pipelines` command. Use an API
key, or `ollama` against a model on the agent.

## Security: Who Can Change the Pipeline

A pull request build in Azure Pipelines runs the YAML from the pull request's
own merge result. This is the opposite of GitHub's `pull_request_target`, where
the base branch's workflow runs. So anyone who can push a branch and open a pull
request can rewrite a pipeline file in that repository. They can keep its
variable mappings, and send every secret those steps can read to a server of
their choosing. `checkout: none` does not help: the YAML itself is the part the
pull request controls.

So a pipeline file in the reviewed repository that maps a secret is only safe
when everyone who can open a pull request there is already trusted with that
secret. Otherwise use the setup above:

- The secret-bearing job lives in a template in a separate repository with
  branch policies, and the reviewed repository only `extends` it.
- The model key sits in a variable group guarded by a **Required template**
  check, so a pipeline that drops the `extends`, or points it at another branch
  or file, is refused the key.
- **Builds of pull requests from forks get no secrets by default. Keep that
  setting off.**
- Grant the build service only **Contribute to pull requests** on the reviewed
  repository. Keep *Limit job authorization scope to current project* turned
  on. Any pipeline can map its own `System.AccessToken`, so its
  permissions are what a rewritten pipeline could use.
- Prefer `System.AccessToken` over a personal access token. If you must use a
  personal access token, give it only **Code (Read & write)** on this
  organisation, a short expiry, and keep it in the protected variable group.
- Use a model key with a spend limit, so a leaked key has a ceiling.

lgtmaybe itself never checks out or executes pull request code. It reads the
change through the API and treats every byte of it as untrusted input.

---

<!-- Source: https://lgtmaybe.coles.codes/how-to/review-on-gitea/ -->

# Review Pull Requests on Gitea

lgtmaybe posts reviews to Gitea as well as GitHub. The review itself is
identical, because none of it depends on the host. It runs the same
[lenses](../reference/glossary.md#lens), the same
[reflection](../reference/glossary.md#reflection) pass, and produces the same
findings. Only the adapter that fetches the diff and posts the comments differs.

## Set It Up

The example workflow needs Gitea 1.21 or later, for the `pull_request_target`
trigger. Read
[Security: Who Can Change the Workflow](#security-who-can-change-the-workflow)
for why it matters.

1. **Create a token.** Sign in as a dedicated account with write access to the
   reviewed repository only. In Gitea, go to *Settings → Applications → Access
   Tokens*. Create a token with the `write:repository`, `write:issue` and
   `read:user` scopes (`read:user` lets lgtmaybe tell its own comments apart).
   Add it to your repository as a secret named `LGTMAYBE_GITEA_TOKEN`. Gitea
   refuses secret names that start with `GITEA_` or `GITHUB_`. The example maps
   this secret to the `GITEA_TOKEN` variable lgtmaybe reads.

    You need all three scopes:

    - `write:repository` also covers reading. Gitea files two endpoints under
      the *repository* category, not *issue*: the review endpoint lgtmaybe
      posts inline comments through (`POST /pulls/{index}/reviews`), and the
      commit-status endpoint. So a token with only `read:repository` is refused
      on the one call the setup exists to make.
    - `write:issue` covers the summary comment and the PR labels.
    - `read:user` lets lgtmaybe ask Gitea who the token is (`GET /user`). Only
      comments that identity wrote count as lgtmaybe's. So nobody else can edit
      the summary through us, or paste a hidden id that hides a finding.
      Without it, every re-run posts a fresh summary and re-posts its findings
      rather than trusting comments it cannot attribute.

2. **Add a provider key.** Add the API key for whichever model you want as a
   second secret, for example `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`. Use a key with a spend
   limit.

3. **Add the workflow.** Copy
   [`examples/gitea/lgtmaybe.yml`](https://github.com/MattJColes/lgtmaybe/blob/main/examples/gitea/lgtmaybe.yml)
   into your repository at `.gitea/workflows/lgtmaybe.yml`.

That is the whole setup. Gitea Actions reimplements the GitHub Actions runtime.
So the example runs lgtmaybe's container image with the same `action` command
and `INPUT_*` variables. lgtmaybe reads `GITHUB_SERVER_URL`, which Gitea points
at your own instance, to know which host to post to.

## Try It Locally First

Reviewing a pull request by URL happens in the Actions run, where the token and
the PR context live. Locally, `lgtmaybe review` reviews the branch you have
checked out against the remote primary branch. It prints the findings instead
of posting them:

```bash
git switch my-feature-branch
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=...
lgtmaybe review --provider anthropic --model claude-sonnet-4-6
```

It runs the same review. Use it to see what a model will say about your change
before you wire up the workflow.

## What Works, and What Does Not

The review itself works in full:

- every lens and the self-reflection pass;
- secret [redaction](../reference/glossary.md#redaction) and
  [prompt-injection](../reference/glossary.md#prompt-injection) hardening;
- [static-analysis fusion](../reference/glossary.md#static-analysis-fusion);
- path filters and finding rules;
- the [change overview](../reference/glossary.md#change-overview) comment;
- PR labels (only labels that already exist in the repository; lgtmaybe does
  not create them);
- the [`fail_on`](../reference/glossary.md#fail-on) merge gate (as a commit
  status);
- the `/review`, `/improve`, `/ask`, `/describe` and `/diagram` slash commands.

A slash command runs only for a commenter with write access to the repository.
Gitea's workflow `if:` cannot read the commenter's role the way GitHub's
`author_association` does. So lgtmaybe checks it itself through the collaborator
permission API. Anyone else's command is ignored with a log line, exits
successfully, and makes no model call.

These are unavailable on Gitea, and lgtmaybe skips them rather than failing:

| Not available | Why | What happens instead |
|---|---|---|
| Incremental review | Gitea's compare endpoint returns commit metadata, not a unified diff | Every run is a full review |
| Resolve-on-fix | Gitea has no thread-resolution API | Fixed findings' comments stay open |
| 👎 feedback (`learn_feedback`) | Not implemented in the Gitea adapter | A downvoted finding can be posted again on a later run |
| Symbol resolution | No base-branch clone in the Gitea adapter | Reflection judges cross-file findings without the symbol's definition |
| Keyless cloud auth | The OIDC/WIF exchange is built into the GitHub composite action | Use an API key, or `ollama` for a local model |

A submitted Gitea review cannot be edited. So lgtmaybe reads the hidden finding
IDs already on the pull request, and does not post the same finding twice. The
summary lives in an ordinary comment, which is editable, so it updates in place
on each run.

## Security: Who Can Change the Workflow

A `pull_request` run in Gitea Actions takes its workflow file from the pull
request's own head commit. A pull request from a branch in the same repository
runs whatever workflow it contains, with the repository's secrets. So anyone who
can push a branch could rewrite the review job. They could then send the model
key and the token to a server of their choosing.

A pull request from a fork also runs its own workflow. But Gitea passes it no
repository or organisation secrets, only the automatic job token, so lgtmaybe
cannot review it.

`pull_request_target`, available from Gitea 1.21, takes the workflow from the
base branch instead, as on GitHub. It gives that workflow the repository's
secrets for pull requests from forks too. That is why the example uses it, and
why it is the same trade-off as on GitHub. lgtmaybe never checks out or executes
pull-request code. It reads the diff through the API and treats every byte of it
as untrusted input.

The `issue_comment` arm always runs the workflow from the default branch, so a
pull request cannot change that either. Gitea still treats a comment on a fork's
pull request as a fork run, and passes it no secrets. So slash commands work
only on pull requests from branches in the repository.

What `pull_request_target` does not cover:

- **Anyone with write access can still read the secrets.** Repository and
  organisation secrets reach every workflow run in the repository. That
  includes a `push` workflow on a branch someone has just pushed, with no pull
  request involved. Give write access only to people trusted with the secrets,
  and take other contributions as pull requests from forks.
- **Gitea before 1.21 has no `pull_request_target`.** There, switch the example
  to `pull_request` only if everyone who can push a branch is trusted with the
  secrets. Pull requests from forks are not reviewed, because their runs get no
  secrets.
- **A fork's pull request starts a paid review without approval.** On an
  instance with open registration, anyone can open one. Use a model key with a
  spend limit.

Keep the token narrow too. A Gitea access token works on every repository its
owner can reach. That is why step 1 creates it on a dedicated account with
write access to the reviewed repository only. It also gives the token only the
three scopes lgtmaybe needs. Do not use `secrets.GITEA_TOKEN` in its place: that
name always resolves to the automatic job token, because Gitea refuses a secret
of your own with that name.

---

<!-- Source: https://lgtmaybe.coles.codes/how-to/review-on-gitlab/ -->

# Review Merge Requests on GitLab

lgtmaybe posts reviews to GitLab as well as GitHub. The review itself is
identical, because none of it depends on the host. It runs the same
[lenses](../reference/glossary.md#lens), the same
[reflection](../reference/glossary.md#reflection) pass, and produces the same
findings. Only the adapter that fetches the diff and posts the comments differs.

## Set It Up

A merge request pipeline runs the CI configuration from the merge request's own
source branch. So where the job lives decides who can read its secrets. Read
[Security: Who Can Change the Pipeline](#security-who-can-change-the-pipeline)
before choosing where it goes.

1. **Create a token.** In your project, go to *Settings → Access Tokens*.
   Create a project access token with the `api` scope, the Developer role and an
   expiry date. Add it under *Settings → CI/CD → Variables* as `GITLAB_TOKEN`.
   Make it masked, with **Environment scope** set to `lgtmaybe`.

2. **Add a provider key.** Add the API key for whichever model you want as a
   second masked variable scoped to the `lgtmaybe` environment, for example
   `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`. Use a key with a spend limit.

3. **Add the job.** Copy
   [`examples/gitlab/.gitlab-ci.yml`](https://github.com/MattJColes/lgtmaybe/blob/main/examples/gitlab/.gitlab-ci.yml)
   into your repository, or merge its `lgtmaybe` job into your existing
   pipeline. If not everyone who can push a branch is trusted with the secrets,
   put it in a separate configuration project instead. See
   [Keep the Pipeline Configuration Outside the Project](#keep-the-pipeline-configuration-outside-the-project).

The job names the environment `lgtmaybe` with `action: access`. That lets it
read the variables scoped to that environment without recording a deployment.
The pipeline's other jobs never receive them.

The job runs `python -m lgtmaybe gitlab-ci`. It finds the merge request from
these GitLab predefined variables:

- `CI_SERVER_URL` or `CI_SERVER_HOST`;
- `CI_MERGE_REQUEST_PROJECT_PATH` or `CI_PROJECT_PATH`;
- `CI_MERGE_REQUEST_IID`.

It must therefore run on merge request pipelines:

```yaml
rules:
  - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"
```

A branch pipeline has no merge request to review. There, lgtmaybe fails with an
error naming the missing `CI_MERGE_REQUEST_IID` rather than guessing.

The example job does not clone the repository (`GIT_STRATEGY: none`), so there
is no `.lgtmaybe.yml` to read. Configure the review with the command's flags:
`--provider`, `--model`, `--fallback-model`, `--api-key`, `--api-base`,
`--config` and `--no-incremental`.

## Try It Locally First

Reviewing a merge request by URL happens in CI, where the token and the MR
context live. Locally, `lgtmaybe review` reviews the branch you have checked out
against the remote primary branch. It prints the findings instead of posting
them:

```bash
git switch my-feature-branch
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=...
lgtmaybe review --provider anthropic --model claude-sonnet-4-6
```

It runs the same review. Use it to see what a model will say about your change
before you wire up the pipeline.

## How It Differs from GitHub

GitLab has no batched review object, so lgtmaybe posts each finding as its own
discussion. The merge request's diff refs and the old or new file line anchor
it. The summary is a note that updates in place on each run.

Resolve-on-fix works here: GitLab discussions resolve over plain REST, where
GitHub needs GraphQL. lgtmaybe resolves a finding's discussion only once the
follow-up validation pass on an
[incremental](../reference/glossary.md#incremental-review) run has confirmed it
is fixed. It never resolves one merely because the finding stopped being
reported.

GitHub also requires the thread to be marked outdated (the code under it
changed). GitLab's API has no such flag, so lgtmaybe works it out. A discussion
counts as outdated when the diff since the commit it was posted on touches the
[hunk](../reference/glossary.md#hunk) around its line.

The GitLab adapter also supports PR labels and the
[`fail_on`](../reference/glossary.md#fail-on) merge gate (reported as a commit
status). Both are config-file settings, so they need a job that provides a file
for `--config`.

### Incremental Re-review

The first pipeline on a merge request reviews the whole change. Every later
pipeline reviews only the commits pushed since the last completed review. It
reads where to start from a hidden
[watermark](../reference/glossary.md#watermark) in lgtmaybe's summary note.
lgtmaybe trusts that watermark only in a note written by its own token's user.
Another user's note therefore cannot skip a review.

It falls back to a full review whenever the increment can't be trusted:

- the branch was rebased or force-pushed (the new commits don't build on the
  last reviewed one);
- the new commits include a merge;
- GitLab no longer knows the last reviewed commit, timed out, or left part of
  the diff out because it is too large;
- any API call fails.

A failed or partial run leaves the watermark where it was. The next run then
still covers the commits it missed. Running a pipeline again on a head that was
already reviewed completely posts nothing.

GitLab has no `/review full`. To force a full re-review, do one of these:

- run the pipeline with the CI/CD variable `LGTMAYBE_INCREMENTAL` set to `false`;
- pass `--no-incremental`;
- set `incremental: false` in the config file.

### 👎 Feedback

Award a 👎 (`thumbsdown`) emoji to the first note of one of lgtmaybe's finding
discussions. Later runs then stop raising that finding on the merge request.
Only a 👎 from a member with the Developer role or above counts, because anyone
can award an emoji on a public project. A high or critical security finding is
never hidden this way. Set `learn_feedback: false` to turn it off.

These are not available:

| Not available | Why | What happens instead |
|---|---|---|
| Slash commands (`/review`, `/ask`, …) | `gitlab-ci` reviews the merge request; nothing routes MR comments to it | Re-run the pipeline to review again |
| Change overview comment | `gitlab-ci` runs the review only | No description or diagram comment is posted |
| Symbol resolution | No base-branch clone in the GitLab adapter | Reflection judges cross-file findings without the symbol's definition |
| Keyless cloud auth | The OIDC/WIF exchange is built into the GitHub composite action | Use an API key, or `ollama` |

## Security: Who Can Change the Pipeline

A merge request pipeline runs the `.gitlab-ci.yml` from the merge request's
source branch, not from the target branch. This is the opposite of GitHub's
`pull_request_target`, where the base branch's workflow runs. GitLab has no
equivalent.

So anyone who can push a branch to the project (the Developer role and above)
can edit the `lgtmaybe` job. They can keep its variables and send the model key
and `GITLAB_TOKEN` to a server of their choosing. A branch pipeline gives them
the same access without opening a merge request at all. `GIT_STRATEGY: none`
does not help: the YAML itself is the part they control.

A job in the reviewed project's own CI configuration is only safe when everyone
who can push a branch there is already trusted with both secrets. For a team
where that holds, the setup above is enough. Otherwise, choose one of the setups
below. Each has a cost, and none of them is as simple as `pull_request_target`.

Scoping the variables to the `lgtmaybe` environment is worth doing either way,
but it is not a defence against this. It keeps the secrets away from jobs that
never ask for them, such as a compromised test tool. A job the merge request
controls can still name the environment.

### Merge Requests from Forks

A merge request from a fork is safe by default. Its pipeline runs in the fork,
with the fork's CI configuration and the fork's variables. It never receives
the parent project's variables. Keep it that way:

- Do not use **Run pipeline** on a fork's merge request in the parent project.
  That runs the fork's CI configuration in the parent project with all of the
  parent's variables, which hands the fork's author your secrets. GitLab shows a
  warning before it does this.
- To remove the option, disable `ci_allow_fork_pipelines_to_run_in_parent_project`
  with the [projects API](https://docs.gitlab.com/api/projects/#update-a-project).

The cost is that lgtmaybe does not review fork merge requests: their pipelines
have no key.

### Protected Variables

Mark `GITLAB_TOKEN` and the model key **Protected**. That keeps them out of
every pipeline on an unprotected branch, so pushing a branch no longer reveals
them. A merge request pipeline receives protected variables only when all of
these hold (the setting below arrived in GitLab 18.1):

- the project allows it, under *Settings → CI/CD → Variables → Access protected
  resources in merge request pipelines*;
- both the source and target branches are protected, and in the same project;
- the user who starts the pipeline can push or merge to the target branch.

A merge request pipeline from a fork never receives them.

The cost: lgtmaybe then reviews only merge requests between protected branches,
opened by people who could already change the pipeline there. A merge request
from an ordinary feature branch gets no token and the job fails. To skip the job
there instead, extend its rule:

```yaml
rules:
  - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event" && $CI_MERGE_REQUEST_SOURCE_BRANCH_PROTECTED == "true"
```

### Keep the Pipeline Configuration Outside the Project

This works on every GitLab tier. In the reviewed project, set *Settings → CI/CD →
General pipelines → CI/CD configuration file* to a file in a separate project.
For example, `.gitlab-ci.yml@my-group/ci-config` (append `:branch-name` to pin a
branch). Every pipeline in the reviewed project then runs that file, merge
request and branch pipelines alike. No commit to the reviewed project can change
a job. Changing the setting needs the Maintainer role. Protect the configuration
project's default branch, and give write access only to people trusted with the
secrets.

The variables stay unprotected, so merge requests from feature branches are
reviewed. What it costs:

- That file is now the project's whole pipeline, so the project's build and test
  jobs must live there too. Do not `include` the reviewed project's own CI files
  from it. A file read at the merge request's commit is the merge request's to
  edit, and its jobs could name the `lgtmaybe` environment.
- Those build and test jobs still run the merge request's code. Keep both
  variables scoped to the `lgtmaybe` environment so those jobs never receive
  them. Keep that environment out of every job but the review.
- Do not let a job that runs merge request code share a shell-executor runner
  with the review job. There, jobs run as the same user on the same host, and
  one can read another's environment.
- Keep *Settings → CI/CD → Variables → Minimum role to use pipeline variables*
  at Maintainer or above (the self-managed default), or `no_one_allowed` (the
  default for new projects on GitLab.com). A pipeline variable outranks a
  project variable, so anyone who can set one can change the review job's
  environment. `AZURE_API_BASE`, for example, tells lgtmaybe where to send the
  key when the job passes no `--api-base`.

### Pipeline Execution Policies

A [pipeline execution policy](https://docs.gitlab.com/user/application_security/policies/pipeline_execution_policies/)
(GitLab Ultimate) can add the `lgtmaybe` job to every pipeline from a separate
security policy project. A merge request then cannot change that job. On its own
it does not keep the secrets safe.

If the policy does not replace the project's configuration entirely
(`override_project_ci`), the project's own `.gitlab-ci.yml` still runs from the
merge request's branch. Its jobs receive the same project and group
variables, or can name the `lgtmaybe` environment to get them. A policy that
does replace the configuration has the same costs as the previous section.

### Tokens and Keys

Whichever setup you choose, assume a secret can leak and limit what it is worth:

- Make `GITLAB_TOKEN` a project access token on this project only, with:
    - the `api` scope (posting discussions needs it; `read_api` cannot);
    - the Developer role and nothing higher;
    - a short expiry.

    On GitLab.com, project access tokens need Premium or Ultimate. On the Free
    tier, use a personal access token of a dedicated account that is a Developer
    of this project alone. A leaked token can post as lgtmaybe. That includes a
    summary note whose watermark makes the next incremental run skip the commits
    before it.
- Use a model key with a spend limit, so a leaked key has a ceiling.

lgtmaybe itself never checks out or executes merge request code. It reads the
diff through the API and treats every byte of it as untrusted input. That is
why the example job sets `GIT_STRATEGY: none` and does not clone the repository
at all.

---

<!-- Source: https://lgtmaybe.coles.codes/how-to/review-with-openai/ -->

# Review with OpenAI

OpenAI is a key-based provider: add an `OPENAI_API_KEY` and pick a model. There
is no OIDC and no endpoint to configure, which makes it the simplest path to a
hosted review.

## Contents

- [Get an API key](#get-an-api-key)
- [GitHub Action](#github-action)
- [Run locally](#run-locally)
- [Choosing the model](#choosing-the-model)
- [Persist non-secret defaults](#persist-non-secret-defaults)

## Get an API Key

Create a key at <https://platform.openai.com/api-keys>. In your repository, add
it as an Actions secret named `OPENAI_API_KEY`
(**Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → New repository secret**).

## GitHub Action

Copy [`examples/workflows/review-openai.yml`][wf] to
`.github/workflows/lgtmaybe.yml`. The core step is:

```yaml
- uses: MattJColes/lgtmaybe@v2
  with:
    provider: openai
    model: gpt-5.5
    api_key: ${{ secrets.OPENAI_API_KEY }}
```

The workflow runs on `pull_request_target`, so the secret is available, but PR
code is never checked out: lgtmaybe reads the diff through the API. See
[Use as a GitHub Action](use-as-github-action.md) for the full workflow,
including [who can trigger a review](use-as-github-action.md#who-can-trigger-a-review).

## Run Locally

```bash
export OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-...

lgtmaybe review --provider openai --model gpt-5.5
```

You can pass the key with `--api-key sk-...` instead of the env var. Either way,
the key is never persisted to config.

## Choosing the Model

Use any chat model your key can access. Name it as you would send it to the
OpenAI API (litellm's native form). Good choices are:

- `gpt-5.5`;
- one of the newer GPT-6 models (`gpt-6-sol`, `gpt-6-luna`, `gpt-6-astra`);
- a smaller model, to cut cost.

[Choose a review model](choose-a-review-model.md) has measured results for the
GPT-6 family.

Under the default `fast` [preset](../reference/glossary.md#preset), a `gpt-5*`
review model runs its [reflection](../reference/glossary.md#reflection)
(false-positive audit) pass on `gpt-5-mini`. So your key needs access to that
model too. Set `reflect_model` to choose a different auditor.

## Persist Non-Secret Defaults

Provider and model are not secrets, so they can live in `.lgtmaybe.yml`. The key
stays in the environment.

```yaml
provider: openai
model: gpt-5.5
```

With that file in place, `lgtmaybe review` needs no flags. See
[Configure .lgtmaybe.yml](configure-lgtmaybe-yml.md) for every setting.

[wf]: https://github.com/MattJColes/lgtmaybe/blob/main/examples/workflows/review-openai.yml

---

<!-- Source: https://lgtmaybe.coles.codes/how-to/review-with-anthropic/ -->

# Review with Claude (Anthropic)

Anthropic is a key-based provider: add an `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` and pick a Claude
model. There is no OIDC and no endpoint to configure.

## Contents

- [Get an API key](#get-an-api-key)
- [GitHub Action](#github-action)
- [Run locally](#run-locally)
- [Choosing the model](#choosing-the-model)
- [Want it through a gateway instead?](#want-it-through-a-gateway-instead)
- [Persist non-secret defaults](#persist-non-secret-defaults)

## Get an API Key

Create a key in the [Anthropic Console](https://console.anthropic.com/). In your
repository, add it as an Actions secret named `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`
(**Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → New repository secret**).

## GitHub Action

Copy [`examples/workflows/review-anthropic.yml`][wf] to
`.github/workflows/lgtmaybe.yml`. The core step is:

```yaml
- uses: MattJColes/lgtmaybe@v2
  with:
    provider: anthropic
    model: claude-sonnet-4-6
    api_key: ${{ secrets.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }}
```

The workflow runs on `pull_request_target`, so the secret is available, but PR
code is never checked out: lgtmaybe reads the diff through the API. See
[Use as a GitHub Action](use-as-github-action.md) for the full workflow,
including [who can trigger a review](use-as-github-action.md#who-can-trigger-a-review).

## Run Locally

```bash
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-...

lgtmaybe review --provider anthropic --model claude-sonnet-4-6
```

You can pass the key with `--api-key sk-ant-...` instead of the env var. Either
way, the key is never persisted to config.

## Choosing the Model

Pass litellm's native Anthropic name as the model. `claude-sonnet-4-6` is a
strong default. Use an Opus-class model (such as `claude-opus-5-5`) for the
deepest review, at a higher price. Use a Haiku-class model (such as
`claude-haiku-4-5`) to cut cost on smaller PRs.

Under the default `fast` [preset](../reference/glossary.md#preset), a Sonnet or
Opus review model runs its [reflection](../reference/glossary.md#reflection)
(false-positive audit) pass on `claude-haiku-4-5`. So your key needs access to
that model too. Set `reflect_model` to choose a different auditor.

## Want It Through a Gateway Instead?

If you reach Claude through OpenRouter, Bedrock or Vertex rather than the
Anthropic API, use that provider instead:

- [OpenRouter](review-with-openrouter.md): `anthropic/claude-sonnet-4.6`
- [Bedrock (keyless OIDC)](review-with-bedrock-oidc.md)
- [Vertex (keyless WIF)](review-with-vertex-wif.md)

## Persist Non-Secret Defaults

Provider and model are not secrets, so they can live in `.lgtmaybe.yml`. The key
stays in the environment.

```yaml
provider: anthropic
model: claude-sonnet-4-6
```

With that file in place, `lgtmaybe review` needs no flags. See
[Configure .lgtmaybe.yml](configure-lgtmaybe-yml.md) for every setting.

[wf]: https://github.com/MattJColes/lgtmaybe/blob/main/examples/workflows/review-anthropic.yml

# Review with OpenRouter

[OpenRouter](https://openrouter.ai/) is a key-based gateway to many model
vendors behind one API. Add an `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`, then pick any model
OpenRouter offers by its `vendor/model` name.

## Contents

- [Get an API key](#get-an-api-key)
- [GitHub Action](#github-action)
- [Run locally](#run-locally)
- [Choosing the model](#choosing-the-model)
- [Credit reservations](#credit-reservations)
- [Rate limits](#rate-limits)
- [Persist non-secret defaults](#persist-non-secret-defaults)

## Get an API Key

Create a key at <https://openrouter.ai/keys>. In your repository, add it as an
Actions secret named `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`
(**Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → New repository secret**).

## GitHub Action

Copy [`examples/workflows/review-openrouter.yml`][wf] to
`.github/workflows/lgtmaybe.yml`. The core step is:

```yaml
- uses: MattJColes/lgtmaybe@v2
  with:
    provider: openrouter
    model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-4.6
    api_key: ${{ secrets.OPENROUTER_API_KEY }}
```

The workflow runs on `pull_request_target`, so the secret is available, but PR
code is never checked out: lgtmaybe reads the diff through the API. See
[Use as a GitHub Action](use-as-github-action.md) for the full workflow,
including [who can trigger a review](use-as-github-action.md#who-can-trigger-a-review).

## Run Locally

```bash
export OPENROUTER_API_KEY=sk-or-...

lgtmaybe review --provider openrouter --model anthropic/claude-sonnet-4.6
```

You can pass the key with `--api-key sk-or-...` instead of the env var. Either
way, the key is never persisted to config.

## Choosing the Model

OpenRouter models are named `vendor/model`. Pick whichever fits your budget and
quality bar, for example:

- `anthropic/claude-sonnet-4.6`
- `openai/gpt-5.5`
- `z-ai/glm-4.6`

Browse the full catalogue and per-model pricing at
<https://openrouter.ai/models>.

One catalogue quirk: a model can accept JSON-schema mode through OpenRouter yet
return replies that parse as empty. The review then comes back with zero
findings and no error (seen with `anthropic/claude-fable-5.1`). If a model is
silent on everything, try one diff with `--no-structured-output` (see
[Configure .lgtmaybe.yml](configure-lgtmaybe-yml.md#structured_output)) before
writing the model off.

## Credit Reservations

OpenRouter checks your balance before it generates anything. It costs the
worst case: the prompt plus the most tokens the reply could use. OpenRouter
assumes a request with no cap wants the model's full output ceiling. So it can
refuse a review for credit the review was never going to spend:

```
This request requires more credits, or fewer max_tokens.
You requested up to 65536 tokens, but can only afford 25905.
```

To keep that reservation realistic, OpenRouter reviews send a default cap of
16384 tokens per call. If a refusal names a larger number, something has
overridden the default. Check the `per-call budget resolved` log line, which
names the ceiling and where it came from:

```
per-call budget resolved  timeout_s=1800  max_tokens=16384  max_tokens_source="provider default"
```

Top up, or lower the cap so the reservation fits your balance:

```yaml
max_tokens: 8192
```

`--max-tokens 8192` does the same for one run. `max_tokens` is also a GitHub
Action input.

Lower it with care:

- A cap that is too low [truncates](../reference/glossary.md#truncation) the
  findings JSON mid-object.
- Reasoning models spend this same budget on thinking tokens, so they need more
  headroom than a plain model.

`max_tokens: 0` removes the cap and puts the reservation back to the model's
full ceiling.

lgtmaybe treats this refusal as permanent and stops after one attempt. Your
balance cannot grow mid-review, so retrying every
[lens](../reference/glossary.md#lens) would only waste runner time before
reporting the same failure.

## Rate Limits

A capacity 429 (the HTTP status for too many requests) is different. It is
temporary, and lgtmaybe handles it for you:

- Rate-limited calls back off on a 20s-60s ladder. That is long enough to reach
  a fresh per-minute window.
- They honour OpenRouter's `Retry-After` header when it sends one (clamped at
  120s).
- A lens that is still failing on the provider when the
  [fan-out](../reference/glossary.md#fan-out) drains is re-run once more.

That rescue covers provider-side failures only. A second attempt would buy the
same answer at full price, so it leaves these alone:

- unparseable output;
- a blown `max_tokens` ceiling;
- a batch the oversized-diff split already retried;
- an unrecoverable failure such as a spent quota;
- any limit you set (`max_review_seconds`, `max_review_tokens`, a cancelled
  job).

Usually you will see none of this. A review that could not recover says so in
its summary and names the lens it lost.

If you are seeing rate limits, check the review's own burst before blaming the
model. Every `(batch, lens)` call shares one concurrency pool and one API key.
So a wide fan-out can throttle itself:

```yaml
max_concurrency: 3
```

Beyond that, it is a question about your OpenRouter account. Limits on free
model variants (the `:free` suffix) are account-wide rather than per-model. The
daily allowance depends on how much credit the account has bought. So a review
is far more likely to be throttled on a free variant than a paid one.

Paid models carry no OpenRouter platform request cap, though the upstream
provider behind a model can still rate-limit you. Neither is the same as a
per-key credit spending cap. That cap limits what a key may spend, not how often
it may call.

## Persist Non-Secret Defaults

Provider and model are not secrets, so they can live in `.lgtmaybe.yml`. The key
stays in the environment.

```yaml
provider: openrouter
model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-4.6
```

With that file in place, `lgtmaybe review` needs no flags. See
[Configure .lgtmaybe.yml](configure-lgtmaybe-yml.md) for every setting.

[wf]: https://github.com/MattJColes/lgtmaybe/blob/main/examples/workflows/review-openrouter.yml

---

<!-- Source: https://lgtmaybe.coles.codes/how-to/review-with-zai/ -->

# Review with z.ai (GLM)

[z.ai](https://z.ai/)'s GLM models (from Zhipu AI) are a first-class provider:
add a `ZAI_API_KEY` and pick a model. lgtmaybe reaches them through litellm's
native `zai/` route, so the international endpoint needs no `api_base`.

## Contents

- [Get an API key](#get-an-api-key)
- [GitHub Action](#github-action)
- [Run locally](#run-locally)
- [Choosing the model](#choosing-the-model)
- [China / coding-plan endpoint](#china-coding-plan-endpoint)
- [Persist non-secret defaults](#persist-non-secret-defaults)

## Get an API Key

Create a key in the [z.ai developer console](https://z.ai/) (see the
[API docs](https://docs.z.ai/)). In your repository, add it as an Actions secret
named `ZAI_API_KEY`
(**Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → New repository secret**).

## GitHub Action

Copy [`examples/workflows/review-zai.yml`][wf] to
`.github/workflows/lgtmaybe.yml`. The core step is:

```yaml
- uses: MattJColes/lgtmaybe@v2
  with:
    provider: zai
    model: glm-4.6
    api_key: ${{ secrets.ZAI_API_KEY }}
```

The workflow runs on `pull_request_target`, so the secret is available, but PR
code is never checked out: lgtmaybe reads the diff through the API. See
[Use as a GitHub Action](use-as-github-action.md) for the full workflow,
including [who can trigger a review](use-as-github-action.md#who-can-trigger-a-review).

## Run Locally

```bash
export ZAI_API_KEY=...

lgtmaybe review --provider zai --model glm-4.6
```

You can pass the key with `--api-key ...` instead of the env var. Either way, the
key is never persisted to config.

## Choosing the Model

Pass any GLM chat model your key can access, such as `glm-4.6`, `glm-4.7`,
`glm-4.5-air`, or a newer `glm-5.x`. Use the name z.ai's API expects; lgtmaybe
adds the `zai/` route prefix for you.

## China / Coding-Plan Endpoint

The native route targets z.ai's international endpoint. To use the China or
coding-plan endpoint instead, point `--api-base` (or `ZAI_API_BASE`, or the
Action's `api_base` input) at it:

```bash
lgtmaybe review \
  --provider zai \
  --model glm-4.6 \
  --api-base https://open.bigmodel.cn/api/paas/v4
```

## Persist Non-Secret Defaults

Provider and model are not secrets, so they can live in `.lgtmaybe.yml`. The key
stays in the environment.

```yaml
provider: zai
model: glm-4.6
```

With that file in place, `lgtmaybe review` needs no flags. See
[Configure .lgtmaybe.yml](configure-lgtmaybe-yml.md) for every setting.

[wf]: https://github.com/MattJColes/lgtmaybe/blob/main/examples/workflows/review-zai.yml

<!-- Source: https://lgtmaybe.coles.codes/how-to/review-with-bedrock-oidc/ -->

# Review with AWS Bedrock (Keyless OIDC)

Use this guide to run lgtmaybe with AWS Bedrock using GitHub's
[OIDC](../reference/glossary.md#oidc) token. No static AWS credentials are stored in secrets.

## Contents

- [How it works](#how-it-works)
- [One-time AWS setup](#one-time-aws-setup)
- [Workflow example](#workflow-example)
- [Choosing a Bedrock model ID](#choosing-a-bedrock-model-id)
- [Running locally with ambient AWS credentials](#running-locally-with-ambient-aws-credentials)
- [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting)

## How It Works

GitHub Actions issues a short-lived OIDC token. AWS STS exchanges it for
temporary credentials for an [IAM](../reference/glossary.md#iam) role you control. Pass
`aws_role_arn` and the Action performs that exchange for you. lgtmaybe then
picks up the credentials through the standard AWS credential chain. There is no
`AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` or `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` in your secrets.

## One-Time AWS Setup

Do this once in your AWS account:

1. Create an IAM OIDC identity provider for `token.actions.githubusercontent.com`.
2. Create an IAM role with a trust policy scoped to your repository
   (`repo:<org>/<repo>:*`).
3. Attach the least-privilege policy below.
4. Confirm the models you want are enabled in the target region (model access
   in the Bedrock console).
5. Note the role ARN (e.g. `arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/lgtmaybe-bedrock`).
   It becomes the `aws_role_arn` Action input.

The role needs only:

```json
{
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Action": [
    "bedrock:InvokeModel",
    "bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream"
  ],
  "Resource": [
    "arn:aws:bedrock:*:<account-id>:inference-profile/*",
    "arn:aws:bedrock:*::foundation-model/*"
  ]
}
```

Both ARNs are required for the recommended inference-profile model IDs (the
`us.`/`eu.`/`apac.`-prefixed IDs below). A cross-region inference profile routes
the call to the foundation model in several regions, so the role needs
`bedrock:InvokeModel*` on both the `inference-profile/*` ARN and the underlying
`foundation-model/*` ARN. Granting only one still fails with
`AccessDeniedException`. A bare `anthropic.…` model ID needs only the
`foundation-model/*` ARN. But most current Claude models can only be invoked
through an inference profile (see the model table below).

Once it works, scope each `Resource` to specific model and inference-profile
ARNs for tighter least privilege, e.g.
`arn:aws:bedrock:*:<account-id>:inference-profile/us.anthropic.claude-opus-5-5*`
and `arn:aws:bedrock:*::foundation-model/anthropic.claude-opus-5-5*`.

## Workflow Example

Copy [`examples/workflows/review-bedrock.yml`][wf] to
`.github/workflows/lgtmaybe.yml`. Store the role ARN in an `AWS_ROLE_ARN`
secret. The Action assumes the role itself, so you need no separate
`configure-aws-credentials` step. But the workflow must grant `id-token: write`
so GitHub will mint the OIDC token:

```yaml
permissions:
  contents: read
  pull-requests: write
  id-token: write # required for the OIDC token exchange (keyless auth)
```

The review step is:

```yaml
- uses: MattJColes/lgtmaybe@v2
  with:
    provider: bedrock
    model: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6
    aws_role_arn: ${{ secrets.AWS_ROLE_ARN }}
    aws_region: us-east-1
```

`aws_region` defaults to `us-east-1`. The example also carries the
trusted-author guard described in
[who can trigger a review](use-as-github-action.md#who-can-trigger-a-review).

## Choosing a Bedrock Model ID

The `model` must be a Bedrock model identifier. Bedrock hosts Anthropic Claude,
Amazon Nova, Meta Llama, Mistral, Cohere, OpenAI GPT and others. Each has
Bedrock's own ID: `openai.gpt-6-sol`, not OpenAI's `gpt-6-sol`. Bedrock rejects
an ID written for another provider's API with
`The provided model identifier is invalid`. Use one of the Claude IDs below:

| Model | Inference-profile ID (recommended) | Base model ID |
|---|---|---|
| Claude Opus 5.5 | `us.anthropic.claude-opus-5-5` | `anthropic.claude-opus-5-5` |
| Claude Sonnet 4.6 | `us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6` | `anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6` |
| Claude Haiku 4.5 | `us.anthropic.claude-haiku-4-5-20251001-v1:0` | `anthropic.claude-haiku-4-5-20251001-v1:0` |

Haiku 4.5 keeps its dated `-20251001-v1:0` suffix on Bedrock. Unlike Opus 5.5
and Sonnet 4.6, it has no undated `anthropic.claude-haiku-4-5` ID.

On Bedrock, Claude Opus 4.7 and later (Opus 5.5 included) take lgtmaybe's
findings schema as a forced tool call rather than native structured output. A
forced tool call makes the model answer by calling one tool whose input is the
schema. There is nothing to configure: litellm picks that route from its model
map.

Prefer the inference-profile form. Most current Claude models on Bedrock can
only be invoked through a cross-region inference profile. They cannot run with
on-demand throughput on the bare model ID. So a bare ID often fails with the
same `invalid model identifier` (or `on-demand throughput isn't supported`)
error.

Prefix the ID with the geography that matches `aws_region`:

- `us.` (US);
- `eu.` (Europe);
- `apac.` (Asia Pacific);
- or the narrower `au.` / `jp.`.

A `global.` prefix lets Bedrock route the call to any commercial region. Use the
bare `anthropic.…` ID only where on-demand access to that model is enabled in
your region.

## Running Locally with Ambient AWS Credentials

If your shell has [ambient](../reference/glossary.md#ambient-credentials) AWS credentials (from
`~/.aws`, SSO, or an assumed role), you can review your current branch with
Bedrock. Bedrock request signing needs `boto3`. So install the `bedrock` extra
(the Action image already bundles it):

```bash
pip install 'lgtmaybe[bedrock]'

lgtmaybe review \
  --provider bedrock \
  --model us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6
```

Bedrock always uses the AWS credential chain. lgtmaybe ignores `--api-key` for
it.

> **`No matching distribution found for lgtmaybe[bedrock]`** (`from versions:
> none`): this is not a packaging problem, because the `bedrock` extra is
> published on PyPI. It means `pip` found no version compatible with your
> environment. The usual cause is a Python older than the required 3.11. Check
> with `python --version`, and install under 3.11 or later (e.g. with `pipx` or
> `uv`). If your Python is fine, `pip` can't reach PyPI. Check your network,
> proxy or `--index-url`.

## Troubleshooting

**`ExpiredTokenException`**: the OIDC exchange failed or the role session
expired. Check that the workflow grants `id-token: write` and that the IAM trust
policy names the correct GitHub repository.

**`AccessDeniedException`**: the role lacks `bedrock:InvokeModel` for the
selected model, or the model is not enabled in the Bedrock console for your
account and region. For an inference-profile ID (`us.`/`eu.`/`apac.`-prefixed),
the policy must allow the `inference-profile/*` ARN as well as
`foundation-model/*`.

**`The provided model identifier is invalid`**: the `model` is not a Bedrock
model ID. It is one of two things:

- Another provider's name, such as `gpt-6-sol` or `claude-sonnet-4-6`.
  Bedrock's are `openai.gpt-6-sol` and `us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6`. Pick an
  ID from the table above.
- A model that needs a cross-region inference profile. Prefix it with
  `us.`/`eu.`/`apac.` (e.g. `us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6`) instead of using
  the bare `anthropic.…` ID.

**`output_config.format: Extra inputs are not permitted`**, **`outputConfig`**,
or a `toolConfig` / "doesn't support tool choice" refusal: the model's Converse
route (Bedrock's chat API) doesn't accept the structured-output shape lgtmaybe
sent. Bedrock rejected the request with a 400.

No action is needed. lgtmaybe re-sends the same schema as a forced tool call
(which Converse does implement). The rest of the [lens](../reference/glossary.md#lens)
[fan-out](../reference/glossary.md#fan-out) uses that shape straight away. Only a route that refuses
the tool call too falls back to prompt-instructed JSON, which the lenient parser
still reads. lgtmaybe logs that fallback as a warning naming the model and the
reason.

If every lens fails at once with `every review call failed` on an older
lgtmaybe, upgrade, or pass `--no-structured-output` (`structured_output: false`)
as a stopgap.

**Structured output stepped down after an odd reply**: an empty reply, or one
that parsed to something other than findings, moves the model one rung down to
the forced tool call and keeps the schema. Only a second such reply gives the
schema up. The provider log says which happened:

- `structured output stepped down to a forced tool call` is the middle rung and
  costs nothing.
- `structured output disabled for this model` is the floor. It carries a
  `reason` worth reading, such as `rejected`, `empty-response`,
  `unparseable-output`, `tool-rejected` or `internal-tool-rejected`.

[wf]: https://github.com/MattJColes/lgtmaybe/blob/main/examples/workflows/review-bedrock.yml

---

<!-- Source: https://lgtmaybe.coles.codes/how-to/review-with-vertex-wif/ -->

# Review with Google Vertex AI (Keyless WIF)

Use this guide to run lgtmaybe with Google Vertex AI using Workload Identity
Federation (WIF), so no service-account JSON or static key is stored in secrets.

## Contents

- [How it works](#how-it-works)
- [One-time GCP setup](#one-time-gcp-setup)
- [Workflow example](#workflow-example)
- [Environment variables](#environment-variables)
- [Available Vertex AI models](#available-vertex-ai-models)
- [Running locally with ADC](#running-locally-with-adc)
- [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting)

## How It Works

GitHub Actions issues an OIDC token. WIF exchanges it for a short-lived GCP
access token that impersonates a service account holding only the Vertex AI
permissions it needs. lgtmaybe picks up those credentials through Application
Default Credentials (ADC).

## One-Time GCP Setup

Do this once in your GCP project:

1. Enable the Vertex AI API on the project.
2. Create a workload identity pool and a GitHub provider in it.
3. Create a service account with `roles/aiplatform.user`, or something narrower.
   That role grants `aiplatform.endpoints.predict`; do not assign broader
   project-level roles.
4. Grant the GitHub principal permission to impersonate that service account,
   scoped to your repository.
5. Note the WIF provider resource name (for `gcp_wif_provider`) and the service
   account email (for `gcp_service_account`).

## Workflow Example

Copy [`examples/workflows/review-vertex.yml`][wf] to
`.github/workflows/lgtmaybe.yml` and store the provider resource name and service
account email in `GCP_WIF_PROVIDER` and `GCP_SERVICE_ACCOUNT` secrets. The Action
authenticates to GCP itself, so you need no separate
`google-github-actions/auth` step, but the workflow must grant `id-token: write`:

```yaml
permissions:
  contents: read
  pull-requests: write
  id-token: write # required for the WIF token exchange (keyless auth)
```

The review step is:

```yaml
- uses: MattJColes/lgtmaybe@v2
  with:
    provider: vertex
    model: gemini-3.8-flash
    gcp_wif_provider: ${{ secrets.GCP_WIF_PROVIDER }}
    gcp_service_account: ${{ secrets.GCP_SERVICE_ACCOUNT }}
```

The example also carries the trusted-author guard described in
[who can trigger a review](use-as-github-action.md#who-can-trigger-a-review).

## Environment Variables

litellm reads the project and region from these variables:

| Variable | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `VERTEXAI_PROJECT` | No | GCP project ID. Defaults to the project your ADC resolves (`GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT`, or your gcloud config). |
| `VERTEXAI_LOCATION` | No | Region (default: `us-central1`) |

In the Action, the authentication step sets the project for you. The Action
forwards only `GOOGLE_*` and `CLOUDSDK_*` variables (plus `AWS_*`, `AZURE_*` and
its own `INPUT_*`) into its container, so `VERTEXAI_*` variables set in your
workflow do not reach lgtmaybe there. The Action therefore always uses
litellm's default region, `us-central1`; to use another region, run the CLI in
a workflow step with `VERTEXAI_LOCATION` set instead.

## Available Vertex AI Models

| Model | Vertex model ID |
|---|---|
| Gemini 3.8 Flash | `gemini-3.8-flash` |
| Gemini 3.5 Flash | `gemini-3.5-flash` |
| Gemini 3.1 Pro (preview) | `gemini-3.1-pro-preview` |
| Gemini 3 Pro (preview) | `gemini-3-pro-preview` |
| Gemini 2.5 Pro | `gemini-2.5-pro` |
| Claude Opus 5.5 | `claude-opus-5-5` |

Use the Gemini 3.x Pro `-preview` IDs as written: litellm's model map has no
bare `gemini-3-pro` or `gemini-3.1-pro` entry, so with those lgtmaybe can't fit
its input budget to the model's window. Claude on Vertex must be enabled in
Model Garden first, and `VERTEXAI_LOCATION` must be a region that serves it.

## Running Locally with ADC

Sign in with `gcloud auth application-default login` so your shell has ADC.
Vertex token minting needs `google-auth`, so install the `vertex` extra (the
Action image already bundles it):

```bash
pip install 'lgtmaybe[vertex]'

export VERTEXAI_PROJECT=my-project
export VERTEXAI_LOCATION=us-central1

lgtmaybe review \
  --provider vertex \
  --model gemini-3.8-flash
```

This reviews your current branch with Vertex. Vertex always uses ambient
credentials; lgtmaybe ignores `--api-key` for it.

## Troubleshooting

**`vertex requires ambient GCP credentials`**: lgtmaybe found no sign of GCP
credentials (`GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS`, a project variable such as
`GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT` or `VERTEXAI_PROJECT`, the ADC file gcloud writes, or
metadata-server credentials, which need the `google-auth` package). Run `gcloud auth application-default login`, set
`GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS`, or (in CI) check the WIF inputs.

**`UNAUTHENTICATED`**: ADC credentials are missing or expired. Run
`gcloud auth application-default login` locally, or check the WIF provider and
the service account impersonation binding in CI.

**`PERMISSION_DENIED`**: the service account lacks `roles/aiplatform.user`, or
the Vertex AI API is not enabled in the project. Enable it with:

```bash
gcloud services enable aiplatform.googleapis.com --project=my-project
```

**`Model not found`**: the model ID may not be available in your selected
region. Check the [Vertex AI Model Garden](https://console.cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/model-garden).

[wf]: https://github.com/MattJColes/lgtmaybe/blob/main/examples/workflows/review-vertex.yml

---

<!-- Source: https://lgtmaybe.coles.codes/how-to/review-with-azure/ -->

# Review with Azure OpenAI (Keyless OIDC)

Use this guide to run lgtmaybe against Azure OpenAI with GitHub's OIDC token
federated to Entra (Azure AD), so no static Azure key is stored in secrets. A
key-based alternative is covered at the end.

## Contents

- [How it works](#how-it-works)
- [One-time Azure setup](#one-time-azure-setup)
- [Workflow example](#workflow-example)
- [Choosing the model name](#choosing-the-model-name)
- [Running locally with ambient Azure credentials](#running-locally-with-ambient-azure-credentials)
- [Key-based alternative](#key-based-alternative)
- [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting)

## How It Works

GitHub Actions issues a short-lived OIDC token. Entra exchanges it for an access
token for your Azure OpenAI resource, through a federated credential on an app
registration or managed identity. Pass `azure_client_id` and `azure_tenant_id`
and the Action sets up that exchange for you; lgtmaybe then picks up the token
through `azure-identity`'s `DefaultAzureCredential`. There is no
`AZURE_API_KEY` in your secrets.

Azure still needs two non-secret values: the deployment name (`model`) and the
resource endpoint (`api_base`, `https://<resource>.openai.azure.com`).

## One-Time Azure Setup

Do this once in your Azure tenant:

1. Register an Entra app (or use a user-assigned managed identity). Note its
   client ID (`azure_client_id`) and your tenant ID (`azure_tenant_id`).
2. Add a federated credential to it for GitHub Actions:
   - Issuer: `https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com`
   - Subject: scoped to your repo, e.g. `repo:<org>/<repo>:pull_request`
     (or `:ref:refs/heads/main`, `:environment:…`)
   - Audience: `api://AzureADTokenExchange`
3. On the Azure OpenAI resource, grant the app the
   **Cognitive Services OpenAI User** role. It is least privilege: it can call
   models but not manage the resource.
4. Deploy the model you want and note the deployment name. That is what you
   pass as `model`, not the upstream OpenAI model ID.
5. Note the resource endpoint (`https://<resource>.openai.azure.com`). It
   becomes `api_base`.

## Workflow Example

Copy [`examples/workflows/review-azure.yml`][wf] to
`.github/workflows/lgtmaybe.yml` and set the `AZURE_CLIENT_ID`,
`AZURE_TENANT_ID` and `AZURE_API_BASE` secrets. The Action performs the OIDC
exchange itself, so you need no separate `azure/login` step, but the workflow
must grant `id-token: write` so GitHub will mint the token:

```yaml
permissions:
  id-token: write          # required for the OIDC token exchange (keyless)
  contents: read
  pull-requests: write
```

The review step is:

```yaml
- uses: MattJColes/lgtmaybe@v2
  with:
    provider: azure
    model: my-gpt-4o-deployment      # your Azure deployment name
    api_base: ${{ secrets.AZURE_API_BASE }}  # https://<resource>.openai.azure.com
    azure_client_id: ${{ secrets.AZURE_CLIENT_ID }}
    azure_tenant_id: ${{ secrets.AZURE_TENANT_ID }}
```

The example also carries the trusted-author guard described in
[who can trigger a review](use-as-github-action.md#who-can-trigger-a-review).

## Choosing the Model Name

For Azure, `model` is the deployment name you chose in the portal, not the
underlying OpenAI model ID. A deployment of `gpt-4o` named `my-gpt-4o-deployment`
is referenced as `model: my-gpt-4o-deployment`, which litellm routes as
`azure/my-gpt-4o-deployment`.

## Running Locally with Ambient Azure Credentials

Keyless works locally too. Install the `azure` extra, sign in (or use a managed
identity), set the endpoint, and review your current branch:

```bash
pip install 'lgtmaybe[azure]'
az login

export AZURE_API_BASE="https://<resource>.openai.azure.com"

lgtmaybe review \
  --provider azure \
  --model my-gpt-4o-deployment
```

`DefaultAzureCredential` finds your `az login` session (or a managed identity,
or `AZURE_*` env vars), and no static key is stored.

## Key-Based Alternative

To use a resource key instead, pass it as `api_key` with the endpoint as
`api_base`. Drop `azure_client_id`, `azure_tenant_id` and the `id-token`
permission. A supplied key always wins over ambient credentials, and the
`azure-identity` package is not needed in this mode.

```yaml
- uses: MattJColes/lgtmaybe@v2
  with:
    provider: azure
    model: my-gpt-4o-deployment
    api_key: ${{ secrets.AZURE_API_KEY }}
    api_base: ${{ secrets.AZURE_API_BASE }}
```

Locally, `export AZURE_API_KEY=… AZURE_API_BASE=…` (or pass `--api-key` and
`--api-base`).

## Troubleshooting

**`azure requires credentials`**: lgtmaybe found neither a key nor an ambient
Entra credential. For keyless, check that `id-token: write` is present and the
federated credential's subject matches the triggering ref or event. For key
mode, set `AZURE_API_KEY` (or the `api_key` input).

**`azure requires the resource endpoint`**: set `api_base` (or `AZURE_API_BASE`)
to `https://<resource>.openai.azure.com`.

**`keyless azure needs the azure-identity package`**: you are running keyless on
the CLI without the extra. Install `lgtmaybe[azure]`. The Action image already
bundles it.

**`AADSTS70021` / no matching federated identity**: the federated credential's
issuer, subject or audience don't match this workflow. The audience must be
`api://AzureADTokenExchange` and the subject must match the repo and event.

**`DeploymentNotFound` / 404**: `model` must be the deployment name on the
resource that `api_base` points at, not the upstream OpenAI model ID.

**`Unsupported API version`**: pin one by setting `AZURE_API_VERSION` (e.g.
`2024-08-01-preview`) in the environment. Otherwise litellm uses its default.

[wf]: https://github.com/MattJColes/lgtmaybe/blob/main/examples/workflows/review-azure.yml
