<!-- Source: https://lgtmaybe.coles.codes/how-to/run-locally-with-ollama/ -->

# Run Locally with ollama

Use this guide to review your local changes with a local ollama model. There is
no API cost, no egress (no data goes to a hosted provider) and no key. The CLI reviews
your `git` diff and prints the findings. To post reviews on pull requests, use
the [GitHub Action](use-as-github-action.md).

> **ollama is the easiest local start.** Are you running a different local
> server (vLLM, llama.cpp or LM Studio), or a hosted OpenAI-compatible API like
> DeepSeek? Use the `openai-compatible` provider instead:
> [Other OpenAI-compatible servers](use-a-custom-openai-compatible-endpoint.md).
> The [model-choice and hardware guidance below](#which-model-and-will-it-fit)
> applies to any local runtime.

## Contents

- [Prerequisites](#prerequisites)
- [Pull the model you want](#pull-the-model-you-want)
- [Which model, and will it fit?](#which-model-and-will-it-fit)
- [Run the review](#run-the-review)
- [Reviewing large files (recursive walk)](#reviewing-large-files-recursive-walk)
- [Use a remote ollama instance](#use-a-remote-ollama-instance)
- [Inside the GitHub Action's container](#inside-the-github-actions-container)
- [Get findings as JSON](#get-findings-as-json)
- [Let an AI agent apply the fixes](#let-an-ai-agent-apply-the-fixes)
- [Concurrency on a local server](#concurrency-on-a-local-server)
- [The output ceiling (why a review can't run forever)](#the-output-ceiling-why-a-review-cant-run-forever)
- [Slow models and timeouts](#slow-models-and-timeouts)
- [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting)

## Prerequisites

- lgtmaybe installed (`pip install lgtmaybe`)
- [ollama](https://ollama.com) installed and running
- A local git repository with changes to review

## Pull the Model You Want

```bash
ollama pull qwen3.6:27b        # strong all-round coding model
ollama pull gemma4:e4b         # smaller, for devices with limited RAM
```

List the models you have:

```bash
ollama list
```

## Which Model, and Will It Fit?

Two rules:

1. **Pick a coding model.** Reviewing a PR is a coding task. Use a model built
   for code (e.g. the Qwen3 coder line), not a general chat model.
2. **Bigger and newer is more accurate.** Use the largest, most recent coding
   model your hardware can run. Our accuracy numbers are for a small model. We
   benchmarked `qwen3.5:4b`, and it did well, but only with recursive review on
   (88% vs 61% recall). A larger, newer model catches more and relies on that
   less.

A solid mid-2026 default is Qwen3.6-27B (`qwen3.6:27b`). On coding benchmarks it
is close to frontier API models (SWE-bench Verified ~77%). Yet it is small
enough for a workstation or a well-specced laptop. So it clears lgtmaybe's bar
across all the review [lenses](../reference/glossary.md#lens) without a
data-centre GPU.

Smaller models work too, but accuracy falls off. You will miss subtler
findings. You may also need `--no-reflect`, because the
[reflection](../reference/glossary.md#reflection) pass over-prunes on a weak
model.

**Hardware, quantised (the usual way to run it locally):**

| You have | What to expect |
|---|---|
| **< 32 GB** RAM/VRAM | Drop to a smaller model (`gemma4:e4b`) or use a hosted provider. 27B at a usable quant won't leave room for the diff. |
| **32 GB** RAM/VRAM | The practical floor. Run `qwen3.6:27b` at a 4-bit quant (≈16-18 GB of weights) with a modest context window. Keep `num_ctx` conservative so the model plus the diff and findings fit. |
| **48 GB+** RAM/VRAM (preferred) | Comfortable. Room for the weights plus the default `--num-ctx` (32k), or a raised 64k window for very large diffs, with headroom for the KV cache. |

This applies to discrete VRAM and Apple Silicon unified memory alike. A bigger
context window costs memory on top of the weights. So if you raise `--num-ctx`
for a large diff (see [Slow models and timeouts](#slow-models-and-timeouts)),
size it to the table above. On a hosted provider none of this matters: the model
runs on the provider's hardware.

## Run the Review

From inside the repository, on the branch you want reviewed:

```bash
lgtmaybe review \
  --provider ollama \
  --model qwen3.6:27b \
  --api-base http://localhost:11434
```

`http://localhost:11434` is the default, so `--api-base` is optional here.

This diffs your current branch against the remote primary branch and prints the
findings. To change what it reviews:

- `--working` reviews the whole worktree (branch commits plus uncommitted edits)
  against that same base.
- `--uncommitted` reviews only your uncommitted edits against HEAD.
- `--base <ref>` diffs against a different base.

## Reviewing Large Files (Recursive Walk)

Sometimes a single file's diff is larger than the per-call token budget
(`--max-input-tokens`). Then lgtmaybe walks it
[hunk](../reference/glossary.md#hunk) by hunk, reviewing each hunk in its own
focused call. Without this, it would send the whole file and the tail would drop
out of the model's attention. The findings are merged, and inline-comment
positions still bind to the real diff.

This recursive (RLM-style) review is on by default (`recursive: true`). Files
that fit the budget are still reviewed whole, so nothing changes for small
diffs.

It helps small local models most, because a smaller prompt is easier to review
thoroughly. In our A/B benchmark a local `qwen3.5:4b` caught all 6 planted bugs
reviewing recursively, versus 4 of 6 reviewing each file whole. The two it
missed were both in the file's tail, even though the diff fit the context
window. So the gain is focus, not only avoiding truncation.

It is a single non-deterministic run on one fixture, so treat it as
directional. The harness is described in
[DEVELOPMENT.md](https://github.com/MattJColes/lgtmaybe/blob/main/DEVELOPMENT.md#benchmarking-the-recursive-rlm-walk).

To review each file whole instead, pass `--no-recursive`. That makes one call
per file, which keeps all of a file's hunks in view together. It tends to miss
more on big files with small models.

```bash
lgtmaybe review --provider ollama --model qwen3.5:4b \
  --api-base http://localhost:11434 --no-recursive
```

```yaml
# or in .lgtmaybe.yml (also how the GitHub Action picks it up):
recursive: false
```

## Use a Remote ollama Instance

If ollama runs on another machine (e.g. a Tailscale peer):

```bash
lgtmaybe review \
  --provider ollama \
  --model qwen3.6:27b \
  --api-base http://100.x.x.x:11434
```

lgtmaybe adds no authentication, and ollama has none built in. Restrict network
access at the host or firewall.

## Inside the GitHub Action's Container

The Action runs lgtmaybe in a container. So it reaches an ollama server on the
runner host at `host.docker.internal`, not `localhost`. Set it with the Action's
`provider`, `model` and `api_base` inputs, or in `.lgtmaybe.yml`:

```yaml
provider: ollama
model: qwen3.6:27b
api_base: http://host.docker.internal:11434
```

## Get Findings as JSON

The CLI prints a readable listing by default and never posts anywhere. Add
`--json` for a machine-readable array you can pipe into other tools:

```bash
lgtmaybe review \
  --provider ollama \
  --model qwen3.6:27b \
  --api-base http://localhost:11434 \
  --json
```

## Let an AI Agent Apply the Fixes

`--format agent` prints the findings as correction instructions. An AI coding
agent (such as Claude Code) can read and apply them. So you can review and fix a
branch locally before opening a PR. See
[Fix findings with an AI agent](fix-findings-with-an-ai-agent.md).

## Concurrency on a Local Server

lgtmaybe [fans out](../reference/glossary.md#fan-out) its review calls across a
pool sized by `max_concurrency`. It is 6 by default on every provider, local
included. That is a ceiling on what lgtmaybe will have in flight. It is not a
promise that your server runs them at once:

- **A default ollama runs one request at a time.** `OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL` is `1`
  unless you set it, so five of six calls queue (up to `OLLAMA_MAX_QUEUE`, 512).
  Nothing is lost and nothing fails. The wall clock is your server's throughput
  either way. Raising `max_concurrency` alone changes nothing.
- **The setting that matters is on the server.** Start ollama with
  `OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL=4` and four calls really do run together.
- **It costs memory in proportion.** ollama allocates the context window per
  parallel slot: four slots at `num_ctx` 32768 need 128k of context, not 32k.
  This is the usual reason a machine that reviewed happily with one slot falls
  over with four.

So the two settings should match. If you have raised the server, tell lgtmaybe:

```bash
lgtmaybe review --max-concurrency 4
```

**How to tell which you got.** `--profile` answers it. Compare the per-call
`elapsed` column with the `review` stage total:

- If the calls' elapsed times sum to roughly the stage time, they ran one after
  another.
- If they sum to well over it, they overlapped.

```
review             95.32s        <- stage total
correctness         52.02s   |
spec                45.64s   |   sum is ~3x the stage,
artefacts           43.67s   |   so these overlapped
security            43.30s   |
```

**Queue time is already covered.** A queued call's timeout clock starts when the
request is sent, not when your server gets to it. So on a single-slot server,
the last call in a six-wide fan-out would otherwise have to finish within the
same budget as the first. lgtmaybe scales the local default timeout by the
fan-out width to cover that (see [below](#slow-models-and-timeouts)). You should
not need to intervene. If you would rather the calls didn't queue at all:

```yaml
# .lgtmaybe.yml
max_concurrency: 1
```

## The Output Ceiling (Why a Review Can't Run Forever)

A local model under structured output sometimes fails to stop and keeps
decoding. With no ceiling, only the per-call timeout ends it. That can mean half
an hour of sustained GPU for a single lens on a one-file diff, and hours for a
whole review.

So a review runs with a default output ceiling of 16384 tokens per call, half
the default 32768 `num_ctx`. Measured findings payloads are hundreds of tokens.
The rest is headroom for a thinking model, which draws its reasoning from the
same budget.

The same ceiling applies to `openai-compatible` and `openrouter`, because the
failure is not specific to local models. Benchmarking found:

- a model behind `openai-compatible` emitting 223,558 tokens on a single lens
  call;
- a hosted model on `openrouter` returning a 393k-token response that parsed
  into 699 false positives on a diff with nothing wrong in it.

The first-party APIs (openai, anthropic, zai, bedrock, vertex, azure) get no
default ceiling. They have not shown this failure, and a cap could truncate long
findings payloads.

The ceiling is a fixed number, not a fraction of your window. Raising `num_ctx`
for a big diff adds room for the prompt, not for a longer answer. Use
`max_tokens` when you want a longer answer.

Every run logs the ceiling it resolved and where it came from:

```
per-call budget resolved  timeout_s=3600  max_tokens=16384  max_tokens_source="provider default"
```

If a lens hits it, you get a truncation notice, not a silent clean review:

```
response hit the 16384-token `max_tokens` ceiling before finishing. The batch
is re-reviewed in smaller pieces automatically, so a lens that keeps doing it is
usually generation instability in the model, which a higher ceiling makes more
expensive rather than prevents
```

**One truncation is not a reason to raise the cap.** The batch is re-reviewed in
smaller pieces on its own, so a lens that trips it occasionally has still been
reviewed. A model that runs away repeatedly is generating past the ceiling, not
being cut short by it. A bigger ceiling only makes a longer wasted call.
Changing the model is what fixes it.

Raising it is right when a genuinely long answer is being cut off: a large diff
with many real findings, where most are salvaged each time. Then raise it. Or
remove the cap with `0`, which leaves the timeout as the run's only stop:

```bash
lgtmaybe review --provider ollama --model qwen3.5:4b --max-tokens 32768
lgtmaybe review --provider ollama --model qwen3.5:4b --max-tokens 0  # uncapped
```

```yaml
# or in .lgtmaybe.yml (also how the GitHub Action picks it up):
max_tokens: 32768
```

Lowering the ceiling is the quickest way to get a result out of a slow model.
`--max-tokens 512` turns a stuck review into one that finishes in minutes and
reports what it truncated.

## Slow Models and Timeouts

Local models are slow, especially large ones on CPU. So ollama gets a long
default per-call timeout of 1800 seconds. You don't need to set anything for a
normal run. (Direct cloud providers default to 600 seconds.)

**That default scales with the fan-out.** Because the calls queue, the budget
has to cover the wait as well as the work:

- At the default width of six, the per-call timeout is `1800 × 6`.
- That is bounded by `max_review_seconds` (3600 seconds by default). `0`
  disables the deadline and with it the bound.
- It is never trimmed below ollama's own 1800 seconds. A deadline set lower than
  that does not shrink it.
- The bound applies to the budget, not the wall clock. The deadline decides when
  a call may start, so a call that begins just inside it still runs its full
  budget.
- At `max_concurrency: 1` there is no queue, and the budget is the plain 1800
  seconds.

Every run logs the number it resolved, and why:

```
per-call budget resolved  timeout_s=3600  timeout_source="provider default"  concurrency=6
```

An explicit `timeout` is never scaled: `timeout: 600` means 600 at any width.

If a big model still times out, you'll see
`litellm.Timeout: Connection timed out after 3600.0 seconds`. Raise the timeout
explicitly:

```bash
# CLI flag (seconds):
lgtmaybe review --provider ollama --model qwen3.6:35b \
  --api-base http://localhost:11434 --timeout 3600
```

```yaml
# or in .lgtmaybe.yml (also how the GitHub Action picks it up):
provider: ollama
model: qwen3.6:35b
timeout: 1800
```

The review makes five lens calls under the default `fast`
[preset](../reference/glossary.md#preset) (one per category under
`--preset full`). On a default ollama those queue rather than overlap. So a slow
model takes roughly `lens calls × per-call time`. That is why `fast` is the
default: five calls instead of one per category is the biggest single local
speed-up.

To go faster:

- Narrow the lenses with `categories:` in `.lgtmaybe.yml` (e.g. just `security`
  and `correctness`).
- Use a smaller model.
- Give ollama more GPU.
- If you have the VRAM to serve requests in parallel, raise
  `OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL` on the ollama server as described
  [above](#concurrency-on-a-local-server). The same five calls then overlap
  instead of queueing. That is close to a 5× wall-clock win with
  `OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL=5`.

Add `--profile` to any run to see the per-call breakdown.

## Troubleshooting

**`Connection refused` on port 11434**: make sure `ollama serve` is running and
the `--api-base` URL is reachable.

**Model not found**: run `ollama pull <model>` before using it.

**`review incomplete: every review call failed`**: every lens call timed out or
returned output that wasn't valid JSON. To fix it:

- raise `--timeout`;
- try a model that follows instructions more reliably;
- or check the `LITELLM_LOG=DEBUG` output for the underlying error.

lgtmaybe reports this and exits non-zero rather than pretending the PR is clean.

For a large diff this can mean the prompt plus the findings don't fit in
ollama's context window, so the output is truncated. lgtmaybe runs ollama with a
32768-token context (`num_ctx`) and structured JSON output, which covers most
reviews.

lgtmaybe does not send ollama's `think` flag. ollama already turns thinking on
for a model that supports it and rejects the flag for one that does not. So
sending nothing is right for both.

For a big multi-file change, raise the context window with `--num-ctx` so the
whole diff and the findings fit. This is ollama-only. Hosted providers manage
their context window server-side and ignore it:

```bash
# A large multi-file diff on a local model: more time and more context
# (32768 is already the default; go above it for very large diffs):
lgtmaybe review --provider ollama --model qwen3.6:35b \
  --api-base http://localhost:11434 --timeout 1800 --num-ctx 65536
```

```yaml
# or in .lgtmaybe.yml (also how the GitHub Action picks it up):
provider: ollama
model: qwen3.6:35b
timeout: 1800
num_ctx: 65536
```

`--num-ctx` needs enough RAM/VRAM on the ollama host, so size it to your
machine.

`--max-input-tokens` is the budget that decides when lgtmaybe splits a diff into
separate model calls. It applies to any provider. Its default (100000) is
lowered automatically to fit the model's window. On ollama that is `num_ctx`
minus the output ceiling, so 16384 tokens at the defaults. Set it explicitly to
send a large diff in fewer calls, or lower it for a small-context model.

If a very large diff still truncates, you can:

- narrow it with `include_paths` / `exclude_paths` in `.lgtmaybe.yml`;
- set a lower `max_files` in `.lgtmaybe.yml`;
- or run a model with a bigger context window.

> **If you set `--max-input-tokens` yourself, keep it under `--num-ctx`.** The
> two are independent. `--max-input-tokens` caps each batch lgtmaybe sends,
> while `--num-ctx` is the window ollama allocates. An explicit value is used as
> given, not fitted. lgtmaybe also estimates tokens with a generic tokeniser,
> and local models tokenise differently. So leave headroom: use a batch budget
> well below the window (e.g. `--max-input-tokens 16000` with
> `--num-ctx 32768`). That avoids ollama silently truncating the findings JSON,
> which otherwise shows up only as an unhelpful "review failed".

**Review is empty or truncated**: the diff may exceed the model's context
window. Add a path filter in `.lgtmaybe.yml` to shrink the diff, or lower
`max_files`.

<!-- Source: https://lgtmaybe.coles.codes/how-to/use-a-custom-openai-compatible-endpoint/ -->

# Local Models and Other OpenAI-Compatible Providers

Many model servers speak the OpenAI `/v1` wire format (the request and reply
shape of OpenAI's API). They include local and self-hosted runtimes like
[vLLM][vllm], [llama.cpp][llamacpp] and [LM Studio][lmstudio]. They also include
hosted APIs like [DeepSeek][deepseek] and many proxies. The `openai-compatible`
provider points lgtmaybe at any of them. You supply the base URL and, if the
server wants one, a key.

Use this provider when the model you want is not in the built-in provider list.

> Some endpoints that could run through here have a first-class provider
> instead, which needs less setup: [z.ai / GLM](review-with-zai.md) (`zai`) and
> [ollama](run-locally-with-ollama.md) (`ollama`).

## Contents

- [Local models at a glance](#local-models-at-a-glance)
- [How it works](#how-it-works)
- [DeepSeek (hosted, keyed)](#deepseek-hosted-keyed)
- [llama.cpp (local, keyless)](#llamacpp-local-keyless)
- [LM Studio (local, keyless)](#lm-studio-local-keyless)
- [vLLM (local or self-hosted, keyless)](#vllm-local-or-self-hosted-keyless)
- [Concurrency: what each server can actually take](#concurrency-what-each-server-can-actually-take)
- [Persist it in `.lgtmaybe.yml`](#persist-it-in-lgtmaybeyml)
- [Gateways that don't support JSON mode (`response_format`)](#gateways-that-dont-support-json-mode-response_format)

## Local Models at a Glance

Run a model on your own hardware, with no cost, no key, and nothing leaving the
machine:

| Runtime | Provider | Key needed? | See |
|---|---|---|---|
| [ollama][ollama] | `ollama` (native) | No | [Run locally with ollama](run-locally-with-ollama.md) |
| [vLLM][vllm] | `openai-compatible` | No | [below](#vllm-local-or-self-hosted-keyless) |
| [llama.cpp][llamacpp] | `openai-compatible` | No | [below](#llamacpp-local-keyless) |
| [LM Studio][lmstudio] | `openai-compatible` | No | [below](#lm-studio-local-keyless) |

ollama has its own `--provider ollama` and [its own guide](run-locally-with-ollama.md).
vLLM, llama.cpp and LM Studio are reached through `openai-compatible` and their
local server's `--api-base`, as shown below.

**Which model, and will it fit?** The ollama guide's model-choice and hardware
advice applies to any local runtime: pick a coding model, prefer bigger and
newer, and size it to your RAM/VRAM. See
[Which model, and will it fit?](run-locally-with-ollama.md#which-model-and-will-it-fit).

## How It Works

`--provider openai-compatible` routes through litellm's OpenAI client. It sends
requests to the `--api-base` you give instead of `api.openai.com`. The base URL
is required (`--api-base` or `OPENAI_COMPATIBLE_API_BASE`). The API key is
optional:

- **Hosted endpoints** (DeepSeek, a paid proxy) need a key. Pass `--api-key` or
  set `OPENAI_COMPATIBLE_API_KEY`.
- **Local servers** (llama.cpp, LM Studio, vLLM) usually need none. lgtmaybe
  then sends a harmless placeholder key, because the OpenAI client rejects an
  empty one.

A key you supply is read from the environment or `--api-key` and is never
persisted to config.

The endpoint might be a slow local model. So `openai-compatible` gets the same
defaults as ollama:

- the same generous 1800-second per-call timeout (scaled for queueing, see
  [Concurrency](#concurrency-what-each-server-can-actually-take));
- the same default output ceiling of 16384 tokens per call.

For a fast hosted endpoint like DeepSeek, you can lower the timeout with
`--timeout` (or `timeout:` in config).

## DeepSeek (Hosted, Keyed)

```bash
export OPENAI_COMPATIBLE_API_KEY=sk-...        # your DeepSeek key

lgtmaybe review \
  --provider openai-compatible \
  --model deepseek-chat \
  --api-base https://api.deepseek.com/v1
```

You can pass the key with `--api-key sk-...` instead of the env var.

## llama.cpp (Local, Keyless)

Start the server:

```bash
llama-server -m ./model.gguf --port 8000        # serves the OpenAI API at /v1
```

Then review against it, with no key:

```bash
lgtmaybe review \
  --provider openai-compatible \
  --model local-model \
  --api-base http://localhost:8000/v1
```

## LM Studio (Local, Keyless)

Enable the local server in LM Studio (it serves the OpenAI API on port `1234` by
default), then:

```bash
lgtmaybe review \
  --provider openai-compatible \
  --model your-loaded-model \
  --api-base http://localhost:1234/v1
```

## vLLM (Local or Self-Hosted, Keyless)

```bash
vllm serve meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct --port 8000
```

```bash
lgtmaybe review \
  --provider openai-compatible \
  --model meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct \
  --api-base http://localhost:8000/v1
```

## Concurrency: What Each Server Can Actually Take

lgtmaybe [fans out](../reference/glossary.md#fan-out) its calls across a pool
sized by `max_concurrency`, 6 by default on every provider. That is a ceiling on
what it will have in flight. Whether your server runs the calls together is up
to the server, and the three above differ sharply:

| Server | Concurrent by default? | Raising it |
|---|---|---|
| **vLLM** | Yes, continuous batching | Close to free; each request keeps the full `--max-model-len` |
| **llama.cpp** | No, one slot | `-np N` adds slots, but **splits one KV cache between them** |
| **LM Studio** | No, single slot | Not exposed; set `max_concurrency` to 1 |

The llama.cpp trap fails as a quality problem rather than an error. `-np`
divides the context you asked for: `-c 32768 -np 4` leaves each slot 8k. A
lgtmaybe review prompt is comfortably larger than that. So the diff is silently
truncated, and the model reviews something it was never fully shown. Size `-c`
as `slots × per-slot context`:

```bash
llama-server -m ./model.gguf --port 8000 -np 4 -c 131072   # 4 slots × 32k each
```

vLLM allocates KV blocks (its per-request memory for the context) dynamically
rather than up front. So concurrent requests each keep the full
`--max-model-len`. That makes it the local server to choose when review latency
matters:

```bash
vllm serve <model> --port 8000 --max-model-len 32768
lgtmaybe review --provider openai-compatible --model <model> \
  --api-base http://localhost:8000/v1 --max-concurrency 6
```

**Queueing does not cost you a timeout.** A queued request's clock starts when it
is sent, not when a slot frees. So lgtmaybe scales the `openai-compatible`
default timeout (1800 seconds) by the fan-out width:

- At the default width, it is `1800 × 6`.
- That is bounded by `max_review_seconds` (3600 seconds). `0` disables the
  deadline and the bound with it.
- It is never trimmed below the 1800-second provider default. A deadline set
  lower than that does not shrink it.
- The bound applies to the budget, not the wall clock. The deadline gates when a
  call may start, and does not cut a running call short.
- An explicit `timeout` is used exactly as written, at any width.

Each run logs the number it resolved and the width it assumed:

```
per-call budget resolved  timeout_s=3600  timeout_source="provider default"  concurrency=6
```

For a single-slot server, you can say so and have lgtmaybe queue nothing:

```yaml
# .lgtmaybe.yml
max_concurrency: 1
```

## Persist It in `.lgtmaybe.yml`

The provider, model and base URL are not secrets, so they can live in config.
The key stays in the environment.

```yaml
provider: openai-compatible
model: deepseek-chat
api_base: https://api.deepseek.com/v1
```

With that file in place, `lgtmaybe review` needs no flags.

In the GitHub Action, set the same values as inputs (or in `.lgtmaybe.yml`). For
hosted endpoints, pass `api_key` from a secret. See
[`examples/workflows/review-openai-compatible.yml`][wf]. Leave `api_key` empty
for a keyless server on the runner host. The Action's container reaches it at
`http://host.docker.internal:<port>/v1`.

## Gateways That Don't Support JSON Mode (`response_format`)

lgtmaybe wants models to return clean findings instead of prose. So it asks
for structured output through the OpenAI `response_format` parameter (JSON
mode). Most endpoints honour it. Some enterprise gateways and custom proxies
don't. They do one of two things:

- ignore it, so the model answers with the JSON in a ```` ```json ```` fence or
  surrounded by prose;
- or reject the request with a `400 Bad Request`.

lgtmaybe handles the first case for you. The parser strips fences and pulls
the JSON out of surrounding prose. So a gateway that ignores `response_format`
still produces a normal review.

A third case is common with LM Studio serving a "thinking" model (e.g.
qwen3.x): the server accepts `response_format`, but the schema-constrained
decoder returns empty content. lgtmaybe handles this too:

1. It retries an empty reply once, with the schema sent as a forced tool call
   instead.
2. If the model answers empty under that as well, lgtmaybe stops sending a
   schema to that model. The parser reads the findings from plain text.

No flag needed.

When a gateway rejects `response_format` with a `400`, lgtmaybe recognises
some refusals that name the parameter. It then steps down by itself. If yours
still fails, turn structured output off so the request never carries the
parameter. The prompt still asks for JSON and the lenient parser still does its
job:

```bash
lgtmaybe review \
  --provider openai-compatible \
  --model gemini-3.5-flash \
  --api-base https://api.myllm.com/v1 \
  --no-structured-output
```

Persist it as `structured_output: false` in `.lgtmaybe.yml`, or set the
Action's `structured_output` input to `false`.

[deepseek]: https://api-docs.deepseek.com/
[llamacpp]: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp
[lmstudio]: https://lmstudio.ai/
[vllm]: https://docs.vllm.ai/
[ollama]: https://ollama.com/
[wf]: https://github.com/MattJColes/lgtmaybe/blob/main/examples/workflows/review-openai-compatible.yml

# Configure .lgtmaybe.yml

Put a `.lgtmaybe.yml` file at the root of your repository to set how lgtmaybe
reviews it. lgtmaybe reads the file from the directory it runs in. For both the
CLI and the GitHub Action, that is the repo root. To read a different file, pass
`--config PATH` (or the Action's `config_path` input). An explicit path must
exist.

The file holds non-secret settings only. API keys stay in the environment or
your CI secrets.

  - [static_analysis](#static_analysis)
  - [triage_model](#triage_model)
