## Full Example

```yaml
provider: openai
model: gpt-5.5
min_severity: low
include_paths:
  - "src/**"
  - "lib/**"
exclude_paths:
  - "**/__pycache__/**"
  - "**/*.min.js"
max_files: 30
max_input_tokens: 80000
categories:
  - security
  - correctness
  - tests
```

## Field Reference

This page covers the fields most teams set. [Reference: Config](../reference/config.md)
lists every field with its type and default, including the tuning knobs not
described here (`max_tokens`, `reasoning_effort`, `temperature`, `language`,
`fail_on`, `max_review_seconds`, `max_review_tokens` and others).

### provider

Which LLM backend, or [provider](../reference/glossary.md#provider), to use. One of `openai`, `openrouter`, `anthropic`, `zai`,
`bedrock`, `vertex`, `azure`, `ollama`, `openai-compatible`.

```yaml
provider: anthropic
```

There is no built-in provider or model. lgtmaybe looks for both in its flags,
`.lgtmaybe.yml` and the user config (written by `lgtmaybe config init`). If
those leave either one unset, lgtmaybe stops before doing any work and tells you
how to configure it. In the GitHub Action, set the `provider` and `model` inputs
instead.

### model

The model identifier for the chosen provider. The format varies by provider:

| Provider | Example model IDs |
|---|---|
| openai | `gpt-5.5` |
| anthropic | `claude-sonnet-4-6`, `claude-haiku-4-5` |
| openrouter | `anthropic/claude-sonnet-4.6` |
| zai | `glm-4.6`, `glm-4.7`, `glm-4.5-air` (GLM / Zhipu AI; newer `glm-5.x` IDs pass through too) |
| bedrock | `us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6`, `us.anthropic.claude-haiku-4-5-20251001-v1:0` (prefer the cross-region inference profile; another provider's name like `gpt-6-sol` is invalid, Bedrock's is `openai.gpt-6-sol` - see [Review with Bedrock](review-with-bedrock-oidc.md)) |
| vertex | `gemini-3.8-flash`, `gemini-3.1-pro-preview` |
| azure | your deployment name, e.g. `my-gpt-4o-deployment`, not the upstream model ID - see [Review with Azure](review-with-azure.md) |
| ollama | `qwen3.6:27b`, `gemma4:e4b` |
| openai-compatible | the served model name, e.g. `deepseek-chat` or `meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct` (also set `api_base` - see [Use a custom OpenAI-compatible endpoint](use-a-custom-openai-compatible-endpoint.md)) |

Write the bare ID. lgtmaybe adds the provider's litellm prefix itself, so
`bedrock/us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6` would end up double-prefixed.

### fallback_model

A second model for a review call the primary model cannot finish. It is off by
default and adds no calls to a healthy review.

Both models go through the same `provider`, `api_base` and credentials. An
OpenRouter review can fall back from a Google model to a Qwen model, because
OpenRouter serves both. An `openai` review cannot fall back to an Anthropic
account. Cross-provider failover needs a separate review run.

```yaml
provider: openrouter
model: google/gemini-3.8-flash
fallback_model: qwen/qwen3.8-max
```

When the fallback runs depends on the failure:

| Primary model result | What lgtmaybe does |
|---|---|
| Transient provider failure, such as a connection error, capacity rate limit, or 5xx | Exhausts the primary model's bounded retries, then tries the fallback. |
| Permanent provider failure, such as an unknown model, rejected request, or exhausted quota | Skips further primary attempts and tries the fallback. A shared credential, quota or endpoint failure usually rejects both. |
| Output hits the `max_tokens` ceiling, or the reply stops mid-JSON | First retries on the primary with a smaller payload or lower `reasoning_effort`, as the token counts suggest. Tries the fallback only if that also fails. |

The fallback does not judge the primary's answer. A clean review, a weak
[finding](../reference/glossary.md#finding) or zero findings never trigger it. Unparseable output has its own
bounded repair path.

The fallback gets a fresh request and retry budget. Its time and tokens add to
what the primary already spent, and its usage counts towards
`max_review_tokens` once the call returns. The review summary names every
[lens](../reference/glossary.md#lens) the fallback answered. `--profile` prints a `models:` line, and
`--profile-json` records the model on each call (see
[Profile Reference](../reference/profile.md#the-models-line)).

If the fallback also fails, lgtmaybe marks the lens incomplete. It does not
walk a list of models or go back to the primary. A review with no usable results
fails rather than posting a clean result. If a lens keeps needing the
second model, make that model the primary.

The `--fallback-model` flag and the Action's `fallback_model` input override
the file:

```bash
lgtmaybe review --fallback-model qwen/qwen3.8-max
```

See [Choose a Review Model](choose-a-review-model.md) for current model results.

### min_severity

The lowest [severity](../reference/glossary.md#severity) to report. lgtmaybe drops findings below
it. From low to high:
`info`, `low`, `medium`, `high`, `critical`.

```yaml
min_severity: medium   # drops info and low findings
```

Default: `low`, which drops only `info` findings. A `project.stage` of
`prototype` raises the default to `medium` (see [project](#project)).

### include_paths / exclude_paths

Glob patterns that limit which changed files lgtmaybe reviews. `include_paths`
is an allowlist. `exclude_paths` is a denylist applied after it, so an exclude
always wins. Both default to empty, which reviews every file.

Patterns match the full repo-relative path. A `**/` prefix also matches at the
repo root, so `**/*.lock` covers a root-level lockfile. The built-in skip
filter for generated, vendored and binary files runs first, so an
`include_paths` entry can't bring back a lockfile.

```yaml
include_paths:
  - "src/**"
exclude_paths:
  - "src/generated/**"
  - "**/*.lock"
```

### max_files

The maximum number of changed files to review. lgtmaybe skips files past the
cap, and the summary says `Reviewed the top N of M changed files`. With
[`triage_model`](#triage_model) set, the cap drops the lowest-risk files.
Otherwise files keep their diff order.

```yaml
max_files: 30
```

Default: `50`. A separate per-file cap, `max_file_diff_lines` (default `2000`,
`0` disables), skips any single file whose diff is longer than that. The
summary names the skipped file. This catches generated data files that the
name-based skip filter can't recognise.

### max_input_tokens

The token budget for each model call. When the diff exceeds it, lgtmaybe splits
the review across [batched](../reference/glossary.md#batch) calls. With `recursive` on (the
default), lgtmaybe walks a single file larger than the budget
[hunk](../reference/glossary.md#hunk) by hunk, instead of cutting it short.

```yaml
max_input_tokens: 80000
```

Default: `100000`. If you leave it unset, lgtmaybe lowers it to fit a model
with a smaller context window. A value you set is used as is.

### preset

How many model calls the review spends. A [preset](../reference/glossary.md#preset) groups the
review's lenses into calls. `fast` (the default) covers the ten everyday
categories in five calls, one per concern:

| Call | Covers |
|---|---|
| security | security |
| correctness | correctness, plus stated intent when the PR states one |
| code health | performance, complexity, ponytail, deprecation |
| artefacts | tests, documentation |
| architecture | architecture |

The same five run on every provider. Worker count only changes whether they
overlap. A sixth `spec` call runs when the repository commits a specification
that matches the PR (see [categories](#categories)).

`full` runs one focused call per category, for release branches and deep
audits.

```yaml
preset: full
```

Default: `fast`. CLI: `--preset fast|full` (`--full` is shorthand); Action
input: `preset`. An explicit `categories` list overrides the grouping.

### categories

Which review lenses to run. Narrowing the list turns off the preset grouping.
Each listed category runs as its own concurrent call, and lgtmaybe merges the
findings. Fewer categories means fewer calls and fewer tokens, at the cost of
coverage.

Choose from `security`, `correctness`, `deprecation`, `tests`, `documentation`,
`performance`, `complexity`, `intent`, `ponytail`, `architecture` and `spec`.

```yaml
categories:
  - security
  - correctness
```

Default: all eleven. Two of them only run when there is something to check:

- `intent` checks the diff against the PR's stated intent: title, description
  and commit names on GitHub, or your `git log` commit names on the CLI. With
  no stated intent (for example, no commits beyond the base branch yet) it is
  skipped and costs nothing. Under `fast` it shares the correctness call.
- [`spec`](../reference/glossary.md#spec-lens) checks the diff against a committed specification
  (OpenSpec, GitHub Spec Kit or Kiro). With no matching spec it is skipped. Turn it off with
  `spec_review: false`, `--no-spec`, or the Action input `spec_review`.

The PR title, description and commit names reach the provider only through the
`intent` lens and the [change overview](../reference/glossary.md#change-overview) (`auto_diagram`). To keep that text from
being sent at all, drop `intent` from `categories` and set `auto_diagram: false`.

[`ponytail`](../reference/glossary.md#ponytail) is the "lazy senior dev" check: *the best code is the code you never
wrote*. It flags code that needn't exist (YAGNI, reinventing the standard
library, code that could be far shorter). See
[What gets reviewed](../explanation/what-gets-reviewed.md#ponytail-the-laziest-senior-dev-in-the-room).

`architecture` flags design decisions in the change that will be expensive to
reverse:

- coupling across boundaries
- dependencies pointing the wrong way
- subclasses that break their base class's contract
- misuse-prone APIs

Each finding has to open with the change it would make painful. See
[What gets reviewed](../explanation/what-gets-reviewed.md#architecture-what-will-this-make-hard-to-change).

### context_lines

The most unchanged lines lgtmaybe adds around each changed hunk, so the model
sees a change in the context of its surrounding code. lgtmaybe reads these lines
from the head revision of the file. The full budget goes before the hunk, where
the enclosing signature and setup are. A quarter of it (at least one line) goes
after. lgtmaybe uses the smaller of this value and what the token budget allows, so
the padding shrinks on large PRs. Set it to `0` to review the bare diff.

```yaml
context_lines: 10   # up to 10 lines before each hunk and 2 after; 0 disables
```

Default: `20`. CLI: `--context-lines`.

### function_context

Extends each hunk's leading padding up to the enclosing function or class
signature, when that signature sits above the `context_lines` window. lgtmaybe
finds the boundary with ast-grep (parsing only, never running code) for Python,
JavaScript, TypeScript/TSX, Go, Rust, Java and Ruby. Its reach is bounded, so a
distant definition can't swamp the diff. Other languages, and any ast-grep
failure, fall back to the fixed-line padding.

```yaml
function_context: false   # fixed-line padding only
```

Default: `true`.

### timeout

The per-request timeout, in seconds, for each model call. Left unset, lgtmaybe
picks a default by provider:

| Provider | Default |
|---|---|
| ollama, openai-compatible | 1800 s, multiplied by `max_concurrency` (calls queue on a single-slot local server) and capped at `max_review_seconds`, but never below 1800 s. With the defaults that is 3600 s. |
| openrouter | 1800 s (it can route to slow reasoning models) |
| other cloud providers | 600 s |

An explicit value is used as is and never scaled. Raise it for a large local
model:

```yaml
timeout: 3600   # an hour per call, e.g. for a big model on CPU
```

CLI: `--timeout`; Action input: `timeout`. See
[Run locally with ollama](run-locally-with-ollama.md#slow-models-and-timeouts).

### structured_output

Asks the provider to return the findings JSON schema through its native JSON
mode (litellm `response_format`). This stops models, especially local ones, from
replying with prose instead of findings. Leave it on unless you hit one of two
failures:

1. The gateway **rejects** `response_format` outright (some
   `openai-compatible` gateways return a `400`). The review fails loudly; turn
   this off.
2. The gateway **accepts** JSON-schema mode but returns replies the parser reads
   as empty. This fails silently: `--profile` shows
   `findings: 0 parsed / 0 returned`, the run exits clean, and a capable model
   looks like one that finds nothing. We saw this with
   `anthropic/claude-fable-5.1` behind OpenRouter on lgtmaybe 2.3.0 and 2.7.0.
   With this off, the same diff returned 11 findings. If a model is unexpectedly
   silent, re-run one diff with `--no-structured-output` before concluding it
   finds nothing.

Either way, the lenient parser still strips code fences and pulls JSON out of
surrounding prose.

```yaml
structured_output: false   # gateway rejects JSON-schema mode, or a model returns nothing under it
```

Default: `true`. CLI: `--no-structured-output`; Action input:
`structured_output`. See
[Use a custom OpenAI-compatible endpoint](use-a-custom-openai-compatible-endpoint.md#gateways-that-dont-support-json-mode-response_format).

### reflect

Runs the [self-reflection](../reference/glossary.md#reflection) pass. It audits the merged findings
and drops the ones the model marks low-confidence, before anything is posted. It
trims [false positives](../reference/glossary.md#false-positive), so leave it on for most models. Turn it off for a weaker or local
model that drops valid findings during the audit.

```yaml
reflect: false   # keep every finding; skip the false-positive audit
```

Default: `true`. CLI: `--no-reflect`.

To audit a weak reviewer with a stronger model instead of turning the pass off,
set `reflect_model`. It uses the same provider and credentials as `model`.
Under the `fast` preset, unless you set `reflect_model`:

- an `anthropic` Sonnet or Opus review audits with `claude-haiku-4-5`;
- an `openai` GPT-5 review (other than a mini or nano model) audits with
  `gpt-5-mini`;
- every other combination audits with the review model.

### min_confidence

During reflection, the auditor gives each kept finding a
[confidence](../reference/glossary.md#confidence) score from 0 (certainly a false positive) to 10
(certainly real). It reaches the score by trying to disprove the finding against
the diff and the file text. lgtmaybe drops findings scored below
`min_confidence`.

The score appears in the CLI output, the JSON output and, as a percentage, in
the posted comment's title next to the lens that raised it:
`**[HIGH · security · 80%] Title**`. A kept finding with no score always passes
the threshold. Its comment leaves out the percentage, as every comment does with
`reflect: false`.

```yaml
min_confidence: 5   # drop findings the auditor scores 0-4
```

Default: `0`, no numeric filtering. Reflection then prunes only through its
keep/drop verdicts. CLI: `--min-confidence`.

### mid_review_retrieval

Lets a review lens ask once for files it can't see.

By default every lens is told the diff is only a slice of the codebase. If a
finding depends on unseen code (a guard, a base class, a helper), the lens must
hedge, lower the severity, or say nothing. That keeps out confident cross-file
mistakes. It also hides a real bug whose evidence is one file away.

With this on, a lens can name the files or symbols it needs alongside its
findings. lgtmaybe fetches them read-only, through the same API or worktree read
the reflection auditor uses, never a checkout of PR code. It
[redacts](../reference/glossary.md#redaction) them and re-runs that one lens with them. lgtmaybe
keeps and de-duplicates the findings from both calls, so a deferral can only add
findings.

```yaml
mid_review_retrieval: true   # trade tokens for cross-file recall
```

Default: `false`, because it can cost up to one extra model call per batch and
lens, carrying the fetched text too. The other bounds are fixed:

- one hop: the re-run can't ask again;
- at most five files, within a quarter of `max_input_tokens`;
- a deferral that arrives past `max_review_seconds` or `max_review_tokens` is
  skipped and reported in the summary.

Read [Reduce Review Cost](reduce-review-cost.md#what-costs-more-on-purpose)
first, and set `max_review_tokens` if the worst case matters. CLI:
`--mid-review-retrieval`; Action input: `mid_review_retrieval`.

### incremental

Commit-scoped review on GitHub, also called
[incremental review](../reference/glossary.md#incremental-review). On a re-run, lgtmaybe reads a
hidden [watermark](../reference/glossary.md#watermark) from its own summary comment. The watermark
is the [head SHA](../reference/glossary.md#head-sha) its last completed review covered. lgtmaybe then
reviews only the commits pushed since, instead of the whole PR.

New findings post as inline comments. Findings on files outside the increment
stay open. Only a run that re-reviewed their file can auto-resolve them.

It falls back to a full review when there is no watermark yet, after a
force-push or rebase, or if the compare call fails. A failed review never moves
the watermark, so no commit is skipped. Comment `/review full` on the PR to
force a full re-review.

```yaml
incremental: false   # every run reviews the whole PR
```

Default: auto. Incremental on a `synchronize` push (new commits on a PR that was
already reviewed); full everywhere else, including open/reopen, slash commands
and the local CLI. Action input: `incremental`.

### static_analysis

Runs fast, deterministic tools over the changed files
([static-analysis fusion](../reference/glossary.md#static-analysis-fusion)).
It is on by default. Each tool feeds the review in one of two modes:

- **`hint`** (the default for every tool): the tool's findings become hints
  the model confirms, puts in context, or discards. This catches mechanical
  bugs models miss, without posting raw linter noise. lgtmaybe reports only
  findings the model confirms.
- **`finding`**: lgtmaybe posts the tool's findings directly, with no model
  call. This is free and gives the same result every run. You opt each tool in
  with `tool_mode`.

Every tool takes one path by default, so the model sees each hit next to the
code it is about. Lockfiles are never reviewed line by line, so a hint about
one (such as an osv-scanner advisory against `uv.lock`) goes to the security
lens once per review. A finding the model confirms there shows in the review
body, because a lockfile has no reviewed line to comment on.

The trade-off: in hint mode the model can discard a real hit, such as a
committed credential. Set `tool_mode` to make a tool post directly, with no
model call:

```yaml
static_analysis:
  tool_mode:
    gitleaks: finding      # post committed secrets directly
    osv-scanner: finding   # post dependency advisories directly
```

| Tool | Checks |
|---|---|
| ruff, bandit, mypy | Python lint, security and type checks |
| gitleaks | secrets, any language |
| zizmor | GitHub Actions workflow security (template injection, unpinned `uses`, broad permissions); runs only when the PR changes a workflow |
| ast-grep | your own structural rules, set with `ast_grep_rules` (skipped when unset) - the deterministic sibling of `extra_lenses` |
| osv-scanner | known vulnerabilities in your dependencies |
| semgrep | multi-language SAST |

```yaml
static_analysis:
  enabled: true
  tools: [ruff, bandit, mypy, gitleaks, zizmor]  # default: all supported tools
  min_severity: low            # floor on mapped tool severity (default info)
  tool_min_severity:           # per-tool overrides of the floor
    ruff: medium               # only medium+ from ruff; bandit keeps low
  tool_mode:                   # per-tool overrides of hint vs finding
    gitleaks: finding          # post secrets directly, with no model call
  # semgrep_rules: .semgrep.yml  # replace the bundled MIT rule pack
  # ast_grep_rules: .ast-grep/   # your own structural rules
```

Default: `enabled: true`, with every tool in `hint` mode. A tool that is not
installed is skipped, so a minimal install runs nothing. To turn it off, set
`enabled: false`, pass `--no-static-analysis`, or set the Action input
`static_analysis: false`.

**Installing the tools.** A tool that isn't installed is skipped silently.
`pip install lgtmaybe[static-analysis]` installs ruff, bandit, mypy, semgrep and
zizmor. ast-grep ships with lgtmaybe. gitleaks and osv-scanner are Go
binaries you install separately. The GitHub Action image includes all eight.

**Sandboxing.** The tools run on the already-fetched file texts in a throwaway
directory. That is never a checkout, and PR code never runs. Each tool runs in a
subprocess with no network, a scrubbed environment and a hard timeout. lgtmaybe
treats their output as untrusted: it is redacted and wrapped before it reaches
the model.

**Direct findings.** Tools read whole files, but only the diff is under review.
So lgtmaybe drops a finding on a line the PR didn't change, and counts it in the
summary. Otherwise a fake credential in a test fixture would post on every PR
that touches the file. Direct findings are also capped per review, most severe
first. They carry a `scan:<tool>` category, so `finding_rules` can drop or
re-grade one scanner without turning it off:

```yaml
finding_rules:
  - match: {category: "scan:gitleaks", path: "tests/fixtures/**"}
    action: {drop: true}
```

**osv-scanner** answers a question a model can't: does a pinned dependency
have a published advisory? That depends on what was disclosed this week, past
any model's knowledge cutoff. osv-scanner reads the manifests and lockfiles the
PR changes through a scan-only channel. The file text never enters the diff, a
prompt or reflection. By default its advisories go to the security lens as
hints, or to the correctness lens when the run has no security lens. With
neither lens, the hints are dropped and the summary says how many. An advisory
the model confirms shows in the review body. With
`tool_mode: {osv-scanner: finding}` the advisories post directly instead, and
only `high` and `critical` ones show (`unanchored_min_severity`).

It needs a local vulnerability database, since the sandbox has no network. The
Action image bakes one in at build time. On the CLI, point
`OSV_SCANNER_LOCAL_DB_CACHE_DIRECTORY` at a directory. Then seed it once from a
project that has your manifests:

```bash
export OSV_SCANNER_LOCAL_DB_CACHE_DIRECTORY="$HOME/.cache/osv-db"
osv-scanner scan source --offline-vulnerabilities --download-offline-databases .
```

Keep the variable set when you run lgtmaybe. It is the one variable passed into
the sandbox. Without a database the scanner reports nothing, and the review says
so rather than calling it clean.

**What the model stops being asked.** When osv-scanner posts findings, the
review prompt stops asking the model two things: whether a version has a known
advisory, and whether a package is abandoned. A knowledge cutoff can't answer
either. The model keeps deprecated APIs, end-of-life runtimes, typosquats and
licence conflicts.

Likewise, when gitleaks posts findings, the model is no longer asked for
hardcoded secrets. lgtmaybe redacts matched secrets before the diff leaves for
the provider, so the model couldn't see them anyway. gitleaks reads the
unredacted text. Secrets written to a log are a different defect that no secret
scanner reports, so the model keeps that one. Set either tool to `hint` and the
model takes those checks back.

**semgrep** runs out of the box with a small, high-precision MIT rule pack that
ships with lgtmaybe. `semgrep_rules` replaces it. Rules are always read from a
local path, because semgrep's registry configs need the network. lgtmaybe
doesn't bundle the well-known semgrep-rules or opengrep-rules collections. They
are LGPL-2.1 plus a Commons Clause, which an MIT package can't redistribute. Point `semgrep_rules` at a fuller pack you have obtained yourself.

**mypy** catches unguarded `Optional` bugs that a review lens reads straight
past, such as a `dict.get()` result dereferenced without a `None` check. It runs
with `--ignore-missing-imports --follow-imports=skip`, because the sandbox holds
only the changed files. So it reports what it can prove from one file and stays
quiet about the rest.

### triage_model

Two-stage routing, so routine PRs don't pay frontier prices while risky ones
still get the strong model. When set, this cheap model runs first over the
per-file diffs. It skips files that plainly need no review (pure formatting,
trivial renames, generated churn). It scores the rest 0-10 by risk. The strong
`model` then reviews only the survivors, riskiest first. The review summary
lists skipped files, and `/review full` reviews everything.

Some files always go to the strong model, whatever triage says:

- security-relevant paths (auth, crypto, session code, migrations, IaC
  (infrastructure as code), CI workflows, dependency manifests);
- patches containing security-relevant tokens;
- files with static-analysis hits;
- large hunks.

Any triage failure, such as an unparseable verdict or a provider error, reviews
everything.

`triage_model`, `model` and `reflect_model` share one provider and set of
credentials, so pointing them all at one ollama model costs nothing. The
trade-off is cheaper, faster reviews against the risk of triage under-rating a
subtle change. The always-review rules bound that risk. For maximum recall,
leave triage off.

```yaml
triage_model: claude-haiku-4-5   # cheap gatekeeper; unset = no triage
```

Default: unset (every file gets the full review). CLI: `--triage-model`; Action
input: `triage_model`.

### auto_diagram

Posts the change overview as one comment, updated in place on every push. The
comment holds:

- a description of the change;
- a [Risk of Change](../reference/glossary.md#risk-of-change) section;
- [High Impact Areas](../reference/glossary.md#high-impact-areas);
- a Mermaid flowchart of the components the PR touches;
- a Mermaid sequence diagram, when the change alters a run-time flow.

`/diagram` posts the same overview on demand.

This is the switch for the whole comment. With it off, lgtmaybe posts only the
review itself automatically. The overview also stands down when the PR
description or another comment already has a diagram. The review summary says
so, and `/diagram` still works.

```yaml
auto_diagram: false
```

Default: `true`. Action input: `auto_diagram`. See
[Generate a change overview](generate-a-change-diagram.md).

### auto_describe

Heads the change overview with a structured description. It contains:

- a suggested title;
- the change type;
- a short summary;
- a per-file walkthrough table;
- when the PR states an intent, a "does it do what it says" check.

The description comes from its own model call, one of the overview's calls. It
is separate from the review's lenses, so this intent check is not the `intent`
lens. It is best-effort: a failure leaves a short note in its place and never
blocks the rest of the comment.

Because it rides the overview comment, it refreshes on every push. `/describe`
posts a description as a separate comment whether or not this is on.

```yaml
auto_describe: false
```

Default: `true`. Action input: `auto_describe`.

### high_impact

Includes the High Impact Areas section in the change overview: changes a
reviewer must not miss. It covers ten areas: infrastructure, security posture,
availability (anything that could cause an outage), data migrations, backups
and recovery, compatibility, observability, dependencies, cost and compliance.

Path patterns ground the model call as untrusted hints. They also set a floor on
its output, so a sensitive file is named even when the model says nothing about
it. Examples are a `*.tf`, a workflow, a migration, a backup policy or a
lockfile. A failed call falls back to that floor instead of dropping the
section. An empty result says what was checked.

```yaml
high_impact: false
```

Default: `true`. Action input: `high_impact`. See
[Generate a change overview](generate-a-change-diagram.md).

### risk

Rates each PR's risk of change as `low`, `medium`, `high` or `critical`, with
the reasons. It is deterministic and makes no model call. It combines:

- how many workspace files import each changed file (Python and TS/JS, via
  ast-grep);
- the High Impact path signals;
- the size of the change;
- code changed without any test changing.

The level and its top reason appear on the review summary line. The change
overview explains every reason. A hidden `<!-- lgtmaybe-risk:<level> -->`
marker lets a workflow read it. With `pr_labels` on, the PR also gets a
`risk/<level>` label.

`core_paths` names central modules that the importer count can't recognise as
central, such as a config loader or a plugin registry. A changed file matching one is at least
`high`.

```yaml
risk:
  core_paths:
    - src/shared/**
    - "**/settings.py"
```

Default: on, with no `core_paths`. Turn it off with `risk: {enabled: false}`,
`--no-risk`, or the Action input `risk: false`. See
[Risk of Change](../explanation/risk-of-change.md) for how the level is decided
and how to gate on it.

### pr_labels

Adds labels derived from the finished review, with no extra model calls:

- `review-effort/1` to `review-effort/5`: a size estimate from the changed lines.
- `possible-security-issue`: the security lens or a security scanner
  (gitleaks, bandit, semgrep, zizmor, osv-scanner) posted a high or critical
  finding.
- `consider-splitting`: the diff spans many unrelated top-level directories.
- `risk/<level>`: the [risk of change](../explanation/risk-of-change.md)
  verdict, when `risk` is on. Only one level is applied at a time.

lgtmaybe reconciles labels on each run: a stale `review-effort/2` is removed
when the score changes. It touches only its own label families. A labelling
failure never fails the review.

```yaml
pr_labels: true
```

Default: `false`. Action input: `pr_labels`.

### finding_rules

Declarative rules applied to findings right before posting. Rules can only drop
or re-grade findings. No user code runs. Each rule has a `match` (every field
given must match) and an `action`. Rules apply in order.

Match fields:

- `path`: a glob; a `**/` prefix also matches at the repo root.
- `category`: the lens that produced the finding (`security`, `correctness`, a
  custom lens ID, or `scan:<tool>`).
- `title_contains`: a case-insensitive substring.
- `min_severity`: matches findings at or above this severity.

Actions: `drop: true` or `set_severity: <level>`.

```yaml
finding_rules:
  # complexity nits in tests aren't worth a comment
  - match: {path: "tests/**", category: complexity}
    action: {drop: true}
  # documentation findings are informational for this repo
  - match: {category: documentation}
    action: {set_severity: info}
```

Default: no rules.

### summary_template

A custom template for the review summary line. Placeholders:

- `{count}`: findings posted
- `{provider}`
- `{model}`
- `{version}`: the lgtmaybe release that produced the review
- `{risk}`: the risk segment, empty when `risk` is off
- `{stack}`: the pull request's layer in a
  [stack](review-stacked-pull-requests.md), such as `layer 2 of 3 in a stack`;
  empty outside a stack
- `{temperature}`: `temperature not sent` when the model's route dropped the
  configured temperature, so the review may not be reproducible; empty
  otherwise

A template that fails to format falls back to the built-in line.

```yaml
summary_template: "🤖 {count} finding(s) · {model} · lgtmaybe {version}"
```

Keep `{version}` if you can. The same model on the same provider reviews
differently across releases, so the version is what makes a surprising review
traceable.

Default: unset, which uses the built-in
`N findings · risk … · provider X · model Y · lgtmaybe Z` line.

### resolve_fixed

Resolves a review conversation once its finding is fixed. On a re-run, two
conditions must both hold:

- a finding lgtmaybe raised is no longer produced;
- GitHub marks its thread outdated (the code under it changed).

lgtmaybe then replies `✅ Looks resolved.` and resolves the conversation.
Because both must hold, a thread is never closed only because nearby lines
moved. Set it to `false` to resolve conversations by hand.

GitHub resolves threads through its GraphQL API. The default `GITHUB_TOKEN`
with `pull-requests: write`, which posting already needs, is enough. The public
`lgtmaybe[bot]` App cannot resolve threads, so under `github_identity: lgtmaybe`
they stay open (see
[What the public App cannot do](use-as-github-action.md#what-the-public-app-cannot-do)).

Other [forges](../reference/glossary.md#forge) (code hosts) work differently:

- GitLab has no "outdated" signal, so there lgtmaybe resolves only threads its
  re-run validated as fixed.
- Azure DevOps has no "outdated" signal either. lgtmaybe compares the file at
  the iteration where it posted the thread against the file now. It marks the
  thread *Resolved* only when the finding is no longer reported **and** the
  flagged line changed. It never does so after a run that failed or finished
  only partly.
- Gitea's API can't resolve threads, so Gitea ignores this setting.

The local CLI has no conversations, so it ignores this setting too.

```yaml
resolve_fixed: false   # leave fixed conversations open for manual resolution
```

Default: `true`. Action input: `resolve_fixed`.

### extra_lenses

Your own review lenses, run alongside the built-in categories. Each one runs as
its own focused model call, and its findings merge into the same review. A lens
needs an `id` and `instructions`. The `id` must be unique, must not be a
built-in category name, and must not start with `scan:`. A `title` and a worked
example (`example_diff` and `example_finding`, supplied together) are optional.
The example noticeably improves a small model's output.

```yaml
extra_lenses:
  - id: simplify
    title: Simplify or delete
    instructions: |
      Flag code that should not exist at all. The best code is the code you never
      wrote: prefer the standard library, an existing dependency, or one line over
      a new abstraction. Call out needless wrappers, premature generality, and
      "just in case" code with no caller.
    example_diff: |
      --- a/util.py
      +++ b/util.py
      @@ -4,1 +4,3 @@
       def get_name(user):
      +    name = user.name
      +    return name
    example_finding:
      path: util.py
      line: 5
      severity: low
      title: Needless local variable
      body: The temporary adds nothing; return user.name directly.
      suggestion: "    return user.name"
```

Lens text reaches the model as trusted instructions. So define lenses only in
files you control (the committed `.lgtmaybe.yml` or repo skill files), never
from PR-author content. See [Add a custom review lens](add-a-custom-lens.md)
for a walkthrough.

Default: none.

### lens_paths

Loads `extra_lenses` from separate skill files instead of inlining them. This
helps when sharing a lens across repos or wiring lgtmaybe into an agent harness.
Each entry is one of:

- a YAML file (one lens or a list of lenses);
- a directory of `*.yml` / `*.yaml` lens files;
- `pack:<name>` for a [lens pack](../reference/glossary.md#lens-pack) bundled with lgtmaybe.

Paths resolve relative to where lgtmaybe runs (your repo root). Loaded lenses
are appended to any inline `extra_lenses`.

```yaml
lens_paths:
  - .lgtmaybe/skills            # a directory of one-lens-per-file skill files
  - team-lenses/house-style.yml # or a single file
  - pack:robustness             # a bundled pack
```

Default: none. See
[Bundled lens packs](add-a-custom-lens.md#bundled-lens-packs-packname).

### directory_rules

Scopes extra review instructions and reference files to part of the repo, for
when `payments/**` and `tests/**` deserve different treatment. Each rule has:

- `paths`: globs. A `**/` prefix also matches at the repo root. An empty or
  missing list applies the rule everywhere.
- `instructions`: free text.
- `context_files`: files read from the checked-out workspace.

A rule reaches every lens call whose batch contains a file it matches.

```yaml
directory_rules:
  - paths: ["payments/**", "billing/**"]
    instructions: |
      Money-handling code. Treat rounding, currency-conversion and retry
      changes as high severity, and flag any write path that is not idempotent.

  - paths: ["tests/**"]
    instructions: |
      Test code. Do not flag duplication, long functions, or missing
      docstrings here.

  - paths: ["src/**"]
    instructions: Check changes against the architecture described below.
    context_files: [ARCHITECTURE.md]
```

Context files are redacted like the diff and share an eighth of
`max_input_tokens`. They are capped at five files per review. A missing or
over-budget file is skipped silently. Instructions and context are trusted
config: on `pull_request_target` they come from the base branch, never the PR
head. See
[Scope review instructions to a directory](scope-review-instructions-to-a-directory.md).

Default: no rules.

### project

Tells the reviewer what kind of project this is, so a weekend prototype and a
regulated payments service don't get the same review. See
[Calibrate reviews to your project](calibrate-reviews-to-your-project.md) for
the walkthrough.

```yaml
project:
  stage: regulated        # prototype | production | regulated
  domain: payments        # a short label, up to 80 characters
  notes: |                # up to 1,000 characters
    PCI-scoped card flows live under payments/. Most traffic is batch.
```

`stage` changes some defaults. A value you set yourself always wins.

| Stage | Default it changes | Review guidance |
|---|---|---|
| `prototype` | `min_severity` defaults to `medium` instead of `low` | Report correctness and security; skip hardening, observability, scalability and documentation polish |
| `production` | none | The standard bar |
| `regulated` | Any PR that isn't only docs and tests is at least `medium` [risk](#risk), with a `regulated workload` reason | Rate data handling, auditability, access control and personal-data exposure one severity step higher where the domain makes them material |

All three fields also add one short paragraph to the system prompt every lens
shares. With [prompt caching](../reference/glossary.md#prompt-cache), that paragraph is paid for once
per run rather than per lens.
Leave the block out and the prompt is unchanged. Like `directory_rules`, this is
trusted config, read from the base branch on `pull_request_target`.

lgtmaybe doesn't read `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md` or `SOUL.md` for this. Those
files are written for coding agents, and most of their text is noise to a
reviewer. The larger ones don't fit the context-file budget either. To put one in front of
the reviewer anyway, name it in a `directory_rules` entry's `context_files`.

Default: no profile.

## Precedence and CLI Overrides

Settings are merged from four layers, highest first:

1. CLI flags, or the GitHub Action's inputs.
2. `.lgtmaybe.yml` (or the file named by `--config` / `config_path`).
3. The user config at `~/.config/lgtmaybe/config.yml`, managed with
   `lgtmaybe config` (local `review` and `diagram` commands only).
4. Built-in defaults.

```bash
lgtmaybe review \
  --provider anthropic \
  --model claude-sonnet-4-6 \
  --min-severity high
```

Most single-value settings have a flag. Run `lgtmaybe review --help-all` for
the list (`--help` alone shows only the everyday ones). List and nested settings
are YAML-only: `include_paths`, `exclude_paths`,
`categories`, `finding_rules`, `extra_lenses`, `lens_paths`, `directory_rules`,
`project`, `spec_paths`, `risk.core_paths` and the `static_analysis` sub-keys.
The `--static-analysis` and `--risk` flags switch those features on or off and
keep the rest of their YAML settings.

## Upgrading from 1.14

Remove `prompt_cache` from `.lgtmaybe.yml` and `--prompt-cache` /
`--no-prompt-cache` from scripts. lgtmaybe 2.0 and later reject them. Prompt
caching is now automatic wherever the provider supports it.

---

<!-- Source: https://lgtmaybe.coles.codes/how-to/add-a-custom-lens/ -->

# Add a Custom Review Lens (BYO Skills)

A [lens](../reference/glossary.md#lens) is one focused review question for the
model. lgtmaybe ships eleven built-in review lenses:

- security, correctness, deprecation, tests, documentation, performance,
  complexity, intent and spec;
- `ponytail`, the "lazy senior dev", write-less-code lens;
- `architecture`, for design decisions that will be expensive to reverse.

A **custom lens** adds your own. It runs alongside the built-ins as its own
focused model call, and its findings merge into the same review. Use one to
enforce a house style or team convention the built-in lenses don't cover.

A custom lens can't reuse a built-in id. So a lens you named `architecture`
before it became built-in needs a new id.

## Contents

- [How a Lens Works](#how-a-lens-works)
- [Inline in `.lgtmaybe.yml`](#inline-in-lgtmaybeyml)
- [As Reusable Skill Files](#as-reusable-skill-files)
- [Bundled Lens Packs (`pack:<name>`)](#bundled-lens-packs-packname)
- [Run It](#run-it)
- [Security: Lenses Are Trusted Input](#security-lenses-are-trusted-input)
- [See Also](#see-also)

## How a Lens Works

Every lens, built-in or custom, has the same shape: a focused set of
instructions and one worked example. Each custom lens is sent as its own model
call, so the model concentrates on a single concern. (Under the default `fast`
[preset](../reference/glossary.md#preset), the built-in lenses share five calls,
plus a sixth when a committed spec matches.
Under `full`, each built-in gets its own call.) A custom lens has these
fields:

| Field | Required | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `id` | yes | A unique short name. It can't be a built-in category name or start with `scan:`. |
| `instructions` | yes | What to look for, in plain language. This is the lens. |
| `title` | no | A human-readable heading (defaults to `id`). |
| `example_diff` + `example_finding` | no (together) | A worked example: a [hunk](../reference/glossary.md#hunk) and the finding the model should return for it. Without one, the lens gets a generic example. Supplying your own noticeably improves smaller models. |

Findings from the lens carry its `id` as their category. So
[`finding_rules`](configure-lgtmaybe-yml.md#finding_rules) can drop or re-grade
them like any built-in lens.

## Inline in `.lgtmaybe.yml`

The quickest way is to define the lens in your repo config:

```yaml
provider: ollama
model: qwen3.6:27b
extra_lenses:
  - id: house-style
    title: House style
    instructions: |
      Enforce our team conventions on changed code. Flag new public functions
      that return bare dicts instead of a typed dataclass, and any logging at
      WARNING or above that doesn't include a correlation id.
    example_diff: |
      --- a/api.py
      +++ b/api.py
      @@ -10,1 +10,2 @@
       def make_user(name):
      +    return {"name": name, "active": True}
    example_finding:
      path: api.py
      line: 11
      severity: low
      title: Public function returns a bare dict
      body: House style returns a typed dataclass from public functions, not a dict.
      suggestion: "    return User(name=name, active=True)"
```

!!! note "The Ponytail lens is built in"
    The "lazy senior dev / write less code" instinct from
    [Ponytail](https://github.com/DietrichGebert/ponytail) ships as the built-in
    `ponytail` lens, so you don't need a custom lens for it. Use `extra_lenses`
    for something the built-ins don't cover, like the house-style rule above.

!!! note "Custom lenses share the never-cut rule"
    Every lens, custom and bundled ones included, runs under one shared rule.
    No lens may recommend removing trust-boundary validation, data-loss error
    handling, security controls, or accessibility support.

    Custom lenses sit outside the deterministic conflict backstop. That
    backstop only arbitrates lens pairs lgtmaybe declares opposed. So write
    instructions that don't contradict the built-ins. See
    [When Lenses Disagree](../explanation/what-gets-reviewed.md#when-lenses-disagree).

## As Reusable Skill Files

You may want to share lenses across repos, or let an agent harness add its own.
Put each lens in its own file, and point `lens_paths` at the file or its
directory:

```yaml
# .lgtmaybe.yml
provider: ollama
model: qwen3.6:27b
lens_paths:
  - .lgtmaybe/skills
```

```yaml
# .lgtmaybe/skills/house-style.yml
id: house-style
title: House style
instructions: |
  Flag new public functions that return bare dicts instead of a typed dataclass,
  and WARNING+ logging without a correlation id.
```

A skill file holds one lens (a mapping) or several (a list). A directory entry
loads every `*.yml` and `*.yaml` file in it. Paths resolve relative to where
lgtmaybe runs, normally the repo root.

Lenses from `lens_paths` are appended to any inline `extra_lenses`. Every `id`
must be unique across the whole set.

## Bundled Lens Packs (`pack:<name>`)

lgtmaybe ships an opt-in library of extra lenses, called
[lens packs](../reference/glossary.md#lens-pack). They are distilled from the
wider engineering-review ecosystem: Ousterhout, Metz, Carmack, the NASA Power of
Ten / TigerStyle, Google's eng-practices, and several skill and rule
collections. See
[ATTRIBUTION.md](https://github.com/MattJColes/lgtmaybe/blob/main/ATTRIBUTION.md).

The packs are off by default for two reasons. They are more opinionated than the
built-ins. And every lens you enable adds a model call per
[batch](../reference/glossary.md#batch).

Enable a pack by name with the `pack:` scheme in `lens_paths`. This works for a
`pip install`, which has no repo-relative path to point at:

```yaml
# .lgtmaybe.yml
provider: ollama
model: qwen3.6:27b
lens_paths:
  - pack:design       # combine as many as you like
  - pack:robustness
```

| Pack | Lenses | Use it when |
|---|---|---|
| `pack:design` | `wrong-abstraction`, `shallow-module`, `information-leakage`, `errors-out-of-existence`, `hidden-state`, `naming` | You want review of structure and taste at a finer grain than the built-in `architecture` lens: the right abstraction, deep modules, explicit state. |
| `pack:robustness` | `assertions`, `bounded`, `idempotency`, `migrations`, `portability`, `observability` | Operational safety: defensive invariants, bounded work, retry-safe side effects, safe migrations. |
| `pack:interface` | `api-design`, `type-safety`, `magic-values`, `comment-why` | Contracts and clarity: backward compatibility, tight types, named constants, comments that explain why. |
| `pack:frontend` | `accessibility`, `i18n` | The diff touches UI or user-facing copy. |

Each pack is a directory of skill files inside the package. You can browse or
copy any single lens from
[`src/lgtmaybe/lenses/`](https://github.com/MattJColes/lgtmaybe/tree/main/src/lgtmaybe/lenses).
An unknown `pack:` name fails with a list of the packs that exist.

## Run It

Once custom lenses are in your config, they run on every review, CLI or GitHub
Action. On the CLI, their findings appear alongside the built-ins:

```bash
lgtmaybe review --provider ollama --model qwen3.6:27b --api-base http://localhost:11434
```

`categories` controls only the built-in lenses. You can narrow it and your
custom lenses still run.

## Security: Lenses Are Trusted Input

A lens's instructions and example reach the model as trusted reviewer
instructions. So treat a lens like code you run:

- Define lenses only in files you control, such as your committed
  `.lgtmaybe.yml` or repo skill files.
- Never source them from a pull request.

On `pull_request_target`, the Action reads config from the base branch, not the
PR head. So a fork PR can't add or change a lens. The diff itself is always
treated as untrusted data, separately from your lenses.

## See Also

- [Configure .lgtmaybe.yml](configure-lgtmaybe-yml.md#extra_lenses) - the field reference.
- [What gets reviewed](../explanation/what-gets-reviewed.md) - the built-in lenses.

---

<!-- Source: https://lgtmaybe.coles.codes/how-to/scope-review-instructions-to-a-directory/ -->

# Scope Review Instructions to a Directory

A monorepo is not uniform. `payments/**` deserves a strictness that would be
pure noise on `tests/**`. And reviewing `src/**` well may need a design document
the diff never shows.

`directory_rules` scopes both **extra instructions** and **reference files** to
path globs (wildcard patterns such as `src/**`). So one repo config can say
different things about different directories.

## Contents

- [The Shape of a Rule](#the-shape-of-a-rule)
- [Scope Instructions to a Directory](#scope-instructions-to-a-directory)
- [Give the Reviewer Background Reading](#give-the-reviewer-background-reading)
- [How Rules Reach the Model](#how-rules-reach-the-model)
- [Limits](#limits)
- [Security: Rules Are Trusted Configuration](#security-rules-are-trusted-configuration)
- [See Also](#see-also)

## The Shape of a Rule

| Field | Required | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `paths` | no | fnmatch globs against the repo-relative path. A `**/` prefix also matches at the repo root. **Omit it** (or leave it empty) and the rule applies everywhere. |
| `instructions` | no | Free text handed to every [lens](../reference/glossary.md#lens) call whose [batch](../reference/glossary.md#batch) contains a file the rule matches. |
| `context_files` | no | Repo-relative files whose text is read from the checked-out workspace and included alongside the instructions. |

A rule needs at least one of `instructions` and `context_files` to do anything.

## Scope Instructions to a Directory

```yaml
provider: bedrock
model: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6

directory_rules:
  - paths: ["payments/**", "billing/**"]
    instructions: |
      This is money-handling code. Treat any rounding, currency-conversion or
      retry change as high severity, and flag any write path that is not
      idempotent under a duplicated webhook.

  - paths: ["tests/**"]
    instructions: |
      Test code. Do not flag duplication, long functions, or missing
      docstrings here. Explicit and repetitive is the house style for tests.
      Do still flag assertions that can never fail.

  - paths: ["infra/**/*.tf"]
    instructions: |
      Terraform. Flag any IAM policy with a `*` action or resource, and any
      storage bucket or database that becomes publicly reachable.
```

Rules are independent, not exclusive. lgtmaybe reviews files in batches. A rule
applies to a whole batch when any file in it matches. A batch touching both
`payments/charge.py` and `tests/test_charge.py` gets both rules, in the order
you wrote them.

## Give the Reviewer Background Reading

`context_files` puts a document in front of the model that the diff would never
show it. Examples are the architecture the code should follow, a data-model
invariant, or a deprecation plan:

```yaml
directory_rules:
  - paths: ["src/**"]
    instructions: |
      Check changes against the architecture described below. Flag a new
      import that crosses a boundary the document forbids.
    context_files:
      - ARCHITECTURE.md
      - docs/data-model.md
```

Paths are repo-relative. The files are read from the workspace lgtmaybe runs
in, the same place your `.lgtmaybe.yml` comes from. They are
[redacted](../reference/glossary.md#redaction) for secrets before they leave the
process, exactly like the diff. A path that resolves outside the workspace is
skipped.

## How Rules Reach the Model

The rules matched for a batch are rendered into one block. The block sits ahead
of the diff in each review call. It is labelled as trusted configuration, so the
model never confuses it with the untrusted diff after it.

The block is part of the same cacheable prefix as the diff. So on providers with
[prompt caching](../reference/glossary.md#prompt-cache), you pay for it roughly
once per batch rather than once per lens.

Instructions and context text both go in as written, with one exception: any
of lgtmaybe's own prompt delimiters are neutralised. So a document that happens
to quote one can't break out of its block.

## Limits

- **Instructions and context only.** A rule cannot change `min_severity`,
  `categories`, or any other setting for a directory. If you want a lens that
  runs everywhere with its own worked example, that is
  [a custom lens](add-a-custom-lens.md).
- **The context budget is small.** Context files share `max_input_tokens / 8`
  (12,500 tokens at the default). They are capped at five files per review. So
  the diff always dominates the call. A file that doesn't fit is skipped whole.
- **A missing path is skipped silently.** A context file is an aid, and a stale
  path must never fail a review. lgtmaybe doesn't log which files it skipped. If
  a document doesn't seem to reach the model, check that the path is
  repo-relative and that the file fits the budget.
- **YAML only.** Like `finding_rules` and `extra_lenses`, `directory_rules` is a
  list of objects. So it has no CLI flag and no Action input. Put it in
  `.lgtmaybe.yml`.

## Security: Rules Are Trusted Configuration

Both the instructions and the context text enter the prompt as **trusted**
content, so they must never come from a pull request's author.

On the recommended `pull_request_target` trigger, the workflow checks out the
**base** branch (the code already merged), never the PR head. `directory_rules`
and the files it names are read from that checkout. That is the same source as
`.lgtmaybe.yml` and `lens_paths`. lgtmaybe never fetches context files through
the host's API, which would resolve them at the untrusted PR head.

On every host, context comes only from the job's workspace. So it is as trusted
as whatever your job checks out. The [GitLab example job](review-on-gitlab.md)
doesn't clone the repository at all. So it has no `.lgtmaybe.yml` or context
files to read.

In practice, a fork PR can change `ARCHITECTURE.md` in its own branch, and
lgtmaybe still reads the base branch's copy. Review changes to your config and
context files the way you review any other change to CI.

## See Also

- [Configure `.lgtmaybe.yml`](configure-lgtmaybe-yml.md) - every field
- [Add a custom review lens](add-a-custom-lens.md) - a whole extra lens, repo-wide
- [Calibrate reviews to your project](calibrate-reviews-to-your-project.md) - stage, domain and notes for the whole repo
- [Configuration reference](../reference/config.md) - generated schema

<!-- Source: https://lgtmaybe.coles.codes/how-to/calibrate-reviews-to-your-project/ -->

# Calibrate Reviews to Your Project

A weekend prototype and a regulated payments service shouldn't get the same
review. The prototype doesn't need to hear about missing metrics. The payments
service shouldn't have an access-control slip rated as a minor issue.

The `project` block tells the reviewer which kind of repository it is looking
at. lgtmaybe then adjusts both its defaults and the model's guidance to match.

## Contents

- [The Shape of a Profile](#the-shape-of-a-profile)
- [Pick a Stage](#pick-a-stage)
- [Add Domain and Notes](#add-domain-and-notes)
- [What Your Settings Still Control](#what-your-settings-still-control)
- [How the Profile Reaches the Model](#how-the-profile-reaches-the-model)
- [Why Not Read AGENTS.md?](#why-not-read-agentsmd)
- [Security: the Profile Is Trusted Configuration](#security-the-profile-is-trusted-configuration)
- [See Also](#see-also)

## The Shape of a Profile

```yaml
provider: bedrock
model: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6

project:
  stage: regulated
  domain: payments
  notes: |
    PCI-scoped card flows live under payments/. Most traffic is nightly batch,
    so latency findings on the batch path matter less than correctness.
```

| Field | Required | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `stage` | no | `prototype`, `production` or `regulated`. Changes defaults and adds fixed guidance. |
| `domain` | no | A short label, up to 80 characters: `payments`, `healthcare`, `internal tooling`. |
| `notes` | no | Free text the reviewer should know, up to 1,000 characters. A longer value fails validation instead of being cut short. |

Every field is optional. Leave the block out and the review is unchanged.

## Pick a Stage

| Stage | Default it changes | Guidance the model gets |
|---|---|---|
| `prototype` | [`min_severity`](configure-lgtmaybe-yml.md#min_severity) defaults to `medium` instead of `low` | Report correctness and security problems, and skip hardening, observability, scalability and documentation polish it doesn't need yet. |
| `production` | none | Hold the change to the standard review bar. |
| `regulated` | Any PR that isn't only docs and tests is at least `medium` [risk](../explanation/risk-of-change.md), with a "regulated workload" reason | Where the domain makes them material, rate data handling, auditability, access control and personal-data exposure one severity step higher. |

`production` changes no settings. It lets a team state the stage explicitly. It
also gives the guidance paragraph a stage to name alongside `domain` and
`notes`.

The `regulated` risk floor stops at `medium` on purpose. Two distinct `high`
reasons make a change `critical`. So a `high` floor would turn every change to a
widely imported module into `critical`. A PR that only touches documentation
and tests stays `low` in any stage.

## Add Domain and Notes

`domain` and `notes` give the model context it can't infer from a diff. Keep
`notes` to what changes how a finding should be judged:

- where the sensitive code lives;
- which paths are hot;
- what the team has decided not to care about.

Some instructions only apply to part of the repo. For those, use
[`directory_rules`](scope-review-instructions-to-a-directory.md) instead. It
reaches only the [lenses](../reference/glossary.md#lens) reviewing matching
files.

## What Your Settings Still Control

A stage only moves defaults. A value you set yourself always wins. It can come
from `.lgtmaybe.yml`, the user config or a CLI flag:

```yaml
project:
  stage: prototype
min_severity: low   # stays low: you set it, so the stage leaves it alone
```

```bash
lgtmaybe review --min-severity info   # beats the prototype default too
```

## How the Profile Reaches the Model

The profile renders one short paragraph at the end of the system prompt that
every review lens shares:

```text
## Project context
From the reviewer configuration (trusted). Calibrate what you report and how
severe you rate it to this project:
This is a regulated workload: where the domain makes them material, rate data
handling, auditability, access control and personal-data exposure one severity
step higher than you otherwise would.
Domain: payments.
Notes from the maintainers: PCI-scoped card flows live under payments/. ...
```

It sits in the shared prompt. So providers with
[prompt caching](../reference/glossary.md#prompt-cache) pay for it once per run
rather than once per lens.

Only the review lenses see it. The
[reflection](../reference/glossary.md#reflection) pass does not. Nor does the
[change overview](../reference/glossary.md#change-overview): its description,
[High Impact Areas](../reference/glossary.md#high-impact-areas) and
diagrams.

The stage's settings changes are deterministic. The guidance paragraph may or
may not shift the severities a given model reports. That depends on the model,
and the eval harness doesn't measure it yet.

## Why Not Read AGENTS.md?

Many repositories already have an `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md` or `SOUL.md`.
Reading one automatically looks like a shortcut. lgtmaybe deliberately doesn't,
for three reasons:

- Those files are written for coding agents: build commands, test runners,
  style rules, personas. Little of it tells a reviewer how strict to be, and
  all of it costs tokens on every call.
- Context files share an eighth of `max_input_tokens` (12,500 tokens at the
  default of 100,000). A file over budget is skipped whole. The repositories
  with the most thorough agent docs are the ones whose file wouldn't fit.
- A stage maps to settings changes that behave the same way every run. Free
  prose can't do that.

You may want one of those files in front of the reviewer anyway. Then name it
in a `directory_rules` entry with no `paths`, which applies everywhere:

```yaml
directory_rules:
  - context_files: [AGENTS.md]
```

## Security: the Profile Is Trusted Configuration

The paragraph enters the system prompt as trusted content. So it must never come
from a pull request's author. On the recommended `pull_request_target` trigger,
`.lgtmaybe.yml` is read from the checked-out base branch, never the PR head.

lgtmaybe still neutralises prompt delimiters in `notes` and `domain`. So nothing
in them can close a prompt block early.

## See Also

- [Configure `.lgtmaybe.yml`](configure-lgtmaybe-yml.md#project), every field
- [Scope review instructions to a directory](scope-review-instructions-to-a-directory.md), for per-path instructions
- [Risk of change](../explanation/risk-of-change.md), how the verdict is built
- [Configuration reference](../reference/config.md), the generated schema

<!-- Source: https://lgtmaybe.coles.codes/how-to/generate-a-change-diagram/ -->

# Generate a Change Overview

lgtmaybe can post a
**[change overview](../reference/glossary.md#change-overview)** on a pull
request. It says what the change is, what is risky about it, and what it
touches. It is one comment, updated in place, for a reviewer to read before the
diff.

The overview is separate from the review. The review finds bugs in the lines it
reads. The overview describes the change as a whole.

## Contents

- [What You Get](#what-you-get)
- [High Impact Areas](#high-impact-areas)
- [Structure and Sequence](#structure-and-sequence)
- [On GitHub: `/diagram` and `auto_diagram`](#on-github-diagram-and-auto_diagram)
- [Locally: `lgtmaybe diagram`](#locally-lgtmaybe-diagram)
- [Why Mermaid (and What the ASCII Is For)](#why-mermaid-and-what-the-ascii-is-for)
- [See Also](#see-also)

## What You Get

One comment holds three model calls, run concurrently, plus one deterministic
section (worked out by code, with no model call). In reading order:

1. **The description head** (`auto_describe`): a suggested title, the change
   type, and a short summary.
2. **Risk of Change** (`risk`): the change's `low` to `critical` verdict and
   every reason behind it, computed without a model call. See
   [Risk of Change](../explanation/risk-of-change.md).
3. **[High Impact Areas](../reference/glossary.md#high-impact-areas)**
   (`high_impact`): the changes a reviewer must not miss. See
   [High Impact Areas](#high-impact-areas) below.
4. **The description detail** (`auto_describe`): a per-file walkthrough, and a
   "does it do what it says?" check when the PR states an intent.
5. **Up to two diagrams**: a Mermaid flowchart of the structure and, when the
   change alters one, a Mermaid sequence diagram of the run-time flow. Mermaid
   is a text format for diagrams that GitHub draws for you. Each diagram also
   comes as plain text. A terminal shows that text, and it is the fallback if
   the Mermaid can't be rendered.

The description, High Impact Areas and diagrams are three calls rather than
one. A single prompt doing three jobs does all three worse. The calls run at the
same time, so the overview takes about as long as its slowest call.

Each section has its own switch. The description and High Impact Areas are
best-effort: if one of those calls fails, its slot says so and the rest of the
comment still posts.

GitHub renders both Mermaid diagrams natively inside the comment, with no image
and no external hosting.

The flowchart is deliberately sparse:

- at most six components;
- short relationship labels;
- Mermaid's automatic layout.

Changed components are marked `(new)` or `(changed)` in their labels.

GitHub's renderer offers zoom buttons but no full screen. So each diagram is
followed by an **⛶ Open full screen** link. It opens the same diagram alone on
[mermaid.live](https://mermaid.live), with pan and zoom. The diagram source
travels compressed in the URL fragment and is decoded in your browser. Nothing
is sent anywhere until you click.

The diff is only a slice of the codebase. So a note under the diagrams calls
out any relationship the model inferred rather than saw in the diff.

Here is the posted comment for a PR that puts a Redis cache in front of a user
service. The Mermaid renders in place. Each text rendering sits in a collapsible
"Text version" underneath:

> ## Cache user lookups in Redis
>
> **Change type:** feature
>
> User reads now check Redis before PostgreSQL, and successful database reads
> populate the cache for later requests.

> ### **Risk of Change: Critical**
>
> - touches infrastructure: `infra/redis.tf`
> - touches backup and recovery: `ops/backup_retention.yaml`

> ### **High Impact Areas**
>
> - **Infrastructure**: New ElastiCache cluster (`infra/redis.tf`). Adds a
>   managed dependency to the production VPC. _Check:_ security group and
>   failover settings.
> - **Availability**: Cache on the user read path (`api/users.py`). User reads
>   now depend on Redis. A Redis outage takes reads down with it. _Check:_
>   confirm a Redis error falls back to the database.
> - **Backup and recovery**: touched `ops/backup_retention.yaml` (not assessed by
>   the model)

> ### Walkthrough
>
> | File | Change |
> |---|---|
> | `api/users.py` | Reads through the Redis cache before querying PostgreSQL |
> | `infra/redis.tf` | Adds an ElastiCache Redis cluster |
> | `ops/backup_retention.yaml` | Excludes the cache from nightly backups |

> ### Structure

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    n0["Client"]
    n1["User API<br/>Python<br/>serves user reads<br/>(changed)"]
    n2["Redis cache<br/>Redis<br/>caches user rows<br/>(new)"]
    n3["User DB<br/>PostgreSQL"]
    n0 -->|"requests"| n1
    n1 -->|"checks"| n2
    n1 -->|"on miss"| n3
```

> [⛶ Open full screen](https://mermaid.live)&nbsp; *(the real link carries the
> diagram source compressed into the URL)*

<details>
<summary>Text version</summary>

```
[Client] --requests--> [User API Python (changed)]
[User API Python (changed)] --checks--> [Redis cache Redis (new)]
[User API Python (changed)] --on miss--> [User DB PostgreSQL]
```

</details>

> ### Sequence

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant n0 as Client
    participant n1 as User API (changed)
    participant n2 as Redis cache (new)
    participant n3 as User DB
    n0->>n1: GET /users/{id}
    n1->>n2: read cached row
    n2-->>n1: miss
    n1->>n3: SELECT user
    n1->>n2: store row, 60s TTL
    n1-->>n0: user JSON
```

<details>
<summary>Text version</summary>

```
1. [Client] -> [User API (changed)]: GET /users/{id}
2. [User API (changed)] -> [Redis cache (new)]: read cached row
3. [Redis cache (new)] --> [User API (changed)]: miss
4. [User API (changed)] -> [User DB]: SELECT user
5. [User API (changed)] -> [Redis cache (new)]: store row, 60s TTL
6. [User API (changed)] --> [Client]: user JSON
```

</details>

> The User DB link is inferred from an import, not shown in the diff.

## High Impact Areas

A review reads the changed lines and tells you what is wrong in them. It cannot
tell you that halving a node count removes your peak headroom. Nor can it tell
you that the PR quietly shortened a backup retention policy.

**High Impact Areas** asks a different question: *what could this change break
beyond itself?* It answers in one section near the top of the overview.

Ten areas are checked:

| Area | What it covers |
|---|---|
| **Infrastructure** | IaC, Kubernetes/Helm, container images, CI/CD pipelines, deploy scripts, networking, DNS, load balancers, resource sizing |
| **Security** | Authentication, authorisation, IAM or permission scope, cryptography, secret handling, removed input validation, CORS/CSP/TLS, CI workflow permissions |
| **Availability** | Anything that could cause a production outage: startup and config defaults, timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, connection pools, rate limits, health checks, removed error handling, concurrency and locking, runtime or major dependency upgrades, hot-path performance, rollback and deploy ordering |
| **Data migration** | Schema or data migrations, destructive or irreversible data operations, backfills |
| **Backup and recovery** | Backup jobs, retention and lifecycle policies, snapshots, restore paths, disaster recovery, failover, replication |
| **Compatibility** | Breaking an external contract: HTTP APIs, event or message schemas, CLI flags, SDK surface, wire formats, feature-flag removal |
| **Observability** | Logs, metrics, alerts, dashboards, tracing, audit trails or runbooks being removed, silenced or changed |
| **Dependencies** | Supply chain: new dependencies, major bumps, loosened pins, lockfiles, base images, build toolchain |
| **Cost** | Autoscaling limits, instance types, provisioned capacity, storage classes, quotas |
| **Compliance** | PII or privacy handling, audit trails, data residency, licence changes |

Each call-out names:

- the area;
- a short headline;
- the files involved;
- the blast radius (what else the change can affect);
- the one thing a reviewer should verify.

A call-out the model rates `medium` or `critical` shows that severity next to
the area name. `high` is the unmarked default. Files the model names that the
PR never changed are dropped.

### The Path Floor

The model is not the only source. Before the call, lgtmaybe matches the PR's
changed paths against fixed patterns per area. Examples are `*.tf`,
`.github/workflows/`, `alembic/`, anything named for backups or retention, and
lockfiles. Those matches do two jobs:

- They are sent to the model as untrusted hints, saying where to look (never
  that anything is wrong).
- They floor the output. Say the model said nothing about a matched file under
  that area. The file is still listed, marked `(not assessed by the model)`. A
  weak model cannot make your Terraform change invisible.

The floor is also the fallback. If the call fails or returns nothing usable,
the section shows the path matches alone, under a "Model assessment
unavailable" note. The section degrades, but it never disappears.

When nothing qualifies, the section says so and names what it checked:

> ### **High Impact Areas**
>
> None detected. Checked: infrastructure, security posture, availability, data
> migrations, backups and recovery, compatibility, observability, dependencies,
> cost, compliance.

### Turning It Off

The section is on by default. To drop it and its model call:

```yaml
high_impact: false
```

The description has its own switch, `auto_describe: false`. Risk of Change has
`risk: {enabled: false}`. With all three off, the comment holds only the
diagrams and costs one call.

## Structure and Sequence

The two diagrams answer different questions, which is why lgtmaybe draws both:

| | Answers | Best on |
|---|---|---|
| **Flowchart** (structure) | What does this change touch, and what talks to what? | Structural PRs: a component added, a dependency introduced, a service split |
| **Sequence** | What happens at run time, in what order, and where did that change? | Behavioural PRs: a retry added, an ordering fixed, a signal now handled |

Most pull requests are behavioural, and structure alone under-describes them.
Take a PR that fixes terminal restoration on `SIGTERM`. It might touch two files
and draw three boxes. Its sequence diagram (signal, flag set, loop exit, guard
dropped, terminal restored) *is* the explanation of the fix.

A PR that puts a cache in front of a service is the opposite. The new box is the
headline, and the flow shows how a request now reaches it.

Some changes have no meaningful run-time flow, such as documentation,
configuration or formatting. For those, the sequence view is omitted rather
than invented. Both diagrams come from one model call and share the same
six-component budget. The sequence view adds at most eight ordered steps.

## On GitHub: `/diagram` and `auto_diagram`

Comment **`/diagram`** on a pull request to post the change overview, or update
it in place. Re-running edits the same comment instead of stacking new ones.
(`/describe` still posts the description alone as its own comment, for when
that is all you want.)

`auto_diagram` is on by default, with no workflow input or `.lgtmaybe.yml`
needed. The overview posts when a PR is opened or reopened. It refreshes after
each push, so every section tracks the head commit. To opt out of the whole
comment, set the input in your workflow:

```yaml
      - uses: MattJColes/lgtmaybe@v2
        with:
          provider: anthropic
          model: claude-sonnet-4-6
          api_key: ${{ secrets.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }}
          auto_diagram: "false"
```

or in `.lgtmaybe.yml`:

```yaml
auto_diagram: false
```

The automatic overview stands back when the pull request already diagrams the
change. That means a fenced `mermaid` block in either:

- the PR description;
- any comment that is not this setup's own overview. That covers yours, a
  teammate's, another review bot's walkthrough, or another lgtmaybe setup's
  overview.

The review still runs, and its summary says where the existing diagram lives.
Once lgtmaybe has posted its own overview on a PR, it keeps refreshing that one
so it never goes stale. Comment `/diagram` to post the overview anyway: slash
commands skip the check.

Gitea runs the same check through the shared Action entrypoint. The
`gitlab-ci` command posts no automatic overview yet.

The description and High Impact Areas are best-effort. A failure is logged and
leaves a visible note in its slot. It never blocks the rest. The diagram is a
required completion step. So a failed diagram leaves the commit unfinished, and
the next run redoes it rather than skipping it.

## Locally: `lgtmaybe diagram`

`lgtmaybe diagram` prints the change overview of your local changes, with no
GitHub involved:

```console
$ lgtmaybe diagram --provider ollama --model llama3
```

It diffs your branch against the base, using the same base resolution as
`lgtmaybe review`:

- `--base` overrides the base;
- `--working` includes uncommitted edits;
- `--uncommitted` uses only the working-tree edits.

The output is the same body the `/diagram` comment carries. In order, that is
the description, Risk of Change, High Impact Areas and walkthrough. Then come
each diagram's Mermaid source, full-screen link and text rendering. There is one
change: a terminal renders no HTML. So the collapsible "Text version" wrapper
becomes a plain labelled section. An excerpt:

````console
$ lgtmaybe diagram --provider ollama --model llama3
...
### Sequence

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant n0 as Order API (changed)
    participant n1 as Payments
    n0->>n1: POST /charge
    n1-->>n0: 503 Unavailable
    n0->>n0: backs off 200ms
```

[⛶ Open full screen](https://mermaid.live/view#pako:…)

Text version:

```
1. [Order API (changed)] -> [Payments]: POST /charge
2. [Payments] --> [Order API (changed)]: 503 Unavailable
3. [Order API (changed)] -> [Order API (changed)]: backs off 200ms
```
````

The Mermaid source stays in the output on purpose. Your terminal can't draw
it, but you can paste it into a GitHub comment,
[mermaid.live](https://mermaid.live), or a Markdown file to render it.

## Why Mermaid (and What the ASCII Is For)

GitHub renders **Mermaid** natively in comments and Markdown, both flowcharts
and sequence diagrams. So a `mermaid` fence renders in the comment, with no
image to generate or host.

That matters for a `pull_request_target` reviewer. Hosting an image would mean
committing a file or calling an external service. Neither fits a fork-safe
comment that is updated in place.

A terminal can't render Mermaid, which is why each diagram also comes as plain
text. In the GitHub comment, that text sits in a collapsible "Text version"
block, out of the way of the rendered diagram. In the terminal, the same block
becomes a labelled section, because HTML tags are noise in a shell. Either way,
the text is what you read without a renderer. It is also the fallback if a
diagram fails to render.

The model never writes Mermaid. It returns typed graph data: components,
relationships and ordered steps. lgtmaybe renders the syntax itself and escapes
every label. A diff that tries to smuggle diagram source or markup into a label
can't reach the fence.

D2 isn't used because GitHub doesn't render it in Markdown, so it would show as
source.

## See Also

- [Configure `.lgtmaybe.yml`](configure-lgtmaybe-yml.md)
- [Use as a GitHub Action](use-as-github-action.md)
- [Configuration reference](../reference/config.md)
