<!-- Source: https://lgtmaybe.coles.codes/reference/profile/ -->

# Profile Reference

`--profile` prints a breakdown of a review at the end of the run. It shows
where the time went, what each model call spent, and what it produced.
`--profile-json PATH` writes the same data as JSON.

Both flags are on the local `lgtmaybe review` command. On the GitHub Action,
set the `profile: true` input to print the table in the Action log. There is no
JSON file there.

**Parse the JSON, not the table.** The table's layout is not a contract and may
change. The JSON payload carries a `schema_version`, so you can pin against it.

## Which Stream the Table Uses

The table goes to **stdout** for a human-format review. It goes to **stderr**
when the findings themselves are machine-readable (`--format json`,
`--format agent`, `--format sarif` or `--json`), so stdout stays parseable.
Without `--profile`, a local review still prints its `tokens:` footer, always
to stderr.

`--profile-json` writes to a **file**, so it never collides with either stream.
If the path can't be written, lgtmaybe logs a warning and carries on. The
review is not lost to a diagnostic file.

## Layout

```text
== lgtmaybe profile ==
total wall time: 41.3s

stage              elapsed
split                0.01s
...

call             batch tries   elapsed   in_tok  out_tok think_tok  think_% cache_rd cache_wr findings  error
security             1     1     8.20s    36918     1286       400       5%        0        0        2  -
reflect              0     1     3.10s     4000      200         -        -        0        0        -  -

cache: 0 tokens read / 0 created across 2 calls
findings: 2 parsed / 1 returned
...
tokens: 42,404 billable (40,918 in / 1,486 out) across 2 calls
```

The stage table lists each pipeline stage (`split`, `expand`, `review`,
`reflect`, `post` and so on) in the order it ran. The call table lists every
model call, slowest first.

## The Call Table's Columns

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `call` | The [lens](glossary.md#lens) ID (`security`, `correctness`, `code-health`, `artefacts`, `architecture`, `spec`, a single category under `full`, or a custom lens ID), or another call: `reflect`, `triage`, `validate`, `repair:<lens>` |
| `batch` | Which [batch](glossary.md#batch) of files the call covered; `0` for calls outside the per-batch fan-out, such as `reflect` and `triage` |
| `tries` | Requests actually issued, including adapter retries (`0` when unknown) |
| `elapsed` | Wall time for the call, including retries |
| `in_tok` | Prompt tokens |
| `out_tok` | Completion tokens, including any reasoning tokens |
| `think_tok` | Reasoning tokens, when the route reports them |
| `think_%` | Reasoning tokens as a share of the call's `max_tokens` ceiling |
| `cache_rd` | Prompt-cache tokens read |
| `cache_wr` | Prompt-cache tokens written |
| `findings` | Findings parsed from this call |
| `error` | The failure reason, when the call failed |

The [change overview](glossary.md#change-overview)'s calls are not in the
profile. Those are the description,
[High Impact Areas](glossary.md#high-impact-areas) and diagrams.

## Summary Lines

These lines follow the call table. A line whose data is missing is left out.

| Line | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `cache:` | Prompt-cache tokens read and written across all calls |
| `findings: N parsed / M returned` | Findings parsed from the calls, and how many survived dedupe, [reflection](glossary.md#reflection) and filtering |
| `models:` | Which models answered, when more than one did (see below) |
| `reasoning:` | Reasoning tokens as a share of output tokens, over the calls that reported a breakdown |
| `largest reasoning share:` | The single call that spent the most of its `max_tokens` ceiling on reasoning, by lens and batch |
| `tokens:` | Billable tokens (input + output) across all calls |
| `estimated cost:` | A price estimate from litellm's pricing map, shown only when it priced at least one call, and noting how many it priced |

### The `models:` Line

When every call was answered by the same model, there is no `models:` line.
A second model can answer some calls through `fallback_model`. That happens
when the engine escalates a truncation to it, or when the adapter falls back on
its own. Either way, a line names each model and how many calls it took:

```text
models: luna (7 calls), sonnet (1 call)
```

There is no per-call model column, because it would repeat one string down
the whole table. The per-call value is in the JSON payload and the structured
`provider call` log line. Both leave it out where the adapter reports no
model.

### What `-` Means

A dash means **unknown**, never zero.

- `think_tok` is a dash when the route reported no reasoning breakdown,
  because `0` would claim the model did no thinking.
- `think_%` is a dash when the call had no ceiling to be a share of.
- `findings` is a dash for a call that doesn't produce review findings at all.
  That differs from a call that produced none, which shows `0`.

This is what breaks naive parsers: `int(row["think_tok"])` raises on a dash. In
the JSON payload the same value is `null`.

## The JSON Payload

```json
{
  "schema_version": 1,
  "wall_seconds": 12.4,
  "total_tokens": 41231,
  "total_cost_usd": null,
  "returned_findings": 3,
  "stages": [{"name": "redact", "elapsed": 0.01}],
  "calls": [
    {
      "label": "security",
      "batch": 1,
      "elapsed": 8.2,
      "attempts": 1,
      "input_tokens": 36918,
      "output_tokens": 1286,
      "cache_read_tokens": 0,
      "cache_creation_tokens": 0,
      "error": null,
      "reasoning_tokens": null,
      "output_ceiling": null,
      "findings": 2,
      "model": "openrouter/google/gemini-3.8-flash",
      "cost_usd": null,
      "reasoning_share": null
    }
  ]
}
```

Notes:

- `reasoning_tokens`, `reasoning_share`, `output_ceiling`, `findings`, `error`,
  `model` and `cost_usd` are `null` when unknown or absent, the JSON
  counterpart of the table's `-`.
- `reasoning_share` is the raw ratio the table rounds into `think_%`.
- `total_tokens` is input + output across all calls. Cache counters are left
  out. Routes disagree on whether a cached read is already inside the prompt
  count, so adding them would double-count on some routes.
- `cost_usd` and `total_cost_usd` are estimates from litellm's pricing map, and
  `null` (never `0`) when nothing was priced.
- `returned_findings` is the count after the whole pipeline, which can be lower
  than the calls' parsed total once dedupe, reflection and filtering have run.

## Stability

`schema_version` is bumped when the payload's shape changes in a way a pinned
consumer would notice. Adding a field is not such a change. Removing a field,
or changing what it means, is.

---

<!-- Source: https://lgtmaybe.coles.codes/reference/glossary/ -->

# Glossary

The terms these docs use, in plain words. Each entry says what the term means
and links to the page where it matters most.

## Ambient Credentials

Credentials the environment already provides, so you store no key. On GitHub
Actions this is a short-lived cloud login made through [OIDC](#oidc) or
[WIF](#wif). On your machine it is your existing `aws`, `gcloud` or `az` login.
See [Auth model](../explanation/auth-model.md).

## Anchor

The exact text of the changed line a [finding](#finding) is about. Models often
miscount line numbers, so lgtmaybe finds the line whose text matches the anchor
and posts the comment there. If no changed line matches, the finding moves into
the review summary instead of landing on the wrong line.

## Architecture Lens

The [lens](#lens) that asks what a change will make hard to change later. It
looks for coupling across boundaries, dependencies that point the wrong way,
subclasses that break their base class, and APIs that are easy to misuse. Each
of its findings opens with the change that would become painful.

## Batch

A group of changed files sent to the model together. lgtmaybe sizes each batch
to fit the model's input limit (`max_input_tokens`). A large pull request
becomes several batches, and every [lens](#lens) reviews every batch.

## Change Overview

One comment that explains a pull request: a description, the
[risk of change](#risk-of-change), the [high impact areas](#high-impact-areas),
and diagrams of what the change touches. It is posted automatically, or on
request with `/diagram`. See
[Generate a change diagram](../how-to/generate-a-change-diagram.md).

## Code Host

Where your pull requests live: GitHub, GitLab, Gitea or Azure DevOps. The code
also calls this a [forge](#forge).

## Composite Action

A GitHub Action built from a list of steps instead of a single program.
lgtmaybe's action first logs in to your cloud without a stored key, then runs
the review in a container. See
[Use as a GitHub Action](../how-to/use-as-github-action.md).

## Confidence

A score from 0 to 10 that [reflection](#reflection) gives each finding it keeps.
Higher means the check could not find a reason the finding is wrong. Set
`min_confidence` to drop findings below a score.

## Diff

The list of lines a change adds and removes. lgtmaybe reads the diff through
your [code host](#code-host)'s API and never checks out or runs the change.

## Fail On

The `fail_on` setting. When it is set, lgtmaybe adds a check to the pull
request that fails if any finding is at or above that [severity](#severity).
Make the check required in branch protection and it blocks the merge.

## False Positive

A finding that is wrong: the code is fine, or the problem is not real. lgtmaybe
works hard to avoid them, because each one costs the reader time and trust.

## Fan-out

Running many model calls at the same time instead of one after another. Each
[lens](#lens) on each [batch](#batch) is its own call, and `max_concurrency`
(6 by default) caps how many run at once.

## Finding

One issue lgtmaybe reports. It has a [severity](#severity), a title, a body
that says what goes wrong and why it matters, and sometimes a suggested fix. On a
code host it becomes an inline comment on the changed line.

## Forge

The code's name for a [code host](#code-host). GitHub, GitLab, Gitea and Azure
DevOps are the forges lgtmaybe supports.

## Head SHA

The [SHA](#sha) of the newest commit on the pull request's branch. lgtmaybe
records the head SHA it reviewed, so a later run knows where to start.

## High Impact Areas

A section of the [change overview](#change-overview) that lists what the change
could break beyond its own lines. It covers areas such as infrastructure,
security, outages, data migrations, cost and compliance. See
[Generate a change diagram](../how-to/generate-a-change-diagram.md).

## Hunk

One block of changed lines in a [diff](#diff). It starts with a line such as
`@@ -10,4 +10,6 @@`, which gives where the block sits in the old and new file.

## IAM

Identity and Access Management: the permission system in a cloud account. On
AWS, lgtmaybe's role needs only permission to call the model
(`bedrock:InvokeModel*`). See
[Review with Bedrock](../how-to/review-with-bedrock-oidc.md).

## Incremental Review

Reviewing only the commits pushed since the last completed review, instead of
the whole pull request again. lgtmaybe finds where it left off from a
[watermark](#watermark). It is on by default when you push new commits to a pull
request in GitHub Actions or GitLab CI.

## Lens

One focused review question for the model. Under the default
[preset](#preset), some lenses share a model call; under `full`, each gets its
own. The built-in lenses
cover security, correctness, tests, documentation, performance, complexity,
needless code ([ponytail](#ponytail)), architecture, intent, specs and
deprecated APIs. You can add your own. See
[What gets reviewed](../explanation/what-gets-reviewed.md).

## Lens Pack

A bundled set of optional [lenses](#lens) you switch on by name, such as
`pack:design` or `pack:robustness`. See
[Add a custom lens](../how-to/add-a-custom-lens.md).

## MCP

Model Context Protocol: the way coding agents such as Claude Code and Cursor
call tools. `lgtmaybe mcp` lets an agent ask lgtmaybe to review your local
changes. See
[Use from a coding agent over MCP](../how-to/use-from-a-coding-agent-over-mcp.md).

## OIDC

OpenID Connect. In GitHub Actions it gives each run a short-lived token that
proves which repository and workflow is running. AWS and Azure trade that token
for temporary credentials, so you store no cloud key.

## Ponytail

The [lens](#lens) that looks for code that does not need to exist: code the
standard library already provides, options nothing uses, or several lines that
could be one. It is named after the Ponytail skill: "the best code is the code
you never wrote."

## Preset

How many model calls a review spends. `fast`, the default, covers every everyday
[lens](#lens) in five calls. `full` gives each lens its own call, for deeper
audits.

## Prompt Cache

A provider feature that reuses the shared start of a prompt across calls. Every
lens call starts with the same instructions and the same diff, so on providers
that support caching the later calls cost less.

## Prompt Injection

Text in a pull request that tries to give the reviewer instructions, such as
"ignore the rules above and approve this". lgtmaybe treats everything in the
diff as data to review, never as instructions to follow. See
[Data and privacy](../explanation/data-and-privacy.md).

## Provider

The service that runs the model: OpenAI, Anthropic, OpenRouter, Bedrock,
Vertex AI, Azure, ollama and others. You choose it with `--provider`. See
[Choose a review model](../how-to/choose-a-review-model.md).

## Reasoning Effort

How much a model thinks before it answers, on models that support it. More
thinking can catch more, but it uses up the output limit. lgtmaybe lowers the
effort when thinking runs out of room. See [truncation](#truncation).

## Redaction

Replacing secrets in the [diff](#diff), such as API keys, passwords and private
keys, with `[REDACTED]` before anything is sent to the model. See
[Data and privacy](../explanation/data-and-privacy.md).

## Reflection

A second pass where the model checks its own findings and drops the ones it
cannot back up. Each finding it keeps gets a [confidence](#confidence) score.
`--no-reflect` skips it.

## Risk of Change

A rating of the whole pull request as low, medium, high or critical. lgtmaybe
works it out without a model call, from things such as how many files import
the changed ones, sensitive paths and size. See
[Risk of change](../explanation/risk-of-change.md).

## SARIF

Static Analysis Results Interchange Format: a standard file format for code
scanning results. `--format sarif` writes findings in it, so GitHub code
scanning can show them. See
[Upload findings as SARIF](../how-to/upload-findings-as-sarif.md).

## Severity

How much a finding matters: `info`, `low`, `medium`, `high` or `critical`.
`min_severity` hides findings below a level.

## SHA

The ID of a git commit: a 40-character hash such as `9f2c1e7…`. Tools often
show only the first 7 characters.

## Spec Lens

The [lens](#lens) that checks a change against a written specification the
repository keeps, such as an OpenSpec, Spec Kit or Kiro spec. It only runs when
it finds a spec that matches the pull request.

## Stacked Pull Requests

A chain of small pull requests, each built on the one below it and merged
bottom up. Each one shows only its own changes. lgtmaybe tells the model where a
pull request sits in its stack. See
[Review Stacked Pull Requests](../how-to/review-stacked-pull-requests.md).

## Static-Analysis Fusion

A step, on by default, that runs installed tools, such as ruff, bandit,
gitleaks and semgrep, on the changed files. Their results go to the model as
hints to confirm or discard. The raw tool output is never posted. A tool you
opt into `finding` mode posts its findings directly instead.

## Symbol Resolution

Finding the file that defines a name. When [reflection](#reflection) needs code
it cannot see, lgtmaybe uses ast-grep to locate the definition and reads that
file, read-only.

## Truncation

A model answer cut off because it reached the output limit (`max_tokens`).
lgtmaybe first retries with smaller pieces or less
[reasoning effort](#reasoning-effort), and only then tries a fallback model.

## Watermark

A hidden marker in lgtmaybe's summary comment that records the last commit it
fully reviewed. [Incremental review](#incremental-review) starts from it. A
failed review never moves it.

## WIF

Workload Identity Federation: Google Cloud's way to let a GitHub Actions run use
a service account without a key file. See
[Review with Vertex AI](../how-to/review-with-vertex-wif.md).

---

<!-- Source: https://lgtmaybe.coles.codes/explanation/what-gets-reviewed/ -->

# What Gets Reviewed

This page explains what lgtmaybe looks at, how it bounds the work, and what the
output looks like on a pull or merge request and on the command line. Each kind
of check below is a [lens](../reference/glossary.md#lens): one focused review
question for the model.

## What It Looks At

lgtmaybe reviews the **diff of a pull request** (or a GitLab merge request): the
lines it adds or changes, not the whole repository. It fetches that diff from
your code host's REST API and **never checks out or runs the PR's code**. A
malicious change therefore can't execute anything in the reviewer's environment.
lgtmaybe treats the diff as untrusted input throughout, including against
[prompt-injection](../reference/glossary.md#prompt-injection) attempts hidden in
PR text.

To review changes in context, lgtmaybe also pads each changed
[hunk](../reference/glossary.md#hunk) with **surrounding lines** read from the
head revision of the changed file. The model uses them to understand the change
(the enclosing function, nearby definitions) but only comments on changed lines.
The padding is budget-scaled and capped by `context_lines` (default 20, `0`
disables it). lgtmaybe fetches it read-only via the API and
[redacts](../reference/glossary.md#redaction) it like the diff.

Before the diff reaches the model it is cleaned:

- **Non-reviewable files are skipped**: lockfiles, minified assets and
  sourcemaps, vendored and build-output directories (`vendor/`,
  `node_modules/`, `dist/`, `build/`, `third_party/`), generated code (protobuf
  output, `.d.ts`, Dart `.g.dart`, test snapshots), generated LLM-index corpora
  (`llms.txt` / `llms-full.txt`), and binaries. Reviewing them is noise and
  wastes tokens.
- **Oversized files are skipped**: a single file whose diff runs past
  `max_file_diff_lines` (default 2000, `0` disables) is dropped and named in the
  summary. Name matching only catches generated files whose name admits it; a
  hand-named 154,000-line data blob is caught on size alone.
- **Secrets are redacted**: anything that looks like a key, token, private key
  or credential is stripped from the diff before it leaves your environment for
  the provider.

By default lgtmaybe also runs any installed static-analysis tools, such as
ruff, bandit, gitleaks and semgrep, over the changed files
([static-analysis fusion](../reference/glossary.md#static-analysis-fusion)).
They run locally in a sandbox with no network. Their results go to the model as
redacted hints to confirm, put in context, or discard, so a tool's raw output
is never posted. A tool you opt into `finding` mode posts directly instead; see
[static_analysis](../how-to/configure-lgtmaybe-yml.md#static_analysis).

## Correctness & Logic

The model is prompted to hunt for the bugs a change introduces and grade them
by impact:

- **Null / None dereferences**: a value that can be empty used without a guard.
- **Off-by-one and boundary errors**: `<` vs `<=`, fencepost mistakes, empty-
  and single-element edge cases.
- **Mismatched or inverted ranges**: `start`/`end` swapped, a lower bound above
  its upper bound.
- **Unhandled error and exception paths**: failures silently swallowed, or state
  left half-updated.
- **Incorrect conditionals**: inverted booleans, `and`/`or` mix-ups, missing
  branches.
- **Resource leaks and ordering**: handles or locks not released,
  use-after-close, bad concurrent sequencing.
- **Races and concurrency**: check-then-act (TOCTOU), shared mutable state
  without synchronisation, coroutines called without `await`, blocking calls in
  async paths.
- **Numeric and date/time bugs**: overflow, float equality, division by zero,
  money in binary floats; timezone-naive datetimes, epoch-unit confusion, DST.
- **Aliasing and mutation**: mutable default arguments, mutating a collection
  while iterating it, sharing a mutable value the caller still owns.

=== "On a pull request"

    ![An inline lgtmaybe review comment flagging a [HIGH] possible None dereference, where get_user can return None but .email is accessed without a guard](../assets/review-correctness.png){ width="660" }

=== "On the CLI"

    ![The lgtmaybe CLI printing a [HIGH] None-dereference finding for demo/orders.py](../assets/cli-correctness.png){ width="660" }

## Security Review

The model is prompted with an OWASP-aligned checklist and told to grade what it
finds `high` or `critical` and name the vulnerability class in the title. It
looks for:

- **Injection**: SQL/NoSQL, OS command, and template/LDAP injection.
- **Cross-site scripting (XSS)**: unescaped user input rendered into HTML/JS.
- **CSRF and open redirect**: unprotected state-changing endpoints,
  user-controlled redirect targets.
- **Hardcoded secrets**: keys, tokens, passwords, or private keys in the diff.
- **Broken authn / authz**: missing permission checks, IDOR, auth bypass, and
  JWT or session pitfalls (unverified signatures, `alg` confusion, missing
  expiry).
- **Path traversal and unsafe file access**: user input in file paths, `../`,
  zip-slip extraction, and unrestricted file uploads.
- **SSRF**: server-side fetches of user-controlled URLs without allow-listing.
- **Insecure deserialisation and unsafe eval**: `pickle`/`yaml.load`/`eval` on
  untrusted data, and XML parsed with external entities enabled (XXE).
- **Mass assignment / over-posting**: request bodies bound straight onto models.
- **Weak cryptography**: MD5/SHA1 for passwords, ECB mode, disabled TLS
  verification, predictable randomness for security tokens.
- **Sensitive-data exposure**: secrets or PII in logs, error responses, or
  analytics (passwords, API keys, tokens/session IDs, SSNs, payment-card data).
- **CI / IaC (infrastructure as code) misconfiguration**: untrusted input
  interpolated into workflow `run:` steps, third-party actions not pinned to a
  SHA, overly broad IAM policies, public buckets, privileged containers, secrets
  echoed into build logs. It also flags:
    - controls that only look enforced, such as an `environment:` key used as an
      approval gate when the environment has no required reviewers, or a budget
      alert treated as a spending cap;
    - checks that cannot fail, such as `continue-on-error: true` or `|| true` on
      a test or scan step. A skipped check that reports a pass is worse than no
      check.
- **Resource / DoS safety**: missing timeouts, unbounded loops or allocations,
  regexes vulnerable to catastrophic backtracking (ReDoS).

=== "On a pull request"

    ![An inline lgtmaybe review comment flagging a [CRITICAL] SQL injection vulnerability in a find_user function, explaining the unsafe string concatenation and suggesting a parameterised query](../assets/review-sql-injection.png){ width="660" }

=== "On the CLI"

    ![The lgtmaybe CLI printing a [CRITICAL] SQL injection finding for demo/db_queries.py](../assets/cli-security.png){ width="660" }

This shapes *what* the reviewer flags. How lgtmaybe protects **itself** from a
malicious PR (secret redaction, prompt-injection defence) is covered in
[Data and Privacy](data-and-privacy.md).

## Deprecation & Dependency Health

The reviewer also flags **factually outdated** code when the diff shows it.
These are objective, not stylistic:

- deprecated language or framework APIs (with the modern replacement when
  known),
- targeting an end-of-life runtime or language version,
- adding or pinning an end-of-life or abandoned dependency,
- pinning a dependency to a version with a known security advisory, and
- a new dependency whose name looks like a typosquat of a popular package, or
  whose licence conflicts with the project's.

It raises these only when the diff itself shows the change, and does not
speculate about code it cannot see.

=== "On a pull request"

    ![An inline lgtmaybe review comment flagging a [MEDIUM] deprecated datetime.utcnow() call and suggesting datetime.now(timezone.utc)](../assets/review-deprecation.png){ width="660" }

=== "On the CLI"

    ![The lgtmaybe CLI printing a [MEDIUM] deprecated-API finding for demo/scheduler.py](../assets/cli-deprecation.png){ width="660" }

## Test Coverage & Documentation

Two lighter checks round out a review:

- **Missing or weak tests**: the diff adds a function, branch, or error case
  with no accompanying test. The reviewer raises a `low`/`medium` finding. Its
  `suggestion` field holds a concrete, runnable test in the project's existing
  test idiom. It also flags tests added in the diff that don't really test
  anything: assertion-free, mocked until only the mock is exercised, or flaky
  (sleep-based waits, wall-clock or ordering dependence). It leaves renames,
  comments, and trivial formatting changes alone.
- **Documentation gaps and stale docs**: a public surface added without a
  docstring, or a name or signature that contradicts what the code does, is
  flagged at `info`/`low`. A docstring or comment the change made wrong is
  flagged up to `medium`, because a comment that lies is worse than none.
  Private helpers and self-evident code are left alone.

A missing test, with a runnable test in the suggestion:

=== "On a pull request"

    ![An inline lgtmaybe review comment flagging a [LOW] new branch added without a test, with a runnable pytest suggestion](../assets/review-tests.png){ width="660" }

=== "On the CLI"

    ![The lgtmaybe CLI printing a [LOW] missing-test finding for demo/discount.py](../assets/cli-tests.png){ width="660" }

A documentation gap on a new public function:

=== "On a pull request"

    ![An inline lgtmaybe review comment flagging an [INFO] public function missing a docstring, with a suggested docstring](../assets/review-documentation.png){ width="660" }

=== "On the CLI"

    ![The lgtmaybe CLI printing an [INFO] missing-docstring finding for demo/client.py](../assets/cli-documentation.png){ width="660" }

## Performance

The reviewer watches for performance regressions the change introduces, graded
by impact (`low`, up to `high` when the cost scales with input size or sits in a
hot path):

- **N+1 queries or calls in a loop**: a query, request, or other expensive call
  issued once per iteration that could be batched or hoisted out.
- **Inefficient algorithms**: accidentally quadratic (`O(n²)`) work where linear
  is feasible, or a linear scan where a set or dict lookup would do.
- **Redundant computation**: recomputing the same value inside a loop instead of
  hoisting or memoising it.
- **Unnecessary allocations and copies**: building large intermediates or
  copying big buffers on a hot path when streaming or in-place work would do.
- **Blocking I/O on a hot path**: synchronous I/O, sleeps, or lock contention
  where non-blocking handling is expected.
- **Unbounded or over-fetching queries**: loading whole tables into memory, or
  missing pagination and limits.
- **Unbounded growth and leaks**: caches without eviction, listeners or
  subscriptions never removed, queues that only grow.

It sticks to changes the diff shows and skips micro-optimisations with no
measurable impact.

=== "On a pull request"

    ![An inline lgtmaybe review comment flagging a [HIGH] N+1 query inside a loop, suggesting a single batched query](../assets/review-performance.png){ width="660" }

=== "On the CLI"

    ![The lgtmaybe CLI printing a [HIGH] N+1-query finding for demo/reports.py](../assets/cli-performance.png){ width="660" }

## Complexity

A restrained lens that flags code harder to read, test, or maintain than it
needs to be (`info`/`medium`), preferring a concrete simplification in the
`suggestion` field:

- **High cyclomatic complexity or deep nesting**: many branches, or deeply
  nested conditionals and loops that would read better with early returns.
- **Over-long, low-cohesion functions**: a function doing several unrelated
  things that should be split.
- **Duplicated logic**: non-trivial logic repeated in the diff that belongs in
  a shared helper.
- **Excessive parameters or boolean-flag arguments**, **convoluted
  expressions**, and **dead or unreachable code**.

Like the documentation lens, it stays quiet on code that is already simple.

=== "On a pull request"

    ![An inline lgtmaybe review comment flagging a [MEDIUM] deeply nested conditional and suggesting guard clauses](../assets/review-complexity.png){ width="660" }

=== "On the CLI"

    ![The lgtmaybe CLI printing a [MEDIUM] deep-nesting finding for demo/router.py](../assets/cli-complexity.png){ width="660" }

## Intent: Does the PR Do What It Says?

The intent lens compares the diff against the PR's **stated intent** and flags
mismatches at `medium`, or `high` when the unexplained change is
security-relevant:

- **Out-of-scope changes**: a hunk unrelated to the stated intent, such as a
  "fix typo" PR that also touches auth logic, CI workflows, dependency pins, or
  permissions. Smuggled security-relevant changes are the most valuable catch.
- **Contradictions**: the code does the opposite of, or something materially
  different from, what the title or commits claim.
- **Unfulfilled intent**: the PR promises behaviour the diff never implements.

Where the stated intent comes from:

- **On a GitHub PR**: the PR title, description, and the first line of each
  commit message, fetched via the API.
- **On the CLI**: the commit subjects from your local `git log` against the
  base branch, so the lens works without GitHub, in `--working` mode too. With
  no commits beyond the base yet (or with `--uncommitted`), nothing states an
  intent and the lens is skipped.

Under the default `fast` [preset](../reference/glossary.md#preset), intent is
folded into the correctness call rather than run as a call of its own.

### The Lens Is Told What It Was Not Shown

An intent lens judging "did the author keep their promise?" against a
*filtered* diff will call a kept promise broken. Files go missing for seven
reasons:

- the generated/binary/vendored skip;
- your `include_paths` / `exclude_paths` globs;
- the `max_file_diff_lines` size cap;
- the `max_files` cap;
- a triage skip;
- an incremental scope;
- being in another [batch](../reference/glossary.md#batch). Lenses run once
  **per batch**, so on a large PR each call sees only part of the change.

So each call is told which of the PR's files it cannot see. The list goes to
every lens. The intent lens also gets the rule that goes with it: a claim about
a file that was not shown is **not shown, not undone**.

lgtmaybe derives the list from what is left of the PR after the batch. It
therefore covers every one of those mechanisms without caring which applied. It
is capped, then wrapped and neutralised as untrusted data, because filenames are
attacker-controlled on a fork PR too. That is why lgtmaybe doesn't report "the
stated intent to regenerate X is not reflected in the diff" when X is a
generated file it was never allowed to read.

The intent text is attacker-controlled on a fork PR, so lgtmaybe treats it
exactly like the diff:

- secrets are redacted;
- it is wrapped as untrusted data with neutralised delimiters;
- the model is told never to follow instructions inside it.

Only the call that carries the intent lens ever sees it. When a PR states no
intent at all, the lens is skipped instead of spending a model call.

## Spec: Does the PR Deliver the Specification It Commits To?

Your repository may drive its work from a committed specification. That spec
is a better statement of intent than a PR description: it is structured, it
predates the code, and its task list records what the author claims to have
finished. The [spec lens](../reference/glossary.md#spec-lens) checks the diff
against it in **both** directions.

lgtmaybe recognises three layouts out of the box, plus your own:

| Workflow | Detected by | Read |
|---|---|---|
| [OpenSpec](https://github.com/Fission-AI/OpenSpec) | `openspec/changes/<id>/`, `openspec/specs/<capability>/` | proposal, delta specs, design, tasks (archived changes are ignored) |
| [GitHub Spec Kit](https://github.com/github/spec-kit) | `.specify/`, or `specs/<slug>/` with a `spec.md` **and** a `plan.md` | spec, plan, tasks |
| [Kiro](https://kiro.dev/docs/specs/) | `.kiro/specs/<feature>/` | requirements, design, tasks |
| Your own layout | `spec_paths` globs in `.lgtmaybe.yml` | whichever of those filenames are present |

### What It Reports

**The diff falling short of the spec**

- **Contradicts an explicit requirement**: the code does the opposite of a
  stated SHALL/MUST or acceptance criterion (`high`).
- **A ticked task that is not delivered** (`medium`); see below.
- **A requirement in scope with nothing implementing it** (`medium`).
- **An acceptance criterion with no test** (`low`).

**The spec falling short of the diff**: the half people miss, and the more
reliable of the two, because the evidence is entirely in the diff.

- **Behaviour no requirement covers**: a new endpoint, state, error path, limit
  or side effect the spec never mentions (`low`/`info`).
- **A requirement the change made stale** (`low`).
- **An unresolved `[NEEDS CLARIFICATION]`** still sitting in a requirement this
  PR implements (`info`).

### Ticked Checkboxes Are Claims

All three workflows track progress with markdown checkboxes, and a PR that
implements tasks *flips* them:

```diff
-- [ ] T014 [US1] Enforce the 30-day link expiry in src/links/service.py
+- [x] T014 [US1] Enforce the 30-day link expiry in src/links/service.py
```

That flip is already in the diff. lgtmaybe extracts it with no model call and
no extra file read, and hands the lens the list as *claims the author made in
this pull request*. That turns a vague question ("did this deliver the spec?")
into a precise one ("is T014 actually here?"). A ticked task is something to
**check**, never to assume false: the lens flags it only when the diff shows
the work is absent.

### Which Spec, and When It Stays Quiet

A monorepo can hold forty spec directories. lgtmaybe ranks them against the PR
on these signals, and sends at most two:

- the PR edits the spec;
- the PR's branch is named after it;
- the PR's title, description or commits name it.

Spec Kit names branches after the spec directory, which is what makes the
branch signal work. **When
nothing matches, the lens does not run at all**: no model call, no prompt bytes.
The same is true when no spec system is present, which is the common case, so
a repository without specs pays nothing.

Because it needs its own large block, the spec lens is a call of its own: a
sixth call under the default `fast` preset, made only when a spec matched. Turn
it off with `--no-spec` on the CLI, or `spec_review: false` in `.lgtmaybe.yml`
or as an Action input.

### The Spec Lens Is Told What It Was Not Shown

A requirement is delivered by *code*, so this lens is even more exposed than
the intent lens to the filtered-diff trap. Told nothing, it reports every
requirement implemented in another batch as undelivered. It gets the same
correction:

- the list of the PR's files this call cannot see;
- the rule that a requirement delivered in one of them is **not shown, not
  undelivered**.

Spec text is treated exactly like the diff: redacted, wrapped as untrusted data
in its own neutralised block, and never obeyed. That is deliberate. A spec is
usually committed in the same PR that implements it, so on a fork PR the author
controls the requirements their own change is judged against.

Files the PR changes are read from its head text for the same reason: the base
branch does not have them yet. Everything else comes from the checked-out
workspace, which on `pull_request_target` is the trusted base branch. The worst
a planted spec can do is suppress a spec finding, because no other lens sees the
block.

## Ponytail: The Laziest Senior Dev in the Room

The best code is the code you never wrote. Inspired by
[Ponytail 5](https://github.com/DietrichGebert/ponytail), this lens reviews new
code with a senior engineer's reflex to **not** add code. It walks Ponytail's
ladder and stops at the first rung that holds:

1. Does this need to exist?
2. Is it already in this codebase?
3. Does the standard library or platform do it?
4. Does an installed dependency do it?
5. Can it be one line?

It flags what skipped a rung (graded `info` to `medium`, and deliberately
restrained):

- **Needless code (YAGNI)**: speculative generality, "just in case" parameters,
  an abstraction with a single caller, or scaffolding for a future that isn't
  here.
- **Re-implementing what exists**: a helper this codebase already has (only when
  that helper is in front of the model), or hand-rolled code that a built-in, the
  standard library, or an already-imported dependency does directly.
- **A new dependency for a few lines**: a package added for what a handful of
  lines or an installed dependency already does.
- **Could be far shorter**: several lines doing what one clear expression would.
- **Premature configurability**: flags, hooks, or options no caller uses yet.

It prefers deleting or collapsing code over adding to it, and puts the smaller
replacement in the suggestion. It also:

- checks the code really is unused before saying so;
- never collapses an existing port, layer, or interface boundary (an adapter
  implementing one is not needless);
- treats a `shortcut:` comment as a recorded decision rather than a finding.

The complexity lens asks "is this code hard to follow?"; Ponytail asks "should
this code exist at all?"

We take Ponytail's leanness rules, not its whole review: Ponytail 5's own
`/ponytail-review` also checks bugs, security, load, and tests, which here are
separate lenses.

## Architecture: What Will This Make Hard to Change?

Architecture is the set of decisions that are expensive to reverse. This lens
flags only decisions the change itself introduces, graded `info` to `medium`.
Every finding has to open with a concrete change scenario: "when X changes, Y
and Z have to change with it". A finding that only names a principle ("this
violates SRP") is not allowed, because the name explains nothing on its own.

- **Coupling across boundaries**: one module reaching into another's internals,
  long call chains across a package or service boundary, or mutable state
  shared between modules. Tight coupling inside one module is fine; the same
  coupling across a boundary, on something likely to change, is the finding.
- **Dependencies pointing the wrong way**: domain code importing a framework,
  adapter, database or HTTP client, an import that closes a cycle, or a stable
  module starting to depend on a volatile one.
- **Broken substitutability (Liskov)**: an override that accepts less than its
  base class, promises less, raises errors the base never did, or quietly does
  nothing, and callers that branch on a concrete subclass instead. It only
  claims this when the base class is in front of it.
- **Misplaced responsibility**: a module gaining a second, unrelated reason to
  change, logic that mostly works on another object's data, or one concept
  spread so a single change needs edits in several places.
- **Sharp edges**: new public surface that is easy to misuse, such as calls
  that must happen in a hidden order, internal mutable state handed out, or
  malformed input accepted silently.
- **Leaky ports**: an interface that forces implementers to stub methods they
  don't need, or vendor types crossing a port so the core is tied to the vendor.

Its evidence bar keeps it from becoming a lecture:

- It never proposes a new abstraction unless the diff shows a second
  implementation or caller, or the coupling crosses a boundary the repository
  already has.
- It reads layers from the repository's own paths and documented architecture
  rather than inventing them.
- It skips tests, scripts and private helpers.
- It hedges to `info` or `low` when the claim depends on code it cannot see.

Most findings carry no one-click suggestion. The finding names a structural fix
instead (move the function, invert the dependency).

The ideas come from the classic literature on design:

- Parnas on information hiding;
- Constantine and Yourdon on coupling and cohesion;
- Liskov and Wing on substitutability;
- Meyer on design by contract;
- Martin on dependency direction;
- Cockburn's ports and adapters;
- Evans on bounded contexts;
- Fowler's refactoring catalogue;
- Bloch on API design;
- Khononov on balancing coupling.

See [ATTRIBUTION.md](https://github.com/MattJColes/lgtmaybe/blob/main/ATTRIBUTION.md).
The complexity lens asks "is this hard to follow?" and ponytail asks "should
this exist?"; architecture asks "what will this make hard to change?". For a
finer grain, the opt-in `pack:design` adds Ousterhout-style checks such as
shallow modules and information leakage.

## When Lenses Disagree

Each lens is prompted on its own and none of them names another. Two lenses
could therefore, in principle, give opposite advice about the same lines. One
says "cut this", another says "this guard is what keeps it safe". Posting both
tells the author two contradictory things, so lgtmaybe stops it at four points:

1.  **Nobody cuts protective code.** A rule shared by every lens covers bundled
    packs and your own custom lenses too. It forbids recommending the removal
    or weakening of:

    - validation at a trust boundary;
    - error handling that prevents data loss;
    - security controls;
    - accessibility support.

    Any shorter replacement must keep every edge case and error path. This is
    Ponytail 5's "never cut" list, applied to all of them.

2.  **Each lens has its own evidence bar.** The bars keep territories apart
    without lenses knowing about each other:

    - ponytail never collapses an existing boundary;
    - architecture never proposes a new one without a visible second
      implementation;
    - complexity only suggests extracting duplicated code when the copies have
      uniform callers (never through a flag argument).

3.  **Reflection referees.** The
    [self-reflection](../reference/glossary.md#reflection) pass sees every
    finding at once. When two give opposite advice about the same code, it
    keeps the one higher on the ladder: correctness, security, performance,
    tests, architecture, complexity, ponytail. That is Ponytail 5's own review
    order (correctness, safety, load, tests, speed, leanness) mapped onto these
    lenses, with design slotted above readability. A finding whose lens is not
    on the ladder, such as a custom or pack lens, is never arbitrated.

4.  **A deterministic backstop.** After reflection (and even with
    `--no-reflect`), `engine/conflicts.py` drops a lower-ranked finding when:

    - it sits within three lines of a higher-ranked one; and
    - the two come from a lens pair declared opposed. Today that is ponytail
      against correctness, security, and architecture.

    Group ids, custom and pack lenses, and scanner hits declare no opposition,
    so the backstop never guesses about them. It sees only where a finding
    sits, not what it advises. That is why it acts only on pairs that oppose
    each other by nature. Reflection reads the advice itself, so it covers the
    rest of the ladder. It drops one of two findings only when they really do
    point opposite ways.

The `counter-advice` eval fixture measures this. It plants a genuine lean catch
beside two traps: upload validation that looks redundant, and an adapter that
looks like a pass-through. The run fails if a model recommends cutting either.

## How the Scope Is Bounded

Every run is bounded so a large PR can't run away on latency. All of these are
configurable in `.lgtmaybe.yml` (see
[Configure .lgtmaybe.yml](../how-to/configure-lgtmaybe-yml.md)):

| Knob | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `preset` | `fast` | `fast` uses five calls (security, correctness, code health, artefacts, architecture) on every provider, plus a sixth spec call when a spec matches; `full` runs one call per lens. |
| `max_files` | 50 | Reviews the top-N changed files and posts a "reviewed top N of M" notice if there are more. |
| `max_file_diff_lines` | 2000 | Skips any single file whose diff is longer, naming it in the summary. `0` disables. |
| `max_input_tokens` | 100,000 | Batches the diff so each model call stays within budget. Left at the default, it is capped at what the model's context window can take. |
| `max_concurrency` | 6, every provider | Concurrent model calls across the whole fan-out (all batches share one pool). Local throughput is set on the server (`OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL`, llama.cpp `-np`, vLLM batching); set this to `1` for serial. |
| `max_review_seconds` | 3600 | Soft wall-clock ceiling: past it, queued calls are skipped and the review posts partial results with a notice. `0` disables. |
| `categories` | all | Which review lenses run (the ten everyday lenses, plus `spec` when a spec matches). An explicit list overrides the preset grouping and runs each listed lens as its own call. |
| `context_lines` | 20 | Ceiling on surrounding lines added around each hunk; the budget may use fewer. `0` disables context expansion. |
| `min_severity` | `low` (`medium` for a [`prototype` project](../how-to/calibrate-reviews-to-your-project.md)) | Drops findings below the floor (`info` → `low` → `medium` → `high` → `critical`). `low` keeps everything except pure-`info` narration. |
| `include_paths` / `exclude_paths` | none | Glob filters to focus the review. |

> These bound a **single run**, not the number of runs. On a public repo,
> anyone who can open a PR or comment can trigger a run, and each run calls your
> chosen LLM provider. See the cost disclaimer in
> [Use as a GitHub Action](../how-to/use-as-github-action.md).

## What a Finding Contains

Every finding is written for an engineer new to the codebase. Its title leads
with the fix when one is known. Its body says what goes wrong and why it
matters, in plain words, and explains a technical term the first time it
appears. The change overview comment follows the same rule.

Findings are structured data, not prose, so they render the same everywhere.
Each finding has:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `path` | File the comment attaches to |
| `line` | Line in the diff |
| `side` | `RIGHT` (added/changed) or `LEFT` (removed) |
| `severity` | `info` / `low` / `medium` / `high` / `critical` |
| `title` | One-line summary |
| `body` | The explanation |
| `failure_scenario` | For defect findings: the trigger, the changed behaviour, and the observable impact |
| `suggestion` | Optional suggested replacement code |
| `anchor` | The flagged line, verbatim, used to place the comment on the right line |
| `anchored` | Whether `anchor` matched a changed line; an unanchored finding moves to the review body |
| `broad` | Set by reflection when the fix needs a broad change (redesign, infra, API contract) rather than a local edit; broad findings go to a collapsed "Broader observations" section |
| `category` | The lens that raised it |
| `confidence` | The self-reflection auditor's 0-10 score (absent when reflection is off) |

The ten everyday review categories are security, correctness, deprecation,
tests, documentation, performance, complexity, intent, ponytail, and
architecture. `spec` is an eleventh that runs only when a committed spec matches
the PR. The default `fast` preset covers the ten in five calls, one per concern:

- security;
- correctness (with stated intent folded in);
- code health (performance, complexity, ponytail, deprecation);
- artefacts (tests, documentation);
- architecture.

The same five run on every provider; worker count changes only how they are
scheduled. `preset: full` runs each category as its own call, with a worked
example of its own finding type.

lgtmaybe drops two kinds of finding:

- security, correctness, deprecation, and performance findings without a
  concrete `failure_scenario`;
- `fast` code-health findings the model left unattributed (any of them may be a
  performance or deprecation one).

It merges and de-duplicates the rest. A self-reflection pass then audits the
rest and drops low-confidence findings. So the model's first guesses are
filtered before anything is posted.

The reviewer only sees the diff and some surrounding context: a *slice* of the
codebase, not the whole thing. A concern may depend on code it can't see, such
as a guard, a base class, or an idempotency check that may live in an unshown
file. Then it hedges and lowers the severity rather than asserting the thing is
missing. The self-reflection pass drops findings that rest on such assumptions.
Genuine gaps in the diff itself are exempt and still raised, such as a changed
path with no test or a new public surface left undocumented.

## What the Response Looks Like

### On a Pull or Merge Request

The rendering below is GitHub's. GitLab, Gitea and Azure DevOps show the same
findings with
the same badges; [how each host posts them](#how-each-host-posts) differs, and
is covered at the end of this section.

lgtmaybe posts **one review** containing:

- an **inline comment** on the exact changed line for each finding, and
- a **summary** that names the model used.

Each finding lands on the line that triggered it. Its severity is in the title
and the explanation in the body. Where the fix is clear, it adds a suggested
change you can commit straight from the PR.

A finding the engine could not place on a changed line is listed in the summary
instead of posted on a guessed line. It is listed only when it is serious enough
(`unanchored_min_severity`, default `high`).

![An inline lgtmaybe review comment flagging a [MEDIUM] server-side request forgery (SSRF) risk where a user_id is concatenated into a URL, with a suggested validation fix](../assets/review-ssrf.png){ width="660" }

![An inline lgtmaybe review comment flagging a [CRITICAL] command injection vulnerability in an archive function using subprocess with shell=True, with a suggested fix that avoids the shell](../assets/review-command-injection.png){ width="660" }

The summary carries a hidden marker (`<!-- lgtmaybe -->`). Re-running at the
same commit **updates** that summary instead of creating a duplicate. A
completed review at a new commit posts a fresh summary and leaves the older one
as history. Findings already posted are never posted twice.

#### Reading the Title Line

A comment's title line carries the finding's provenance in its brackets:

```
**[HIGH · security · 80%] User input is concatenated into the SQL string**
```

- **`HIGH`** is the severity.
- **`security`** is the lens that raised it: one of the review categories (or
  your own id if you added a [custom lens](../how-to/add-a-custom-lens.md)).
  It is the same value you match on in `finding_rules`, so a badge you keep
  seeing and don't want tells you exactly which rule to write.
- **`80%`** is the self-reflection auditor's confidence that the finding is
  real, reached by trying to disprove it. It is the auditor's 0-10 score shown
  as a percentage, so `min_confidence: 5` is the same floor as `50%`. Set that
  floor to drop everything below a score you choose.

Each part drops away when it isn't there: with `reflect: false` there is no
score, and the badge is the lens alone.

Neither GitHub's nor Gitea's review API can edit an inline comment once it is
posted. So an inline comment's score is **frozen at first post**: a later run
that judges the same finding differently won't change it. Findings in the
summary body (the "Additional findings" and "Broader observations" sections)
are rewritten on every run, so those badges do track. Severity and title have
always behaved this way; the badge makes it visible.

### Resolving Conversations Once They're Fixed

Each inline comment also carries hidden per-finding ids. When you push a fix and
lgtmaybe runs again, it checks its own open conversations. lgtmaybe treats a
finding as fixed when both of these hold:

- the finding it raised is **no longer produced**;
- GitHub marks that thread **outdated** (the code under it changed).

It then replies `✅ Looks resolved.` and resolves the conversation. Because both
conditions must hold, a thread is never collapsed only because the lines around
it shifted. Nor is it collapsed because one run happened not to re-flag it
while the code stayed the same.

This is on by default. To leave conversations for manual resolution, set
`resolve_fixed: false` in `.lgtmaybe.yml` (or the Action's `resolve_fixed`
input). Resolving a thread uses GitHub's GraphQL API; the workflow's default
`GITHUB_TOKEN` (with `pull-requests: write`, already needed to post the review)
is enough. The step is best-effort: if it can't run, the review still posts
normally.

On **GitLab** the same thing happens over plain REST. On **Gitea** it does not
happen at all: Gitea has no thread-resolution API, so finding comments stay open
for a human to close. On **Azure DevOps** the thread is set to *Resolved*.
Azure DevOps has no "outdated" flag, so lgtmaybe records the iteration each
finding thread was posted at and compares the file then against the file now.
It only resolves threads its own token opened, and only after a complete run.

### How Each Host Posts

The findings are identical everywhere. What each host's API allows is not:

| | GitHub | GitLab | Gitea | Azure DevOps |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Inline comments | one batched review | one discussion per finding | one batched review | one thread per finding |
| Summary | the review body, edited in place | a note, edited in place | an issue comment, edited in place | a general thread, edited in place |
| Avoiding duplicates on a re-run | skips ids already posted | skips ids already posted | skips ids already posted | skips ids it posted itself, once the token's identity is known |
| Auto-resolve a fixed finding | ✅ GraphQL | ✅ REST | ✗ no API | ✅ REST |
| Incremental review of new commits | ✅ | ✅ | ✗ no compare diff | not yet |
| Learn from 👎 on a finding | ✅ reactions | ✅ award emoji | ✗ | not yet |

A submitted **Gitea** review can't be edited, so its summary moves to an
ordinary comment and duplicate findings are filtered *before* posting.
**GitLab** has no batched review object, so each finding becomes its own
positioned discussion. **Azure DevOps** serves no diff at all, so lgtmaybe
builds one from the file contents before and after the change, and each finding
becomes its own positioned thread.

When a PR is clean (no findings, and every file was within the caps), the
summary is short:

```
👍 LGTM!

0 findings · risk low (no risk signals) · provider anthropic · model claude-sonnet-4-6 · lgtmaybe 2.11.1
```

The risk segment comes from the [risk of change](risk-of-change.md) assessment
and is absent when that is turned off (`--no-risk`, or `risk.enabled: false`).
If the file cap kicked in, the summary says so (for example "Reviewed the top 50
of 120 changed files"). lgtmaybe never fails
silently: any error is posted back to the PR as a short comment.

### On the Command Line

`lgtmaybe review` runs the same pipeline over your local `git` diff and prints
the findings. It posts nothing and needs no GitHub token. By default it diffs
the current branch against the remote primary branch (`origin/HEAD`, falling
back to `origin/main`/`origin/master`, then a local `main`/`master`). An empty
diff makes no model call; when none of those branches exists it exits non-zero
and asks for `--base`.

- `--working` reviews the whole worktree (branch commits plus uncommitted
  edits) against that same base.
- `--uncommitted` reviews only the uncommitted edits against `HEAD`.
- `--base <ref>` picks a different base.

Both worktree modes include files you haven't `git add`ed yet. A brand-new file
is often the one you most want a second pair of eyes on. Anything `.gitignore`
excludes stays out. The default output is a readable listing
followed by the summary line:

```console
$ lgtmaybe review --provider ollama --model qwen3.6:27b --api-base http://localhost:11434
src/app.py:2  [MEDIUM] Import order (confidence 6/10)
  sys should be sorted before os

1 finding · risk low (no risk signals) · provider ollama · model qwen3.6:27b · lgtmaybe 2.11.1
```

![The lgtmaybe review command running in a terminal, printing a [MEDIUM] import-order finding with its file and line, then a summary line naming the model](../assets/cli-example.png){ width="660" }

`--format` selects the output. `--json` is shorthand for `--format json`, which
prints the findings as a JSON array (every field in the table above) so the same
structured data can be piped into other tooling:

```console
$ lgtmaybe review --provider ollama --model qwen3.6:27b --api-base http://localhost:11434 --json
[{"path": "src/app.py", "line": 2, "side": "RIGHT", "severity": "medium",
  "title": "Import order", "body": "sys should be sorted before os",
  "failure_scenario": null, "suggestion": null, "anchor": "import sys",
  "anchored": true, "broad": false, "confidence": 6, "category": "complexity"}]
```

`--format agent` turns the findings into plain correction instructions an AI
coding agent can read and apply, for a local review-and-fix loop. See
[Fix findings with an AI agent](../how-to/fix-findings-with-an-ai-agent.md).
`lgtmaybe mcp` serves both shapes to a coding agent as MCP tool calls; see
[Use from a coding agent over MCP](../how-to/use-from-a-coding-agent-over-mcp.md).

`--format sarif` prints a SARIF 2.1.0 log for GitHub code scanning or an IDE
SARIF viewer. The log has:

- one rule per lens;
- the severity folded onto SARIF's three levels;
- the finding's fingerprint and identity as `partialFingerprints`.

See [Upload findings as SARIF](../how-to/upload-findings-as-sarif.md).

## See Also

- [Getting Started](../tutorial/getting-started.md): run your first review
- [Architecture](architecture.md): the review pipeline, stage by stage
- [Data and Privacy](data-and-privacy.md): what is sent where
