<!-- Source: https://lgtmaybe.coles.codes/explanation/risk-of-change/ -->

# Risk of Change

Every review carries a **risk of change** verdict: `low`, `medium`, `high` or
`critical`, with the reasons that produced it. It answers a different question
from the [findings](../reference/glossary.md#finding). A finding says "this line is wrong". The verdict says "this
change can reach a long way, so read it carefully", even when every line is
right.

The verdict is deterministic: it comes from fixed rules. It makes no model
call, so it costs nothing. It reads the same on every re-run of
the same head commit, so a workflow can rely on it.

## Where You See It

The review summary line names the level and its top reason:

```text
3 findings · risk high (`src/core/models.py` is imported by 84 files, +2 more) · provider … · model … · lgtmaybe …
```

The [change overview](../reference/glossary.md#change-overview) lists every
reason in a **Risk of Change** section above
[High Impact Areas](../reference/glossary.md#high-impact-areas). The summary
carries the verdict even when the overview is
turned off or skipped, so every review has it.

The summary also carries a hidden marker, `<!-- lgtmaybe-risk:high -->`. With
`pr_labels` on, the PR gets a `risk/<level>` label. Locally, `lgtmaybe
review` prints the same summary line.

## How the Level Is Decided

Each factor raises the level, and the verdict takes the highest:

| Factor | Raises to |
|---|---|
| A changed file imported by 5 or more files in the repository | `medium` |
| A changed file imported by 20 or more files, or matching a `risk.core_paths` glob | `high` |
| Touching an infrastructure, security, data migration, or backup and recovery path | `high` |
| Touching a path for any other High Impact area (dependencies, compatibility, cost, …) | `medium` |
| 500 or more changed lines | `medium` |
| 50 or more changed lines of code with no test file changed | `medium` |
| A [`regulated` project stage](../how-to/calibrate-reviews-to-your-project.md) | `medium` |

The area rows use the same path patterns as the
[High Impact Areas](../how-to/generate-a-change-diagram.md#high-impact-areas)
floor, applied to changed files that are not tests or documentation.

Two distinct `high` reasons make the change `critical`: a widely imported
module and a Terraform file, say, or an auth change and a database migration.
Two files in one area count once. A change touching only documentation and
tests is `low`, whatever the project stage. The `regulated` floor never goes
above `medium`, so it can't combine with one other `high` reason to make a
change `critical`.

## Blast Radius

The blast radius is how much existing code a change can reach. lgtmaybe
measures it by counting the files that import each changed file.

The importer count comes from one [ast-grep](https://ast-grep.github.io/) scan
of the checked-out repository for Python, TypeScript and JavaScript imports. It
parses files and runs nothing. On `pull_request_target` the checkout is the
trusted base branch, and nothing from the scan is sent to the model.

The count measures the code that already depends on a file:

- A file the PR adds has no existing importers.
- Importers the PR itself changes are left out, because they are already in the
  diff.
- Test files don't count as importers.

When a blast radius can't be measured, the verdict names the file instead of
guessing. This happens:

- for a language the scan doesn't read;
- when there is no checkout;
- when the ast-grep binary is missing or the scan fails;
- when the scan runs past its 20-second limit.

A `low` verdict with unmeasured files always says so:

```text
risk low (blast radius not assessed: `lib/billing.rb`)
```

The import count can't see modules reached by dynamic import, TypeScript path
aliases or barrel re-exports. Name those in `risk.core_paths` (see
[`risk`](../how-to/configure-lgtmaybe-yml.md#risk)).

## Gating on the Verdict

lgtmaybe never approves or blocks a PR on its risk. The marker lets you decide
what a level means for your team. For example, a step after the lgtmaybe step
can request a second reviewer when the latest review summary carries
`lgtmaybe-risk:critical`:

```yaml
- name: Require a second reviewer on critical changes
  env:
    GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
    PR: ${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}
  run: |
    latest=$(gh pr view "$PR" --json reviews \
      --jq '[.reviews[].body // "" | select(contains("lgtmaybe-risk:"))] | last // ""')
    if grep -q 'lgtmaybe-risk:critical' <<<"$latest"; then
      gh pr edit "$PR" --add-reviewer my-org/platform-leads
    fi
```

Reading only the latest summary matters: each new head commit gets a fresh
summary, so an older review can still carry a level the current change no
longer has.

If the assessment itself fails, the summary reads `risk unavailable` and no
marker is written, so a gate reads a missing marker as "unknown", never as a
level.

---

<!-- Source: https://lgtmaybe.coles.codes/explanation/architecture/ -->

# Architecture

lgtmaybe uses a **hexagonal architecture**, also called ports and adapters. A
port is an interface the core defines. An adapter implements a port for a real
service. The core defines the ports in `core/ports.py` and never imports an
adapter. Tests swap in fakes without patching. A new model backend or code host
plugs in without touching the engine.

## Ports and Adapters

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph core["core - never imports an adapter"]
        ports["ports.py<br/>ProviderClient · ReviewGateway · ReviewEngine"]
        models["models.py<br/>ReviewConfig · ReviewFinding · ProviderResult · PRContext"]
    end
    providers["providers/<br/>litellm adapter"] -- implements --> ports
    github["github/<br/>GitHub REST adapter"] -- implements --> ports
    gitlab["gitlab/<br/>GitLab REST adapter"] -- implements --> ports
    gitea["gitea/<br/>Gitea REST adapter"] -- implements --> ports
    azure["azure_devops/<br/>Azure DevOps REST adapter"] -- implements --> ports
```

Two independent choices meet at these ports:

- which **model** reviews the code (`ProviderClient`);
- which **[code host](../reference/glossary.md#code-host)** the review is
  posted to (`ReviewGateway`).

Any combination works, because neither side knows about the other.

`core/ports.py` defines three structural protocols (`typing.Protocol`). An
adapter satisfies one by having the right methods. It never inherits from it.

- `ProviderClient` has one method. `complete(messages, model, **opts)` returns
  a `ProviderResult` (text plus token usage).
- `ReviewGateway` has three:
    - `get_pr_context()` fetches the change diff and metadata.
    - `post_review(findings, summary)` posts batched inline comments and a
      summary.
    - `post_issue_comment(body)` posts a standalone comment. `/ask` and failure
      notices use it, and it is the describe/diagram fallback.
- `ReviewEngine` has `review(ctx, cfg)`, which returns `(findings, summary)`.
  The engine takes a `PRContext` and never sees a gateway. That is why the
  local CLI can build a `PRContext` from `git` with no code host at all.

The ports are frozen. The providers,
[forge](../reference/glossary.md#forge) adapters, engine and CLI all build
against these signatures, so change one only deliberately. `GitHubGateway`
survives as an alias of `ReviewGateway`, for adapters written before lgtmaybe
supported more than one host.

## Code Hosts (Forges)

Internally lgtmaybe calls a code host a **forge**. This keeps it distinct from
a model *[provider](../reference/glossary.md#provider)*. `core/forge.py` holds
the host-specific logic that lives outside the adapters:

- a `Forge` enum;
- a `PRLocator` (forge, host, repo, number) parsed from a change-request URL;
- the environment variable that holds each host's token.

The URL is all lgtmaybe needs:

| URL shape | Forge | Token |
|---|---|---|
| `github.com/org/repo/pull/42` | GitHub | `GITHUB_TOKEN` |
| `gitlab.com/group/sub/project/-/merge_requests/42` | GitLab | `GITLAB_TOKEN` |
| `gitea.example.com/org/repo/pulls/42` | Gitea | `GITEA_TOKEN` |
| `dev.azure.com/org/project/_git/repo/pullrequest/42` | Azure DevOps | `AZURE_DEVOPS_TOKEN` or `SYSTEM_ACCESSTOKEN` |

lgtmaybe parses the host from the URL rather than assuming it, because
self-hosted GitLab and Gitea are the normal case. `cli._GATEWAY_BUILDERS` maps
the resolved forge to its adapter.

### Required Surface vs Optional Capabilities

`ReviewGateway` is deliberately three methods. Everything richer is an optional
`Supports*` protocol. The CLI probes for each one and skips it when absent. So
an adapter is useful long before it is complete. It can also be honest about
what its host cannot do, instead of failing at run time.

| Capability | GitHub | GitLab | Gitea | Azure DevOps |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `SupportsFileContents`: read head text for context | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| `SupportsDescribe` / `SupportsDiagram`: upserted comments | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| `SupportsConversation`: read existing comments | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| `SupportsLabels` | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | not yet |
| `SupportsChecks`: check run / commit status | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | not yet |
| `SupportsThreadResolution`: auto-resolve a fixed finding | ✅ GraphQL | ✅ REST | ✗ no API | not yet |
| `SupportsIncremental`: review only new commits | ✅ | ✅ | ✗ no compare diff | not yet |
| `SupportsPermissions`: only writers run slash commands | ✅ | ✗ no slash commands | ✅ | ✗ no slash commands |
| `SupportsFeedback`: learn from 👎 reactions | ✅ | ✅ award emoji | ✗ | not yet |
| `SupportsBaseCheckout`: clone base for symbol lookup | ✅ | ✗ | ✗ | not yet |

`tests/test_ports.py` asserts the GitHub adapter satisfies every capability.
The GitLab, Gitea and Azure DevOps tests assert those adapters do **not** claim
what they cannot serve. That keeps this table honest.

### Where the Hosts Differ

Gitea is close to GitHub; GitLab and Azure DevOps are not.

- **GitHub** batches every inline comment into one review object. It resolves
  threads over GraphQL.
- **Gitea** mirrors GitHub's API, but a submitted review is immutable. So the
  summary lives in an ordinary issue comment, which can be edited. The adapter
  de-duplicates findings *before* posting, by reading the hidden ids already on
  the pull request.
- **GitLab** has no batched review object. Each finding is its own
  **discussion**, positioned by old/new path and line plus the merge request's
  `base_sha`/`start_sha`/`head_sha`. Threads resolve over plain REST. Its
  compare API returns per-file patches and no "ahead" status. So the adapter
  reassembles the increment into a unified diff. It checks from the commits'
  parent ids that the new head builds on the last reviewed one. It also works
  out the "lines moved" signal GitLab doesn't expose, from the diff since each
  discussion was posted.
- **Azure DevOps** serves no unified diff. The adapter lists the latest
  iteration's changed files against the merge base. It fetches each file's text
  on both sides. It renders the diff with `core/diffbuild.py`, so the shared
  parser reads it like any other. Each finding is its own thread, positioned by
  `threadContext`. The summary is a general thread edited in place.

lgtmaybe uses GitHub's `RIGHT`/`LEFT` side vocabulary internally. Each adapter
translates it at its boundary:

- `new_position`/`old_position` on Gitea;
- `new_line`/`old_line` on GitLab;
- right-file/left-file ranges on Azure DevOps.

### Entrypoints

GitHub and Gitea share one entrypoint. Gitea Actions reimplements the GitHub
Actions runtime, so the same `action` command and container work on both. The
only variable that differs is `GITHUB_SERVER_URL`, which Gitea points at your
own instance.

GitLab CI has neither an event payload file nor `INPUT_*` variables. So it gets
its own `gitlab-ci` command, which reads GitLab's predefined `CI_*` variables.
Everything downstream (locator, gateway registry, engine) is shared. There is
no `synchronize` action to key on, so `gitlab-ci` treats an unset `incremental`
as on. The first pipeline has no
[watermark](../reference/glossary.md#watermark) yet, so it is a full review
anyway.

Azure Pipelines is in the same position, so `azure-pipelines` reads its
predefined `SYSTEM_*` and `BUILD_*` variables.

## Review Pipeline

The engine runs a pipeline of composable stages:

```
fetch → redact → compress → prompt → parse → re-anchor → suppress
      → evidence gate → merge/dedupe → reflect → arbitrate → filter → post
```

The prompt/parse stage [fans out](../reference/glossary.md#fan-out): it makes
one concurrent model call per review [lens](../reference/glossary.md#lens).
The findings then funnel back into a single stream:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    fetch["fetch<br/>diff via API, never a checkout"] --> compress["redact + compress<br/>skip generated files · pad context · batch to budget"]
    compress --> security["security lens"]
    compress --> correctness["correctness lens<br/>+ stated intent"]
    compress --> codehealth["code-health lens<br/>performance · complexity · ponytail · deprecation"]
    compress --> artefacts["artefacts lens<br/>tests · documentation"]
    compress --> design["architecture lens<br/>coupling · dependency direction · substitutability"]
    security --> anchor["re-anchor<br/>snap lines to the real diff"]
    correctness --> anchor
    codehealth --> anchor
    artefacts --> anchor
    design --> anchor
    anchor --> suppress["suppress<br/>ignored fingerprints · pragmas · 👎"] --> evidence["evidence gate<br/>defects need a failure scenario"] --> dedupe["merge / dedupe"] --> reflect["reflect<br/>validate scenarios · drop low-confidence"] --> arbitrate["arbitrate<br/>no opposite advice on the same code"] --> filter["filter<br/>severity floor · finding rules"] --> post["post<br/>inline comments + summary"]
```

The five lens calls shown are the default `fast` grouping. The same five run on
every provider; worker count decides only whether they overlap. The `full`
[preset](../reference/glossary.md#preset) fans out one call per category. A
[spec lens](../reference/glossary.md#spec-lens) (when a committed spec matches
the PR) and any custom lenses join the same fan-out.

1. **fetch**: `ReviewGateway.get_pr_context()` retrieves the change diff and
    metadata from the forge's API. lgtmaybe never checks out or executes the
    change's code. It treats the diff as untrusted input throughout.

2. **redact + compress**: this stage prepares the diff for the model.

    - It [redacts](../reference/glossary.md#redaction) secrets from the diff
      before anything else sees it.
    - It skips generated files, lockfiles, minified assets and vendored code.
    - It then applies the `include_paths` / `exclude_paths` filters and the
      `max_file_diff_lines` and `max_files` caps.
    - It pads each remaining [hunk](../reference/glossary.md#hunk) with
      surrounding lines from the file's head revision. The gateway fetches
      those lines, never a checkout. `context_lines` and the token budget cap
      the padding.
    - It batches the result to fit `max_input_tokens`. When that is left at its
      default, it is first capped at what the model's context window can take.
    - With `recursive` on (the default), it walks a single file over budget
      hunk by hunk instead of sending it whole.

    The padded diff is for the model only. Inline-comment positions are rebuilt
    from the **real** diff at post time. So a finding on a padding line maps to
    nothing and is dropped rather than mis-posted.

3. **prompt + parse**: this stage **fans out one model call per review lens**,
    and `preset` decides the lens set. `fast` (the default) covers all ten
    everyday categories in **five calls**, one per concern:

    - security;
    - correctness, with stated intent when present;
    - code health: performance, complexity, ponytail, deprecation;
    - artefacts: tests, documentation;
    - architecture.

    `full` runs one call per category. Every (batch, lens) task shares **one
    `ThreadPoolExecutor`** over the synchronous provider port. It is sized by
    `max_concurrency` (default 6 for every provider, local included), so
    batches never wait on each other.

    Each call starts with a shared
    [cacheable prefix](../reference/glossary.md#prompt-cache): a
    lens-independent system preamble, then the wrapped diff. The lens-specific
    instructions follow as the final user block.

    Some routes take an explicit cache breakpoint: anthropic, bedrock
    Claude/Nova, vertex Claude and Gemini, zai GLM, and openrouter's
    claude/gemini/glm/minimax families. On those, lgtmaybe marks the prefix
    with `cache_control`. Backends that cache automatically (OpenAI, Azure,
    DeepSeek) need no marker. On a cache-capable route, every call after a
    batch's first reads the preamble and diff from cache. Other routes get the
    blocks merged into one plain message and make no caching promise. On big
    diffs a warm-up primer runs the first lens alone. That way a concurrent
    first wave doesn't pay for several cache writes.

    Each lens prompt asks for JSON matching the `ReviewFinding` schema (`path`,
    `line`, `side`, `severity`, `title`, `body`, `failure_scenario`,
    `suggestion`, `anchor`). It also carries
    [prompt-injection](../reference/glossary.md#prompt-injection) defence
    instructions. Pydantic parses and validates each response. A reply that
    does not parse is sent back once for repair (`repair_unparseable`, default
    on). A call that still fails is named in the summary's incomplete-results
    notice, rather than silently discarded.

    With `mid_review_retrieval` on (default **off**), a lens has a third option
    besides asserting or hedging a cross-file claim: **ask to read the code**.
    Alongside its findings it may return `needs`, the file paths or symbols it
    must see. The engine fetches them through the same read-only, redacting
    boundary that [reflection](../reference/glossary.md#reflection) uses (never
    a checkout). It then re-runs *that one lens* with the text added to its own
    uncached block. The shared prefix is untouched, so the batch's other lenses
    still read it from cache.

    This retrieval is bounded to **one hop**:

    - the re-run cannot defer again;
    - it fetches at most five files within a quarter of `max_input_tokens`;
    - a deferral that arrives past the review deadline or token budget is
      skipped with the usual incomplete-results notice.

    Both calls' findings are merged, so a deferral can only add findings. The
    cost is up to one extra model call per (batch, lens), which is why it ships
    off.

4. **re-anchor**: `_snap_findings` rebinds each finding's `line` to the changed
    line whose content matches the finding's verbatim
    [`anchor`](../reference/glossary.md#anchor). It does this rather than trust
    the model's line arithmetic. A finding whose anchor matches nothing is
    marked `anchored=False`. It must clear `unanchored_min_severity` (default
    `high`). It is then demoted to the review body instead of posted on a
    guessed line.

5. **suppress**: findings a team has marked known-fine are dropped before they
    cost any reflection tokens. Three things suppress a finding:

    - its fingerprint is in `ignore_fingerprints`;
    - a `# lgtmaybe: ignore` pragma sits on (or directly above) the flagged
      line;
    - a reviewer reacted 👎 to it on an earlier run (`learn_feedback`).

    Neither a 👎 nor a pragma (which the PR's author writes) suppresses a high
    or critical security finding. Only `ignore_fingerprints` in trusted config
    can.

6. **evidence gate**: security, correctness, deprecation and performance
    findings must carry a concrete `failure_scenario`. That means the trigger,
    the changed behaviour, and the observable impact. The rule applies
    regardless of the severity the model chose, so lowering a finding to `low`
    cannot bypass it. Gap and maintainability findings (tests, documentation,
    complexity) do not need a runtime failure. A fast-preset code-health
    finding the model left unattributed does, since it may be a performance or
    deprecation one.

7. **merge/dedupe**: findings from every lens are merged and de-duplicated by
    `_dedupe`. It keys on path/line/side, and scan findings on their title too,
    so distinct tool hits never merge. It runs after the two filters above. So
    a copy they would drop never displaces the finding that shares its line.

8. **reflect**: a self-reflection pass (`engine/reflect.py`) asks the provider
    to audit its own findings. It scores each 0-10 and drops the ones it marks
    low-confidence, plus any below `min_confidence`. If the verdict can't be
    parsed, every finding is kept. `--no-reflect` skips the pass. The auditor
    also tries to disprove each claimed failure scenario against the diff and
    the grounded file text.

    Sometimes the auditor would drop a finding *only* because it can't see code
    outside the diff. Then it **defers** by naming what it needs: a file path or
    a **symbol**. A path is fetched read-only (`get_file_contents`). A symbol is
    located by **ast-grep** (`engine/astgrep.py`), which structurally searches
    a corpus for the file that *defines* it. The corpus is the local worktree
    for the CLI, or a read-only shallow clone of the trusted **base** branch on
    GitHub. That file is fetched through the same read-only boundary. The
    auditor then re-judges with the real definition in front of it, instead of
    guessing about an unseen guard or base class.

    This stays inside the fork-safety model: ast-grep only *parses* the corpus
    (never executes it), and the base clone is never the PR head.
    [Symbol resolution](../reference/glossary.md#symbol-resolution) needs the
    bundled `ast-grep` binary and a corpus. Without either it falls back to the
    path-only fetch. `--no-symbol-resolution` disables it. It is bounded by the
    same hop and file caps as the path fetch.

    The auditor is also the first referee for opposing advice. Two findings
    from lenses on the precedence ladder may point opposite ways about the same
    code. Then it keeps the higher-ranked one.

9. **arbitrate**: this is the deterministic referee behind it
    (`engine/conflicts.py`). It also runs under `--no-reflect`. Some lens pairs
    are declared opposed: [ponytail](../reference/glossary.md#ponytail) against
    correctness, security or architecture. A finding from such a pair within
    three lines of a higher-ranked one is dropped. Each drop is logged with the
    finding and the lens that outranked it. See
    [When Lenses Disagree](what-gets-reviewed.md#when-lenses-disagree).

10. **filter**: findings below `min_severity` are dropped. Then any
    `finding_rules` apply, which drop or re-grade findings by path, lens, title
    or severity.

11. **post**: findings are posted as one batched review on GitHub. Per-host
    differences are in
    [What gets reviewed](what-gets-reviewed.md#how-each-host-posts).

    A hidden marker identifies lgtmaybe's summary. A re-run at the same commit
    edits it in place. A completed review at a new commit posts a fresh
    summary, leaving the older ones as history. Each inline comment carries two
    hidden per-finding ids, so a re-run never re-posts a finding it already
    made.

    On a re-run, conversations whose finding is gone **and** whose thread
    GitHub marks outdated are replied to and resolved (`resolve_fixed`, default
    on). The REST review API can't resolve a thread, so this step uses GitHub's
    GraphQL API. It is best-effort: a failure never blocks the review.

## Provider Strategy and Factory

Provider selection uses the **strategy pattern**: one interface with
interchangeable implementations. `--provider` picks a `ProviderClient`
strategy, and a small factory (`providers/factory.py`) builds it. The litellm
library normalises every provider to one `completion()` call. So the factory
stays small and the engine stays provider-agnostic.

Credential resolution is a **chain of responsibility**
(`providers/credentials.py`): each provider knows how to find its own
credentials. That is an API key,
[ambient cloud credentials](../reference/glossary.md#ambient-credentials), or
none for ollama. lgtmaybe never stores or logs credentials.

## Reliability: Retries, Timeouts and Concurrency

The provider wrapper (`LiteLLMProvider`) and the engine cooperate. A flaky
network recovers, but a dead-end failure surfaces fast.

- **Retries are classified, not blanket.** Transient failures are retried with
    exponential backoff and jitter, up to four attempts. These count as
    transient:

    - capacity rate limits (`429 rate_limit_exceeded`);
    - the provider's own connect/read timeouts;
    - connection errors, such as an ollama server still warming up;
    - 5xx responses.

    **Permanent** failures are not retried:

    - bad credentials (`AuthenticationError`);
    - malformed or unsupported requests (`BadRequestError`, including
      content-policy blocks);
    - unknown models (`NotFoundError`);
    - denied permissions;
    - **quota/billing** limits (`429 insufficient_quota`).

    A quota error can never succeed on retry. Across every lens it would only
    turn an instant "out of credit" into many minutes of wasted runner time. So
    lgtmaybe raises it immediately. An optional `fallback_model` is still tried
    once.

- **A blown wall clock is permanent too.** When a call outlives lgtmaybe's own
    per-request timeout, a retry would send the identical request to the
    identical model against the identical budget. It would fail the same way
    after another full timeout. So the wall timeout is raised after one
    attempt, and the failure reports how many attempts it used. The
    `fallback_model` is a different request, so it still gets its turn with a
    fresh budget.

- **Retried smaller, not repeated.** A wall timeout says something about the
    *payload*, and the payload is the one thing the engine can change. So the
    engine splits the batch: it halves it by file, or by hunk for a
    single-file batch. Each piece is reviewed with a fresh budget. A slow lens
    no longer discards the whole batch's review.

    The split goes **one** level deep. A piece that times out again fails with
    no further split. So a model that cannot answer at any size can't cascade
    through the review budget. The summary says when a batch had to be shrunk.
    A silent split would hide that every run is at the edge of what the model
    can finish in time.

- **A second model is the last remedy for a
    [truncation](../reference/glossary.md#truncation), not the first.** A
    truncated lens has two remedies that stay on the model you chose:

    - shrink the payload (the split above) when the *answer* outgrew the
      output ceiling;
    - lower `reasoning_effort` when the *thinking* did. If the lower setting
      also spends the ceiling on thinking, one more call runs with reasoning
      switched off (`disable_reasoning`). Some models treat effort as an on or
      off switch, so a lower setting alone changes nothing.

    Both are cheap, and both act on what the token counts say went wrong.
    Switching to `fallback_model` says nothing about the failure. It re-sends
    the same request at the same ceiling and hopes a second model finishes it.
    So it runs only after the targeted remedy has failed. It runs once for the
    whole batch, not once per split piece. The adapter still rescues every
    other kind of failure itself. Either way, the summary names the lens and
    the model that answered it. A review the primary model could not finish
    must not read like one it did.

    Reach for this rule before routing on diff size. Truncation does not track
    size. In our measurements a fifteen-line diff truncated at the same ceiling
    as a large multi-file one, because the ceiling goes on thinking. A size
    threshold spends the strong model on diffs that were already fine. A
    fallback keyed on the failure costs nothing until one happens.

- **A rate limit waits on its own, slower ladder.** The general ladder starts at
    a tenth of a second, which suits a blip such as a connection reset. A
    capacity 429 is not a blip. Gateways that meter an API key meter it *per
    minute*. A ladder that fits four attempts into a few seconds lands them all
    in the same window, where they fail identically.

    So rate limits back off on a 20s-60s ladder. They prefer the server's own
    **`Retry-After`** when it sends one, in either RFC form. That wait is
    clamped at 120s, so a gateway asking for an hour can't eat the run's wall
    clock. Both ladders stay inside the 2.5× retry budget below. The budget is
    checked against the *upcoming* wait, so a backoff that would exceed it ends
    the call instead of sleeping.

- **A call that failed on the provider gets one more go.** Once the fan-out has
    drained, the calls that failed *provider-side* are re-run once, in a narrow
    pool of their own. Without this, a single flaky call voided that lens's
    findings for the round until somebody re-ran by hand.

    Nothing else is re-run, because a second attempt would repeat the same
    failure at full price:

    - unparseable output returns the same answer at temperature 0;
    - a truncation hits the same ceiling;
    - a batch the split already retried has had the one retry that can help;
    - a dead key or spent quota won't fix itself mid-review;
    - a ceiling you set is not a fault to retry past.

    Every rescue re-checks the deadline, the token budget and the interrupt
    first. A healthy run costs **zero** extra calls.

- **One retry layer.** litellm's own internal retry loop is disabled
    (`num_retries=0`), so failures aren't ground through two stacked backoff
    layers. lgtmaybe owns the retry policy in one place.

- **Per-request timeout and a shared retry budget.** Every model call carries
    a timeout:

    - 600s for direct cloud providers;
    - 1800s for providers that may front a slow model: ollama,
      openai-compatible (local servers) and openrouter (a gateway to arbitrary
      models, including slow reasoning ones).

    For ollama and openai-compatible, the default is multiplied by the fan-out
    width. A single-slot local server queues the other calls while their clocks
    run. `timeout` / `--timeout` overrides all of this. All attempts for one
    call share a wall-clock budget of **2.5× the timeout**. So a flaky model
    can't burn four full timeouts plus backoff per lens.

    lgtmaybe's own workflows also set a job-level `timeout-minutes` (75) above
    `max_review_seconds`. So the soft deadline, which still posts partial
    findings, fires before the runner kills the job. Do the same in yours. If
    the runner does cut the job short, the CLI's signal handler is the backstop
    (below).

- **A whole-review deadline.** `max_review_seconds` (default 3600, `0`
    disables) is a soft ceiling on the run. Once it passes, queued model calls
    are skipped, in-flight ones finish and their findings post, and the summary
    carries an explicit incomplete-results notice. It can never produce a
    silent LGTM: a run where every call failed or was skipped still fails
    loudly.

- **A termination signal does the same thing.** The CLI installs a
    SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that sets the deadline's state. So a job the runner
    cancels or times out stops dispatching model calls. It posts what it
    already has, with a notice naming the interruption. Only the CLI entrypoint
    installs the handler. Importing lgtmaybe as a library never touches your
    signal handlers. The handler restores the previous handler as it fires, so
    a second signal still kills the process.

- **Incompleteness is visible on the PR, not only in the log.** A failed lens
    call of *any* kind raises the incomplete-results notice: a per-call
    timeout, a provider error, or unparseable output. The notice names the
    lenses it lost and why. A missing security lens and a missing
    documentation lens are the same count and very different news. The engine
    also stamps a hidden `<!-- lgtmaybe-incomplete -->` marker.

    Later findings arrive as separate review comments, while the first run's
    summary is only edited in place. So an incomplete run also posts the notice
    as its own PR comment. A review that failed outright does the same.

    The summary also carries a hidden `<!-- lgtmaybe-lenses:… -->` list of the
    lenses that completed every call. A gate that wants "every lens ran" can
    require the set it expects. It need not infer it from the absence of a
    notice. A matched spec that did not fit the spec budget is named the same
    way. A spec lens that should have run and did not is a gap, not a no-match.

- **A diff the host will not serve is a review that did not happen.** GitHub
    answers the diff request with 406 once a PR passes 300 files or 20,000
    lines. lgtmaybe reads PR content through that API only, never a checkout.
    So there is nothing to review, and no retry will change it. The run:

    - posts a "not reviewed" notice quoting GitHub's reason, with a hidden
      `<!-- lgtmaybe-skipped -->` marker;
    - stamps nothing complete;
    - exits zero.

    It is not a failure: a red job for a PR the reviewer could never read only
    teaches people to ignore red jobs. It is never an LGTM either. The fix is a
    smaller PR; no reviewer setting moves the host's limit.

- **One global fan-out pool.** Every (batch, lens) call runs through a single
    `ThreadPoolExecutor` sized by `max_concurrency`. The default is **6
    workers** for every provider. An extra worker can cut a full-latency wave
    off the wall clock. But the fan-out shares *one* API key. Past some width,
    the burst rate-limits itself against a gateway that meters per minute.
    Raise it if your rate tier is generous.

    Local providers get the same 6. A default ollama serves one request at a
    time, but that is a property of the *server*. One that can batch would be
    capped for nothing. One that can't loses nothing by having work queued,
    because ollama queues up to `OLLAMA_MAX_QUEUE` rather than failing.

    Local throughput is decided by `OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL`, llama.cpp's `-np` or
    vLLM's batching. Raising those costs memory per slot; see
    [running locally](../how-to/run-locally-with-ollama.md). Drop
    `max_concurrency` to 1 for a very slow local model, where six queued calls
    could each wait out the timeout. The pool is shared across batches. So wall
    time is `ceil(batches × lenses / workers)` call-latencies rather than
    `batches × ceil(lenses / workers)`.

## Dependency Injection

The engine receives its ports by injection: it is handed them rather than
building them itself. `LLMReviewEngine` takes a `ProviderClient`, plus optional
file-fetch and symbol-resolver callables. `review()` takes a `PRContext`. In
production the CLI wires the real adapters. In tests, the fakes in
`tests/fakes/` (`FakeProvider`, `FakeGitHub`, `FakeEngine`) drop in directly.
So swapping a port never needs patching.

## Why Not a Plugin Framework or Event Bus

We considered both and skipped them. The current providers fit cleanly in a
strategy and factory. A plugin registry would add indirection with no present
benefit. An event bus would complicate the linear pipeline without enabling any
feature the product needs. Either can be revisited if a concrete requirement
arises.

---

<!-- Source: https://lgtmaybe.coles.codes/explanation/auth-model/ -->

# Auth Model

lgtmaybe supports seven hosted [providers](../reference/glossary.md#provider)
plus local ollama. It also has an `openai-compatible` escape hatch for any
server that speaks the OpenAI `/v1` wire format (DeepSeek's API, llama.cpp, LM
Studio, vLLM).

The design principle is **no static cloud credentials**. A static credential is
a long-lived key you store and rotate by hand.

- Cloud providers use [ambient](../reference/glossary.md#ambient-credentials),
  short-lived tokens that the environment already provides.
- Key-based SaaS providers (openai, anthropic, openrouter, zai) need an API key.
  The key lives in a secret store, never in committed config.
- Azure sits between the two. It accepts a resource key but falls back to
  ambient Entra (Azure AD) credentials. It always needs the resource endpoint
  (`AZURE_API_BASE`), because each Azure OpenAI deployment lives at its own URL.

## Why Keyless for Cloud

Static credentials, such as an AWS access key pair or a GCP service-account
JSON file, have a long lifetime and broad scope. If one leaks from a CI log, a
misconfigured secrets manager, or a compromised runner, an attacker keeps
access until someone rotates the key by hand.

[OIDC](../reference/glossary.md#oidc) (AWS),
[Workload Identity Federation](../reference/glossary.md#wif) (GCP), and
federated credentials on an Entra app (Azure) issue tokens that:

- expire in minutes, not years;
- are scoped to a single workflow run;
- are never stored as static secrets, so there is no long-lived key to leak;
- are tied to the specific repository and branch through the OIDC claims.

The exchange has the same shape on all three clouds, and no secret ever enters
the workflow:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant W as GitHub Actions run
    participant O as GitHub OIDC issuer
    participant STS as Cloud token service<br/>(AWS STS / GCP STS / Entra)
    participant M as Model API<br/>(Bedrock / Vertex / Azure OpenAI)
    W->>O: request identity token (id-token: write)
    O-->>W: signed JWT with repo + branch claims
    W->>STS: exchange JWT for cloud credentials
    STS-->>W: short-lived, scoped credentials
    W->>M: lgtmaybe review calls with ambient creds
```

In the GitHub Action, pass `aws_role_arn`, `gcp_wif_provider` or
`azure_client_id` and the action runs this exchange for you. The workflow needs
`permissions: id-token: write`.

For these reasons, Bedrock and Vertex accept only ambient credentials:
`--api-key` is ignored for them. Azure defaults to the same keyless path
(GitHub OIDC to Entra, through `azure-identity`'s `DefaultAzureCredential`) but
also accepts a resource key for teams that can't adopt federation yet.

## Chain of Responsibility

When lgtmaybe starts, it resolves credentials for the selected provider. Each
provider has its own rule for where to look:

1. **Bedrock** hands credential discovery to the AWS SDK, which finds GitHub
   OIDC role credentials, `~/.aws` profiles, environment variables, or an
   ECS, EKS or EC2 role. lgtmaybe never asks for a key, and missing
   credentials surface as an error from the first model call.
2. **Vertex** checks for ambient GCP credentials first: Workload Identity
   Federation, Application Default Credentials from
   `gcloud auth application-default login`, or a project set in the
   environment. Failing those, it asks `google-auth`, which also finds the
   metadata-server credentials of GCE, GKE Workload Identity, Cloud Run and
   Cloud Build. If there are none, lgtmaybe fails immediately with a message
   explaining how to authenticate. It never falls back to a key.
3. **Azure** always needs the resource endpoint (`AZURE_API_BASE` or
   `--api-base`). It uses a key when one is supplied (`AZURE_API_KEY` or
   `--api-key`). Otherwise it goes keyless and mints an Entra token from
   ambient credentials: GitHub OIDC federation in CI, or `az login` or a
   managed identity locally. The token is refreshed as it nears expiry, so a
   review that runs past an hour keeps working. Keyless needs the
   `azure-identity` package (`pip install 'lgtmaybe[azure]'`; the Action image
   includes it). With neither a key nor an ambient credential, lgtmaybe fails
   at start-up with a message naming both options and the SDK's own reason.
4. **ollama** needs no credentials. `--api-base` points it at the server and
   defaults to `http://localhost:11434`.
5. **zai** (GLM / Zhipu AI) needs `ZAI_API_KEY` or `--api-key`. Without an
   endpoint override, litellm's native `zai/` route targets the international
   endpoint; set `--api-base` or `ZAI_API_BASE` for the China or coding-plan
   endpoint.
6. **openai-compatible** always needs the endpoint (`--api-base` or
   `OPENAI_COMPATIBLE_API_BASE`), since choosing your own is the point. The key
   is optional. Hosted endpoints like DeepSeek take one (`--api-key` or
   `OPENAI_COMPATIBLE_API_KEY`). Local servers (llama.cpp, LM Studio, vLLM)
   need none, and lgtmaybe sends a harmless placeholder key because the
   underlying OpenAI client rejects an empty one.
7. **openai, anthropic and openrouter** read the key from `--api-key`, or else
   from `OPENAI_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` or `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`. With
   neither, lgtmaybe fails with a message naming the variable to set.

!!! note "In the GitHub Action, use the `api_key` and `api_base` inputs"

    The Action's container receives only its `INPUT_*` variables and the
    cloud-auth `AWS_*`, `GOOGLE_*`, `CLOUDSDK_*` and `AZURE_*` variables. A
    provider key set as a step `env:` variable such as `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` does
    not reach it, so pass the key with `api_key: ${{ secrets.… }}` and any
    endpoint with `api_base`.

## Provider Auth Summary

| Provider | Credential type | How to supply |
|---|---|---|
| openai | API key | `OPENAI_API_KEY` env var or `--api-key` |
| anthropic | API key | `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` env var or `--api-key` |
| openrouter | API key | `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` env var or `--api-key` |
| zai | API key (+ optional endpoint) | `ZAI_API_KEY` env var or `--api-key`; optional `ZAI_API_BASE` / `--api-base` for the China / coding-plan endpoint |
| bedrock | Ambient AWS creds | GitHub OIDC role or local `~/.aws`; IAM needs only `bedrock:InvokeModel*` |
| vertex | Ambient GCP creds | GitHub WIF or local ADC (`gcloud auth application-default login`) |
| azure | Ambient Entra creds (keyless) or API key, + endpoint | GitHub OIDC to an Entra federated credential, or local `az login` / managed identity; or `AZURE_API_KEY`. Always with `AZURE_API_BASE` / `--api-base` |
| ollama | None | `--api-base` pointing at the local or remote server (default `http://localhost:11434`) |
| openai-compatible | Optional key, + endpoint | `--api-base` / `OPENAI_COMPATIBLE_API_BASE` (e.g. `https://api.deepseek.com/v1` or `http://localhost:8000/v1`); key via `--api-key` / `OPENAI_COMPATIBLE_API_KEY`, or none for keyless local servers |

## Code-Host Auth

Everything above authenticates lgtmaybe to a **model provider**. Reading the
diff and posting the review need a separate credential for the
[code host](../reference/glossary.md#code-host). The host in the change-request
(pull or merge request) URL decides which one:

| Host | Variable | What it needs |
|---|---|---|
| GitHub | `GITHUB_TOKEN` | `contents: read` and `pull-requests: write`. The Action's default token is enough |
| GitLab | `GITLAB_TOKEN` | A project access token with the `api` scope, Developer role or above |
| Gitea | `GITEA_TOKEN` | A token with `write:repository`, `write:issue` and `read:user` |
| Azure DevOps | `AZURE_DEVOPS_TOKEN`, else `SYSTEM_ACCESSTOKEN` | A personal access token with Code (Read & write) scope, or the pipeline's own token with *Contribute to pull requests* granted to the build service |

These are always tokens. There is no keyless path to a code host, and lgtmaybe
does not attempt one. The token is read from the environment only and, like a
provider key, is never written to `.lgtmaybe.yml` or logged.

!!! note "Keyless cloud auth is GitHub-only"

    Bedrock, Vertex, and Azure go keyless by exchanging a **GitHub Actions**
    OIDC token. GitLab CI, Gitea Actions and Azure Pipelines have no equivalent
    exchange wired up, so on those hosts use an API-key provider, or `ollama` against a
    runner-local model, which needs no credential at all.

## Least-Privilege IAM

For Bedrock, the minimum [IAM](../reference/glossary.md#iam) policy is `bedrock:InvokeModel` and (if streaming)
`bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream` on the specific model ARN. No other AWS
permissions are needed or requested.

For Vertex, `roles/aiplatform.user` on the project is enough. Do not use
`roles/editor` or `roles/owner`.

For keyless Azure, the Entra app needs only the **Cognitive Services OpenAI
User** role on the Azure OpenAI resource (enough to call deployments, not to
manage them) plus a federated credential scoped to your repository. No owner or
contributor role is required.

## API Keys in Secrets, Not Config

Every API key (openai, anthropic, openrouter, zai, an Azure resource key, or a
hosted `openai-compatible` key) belongs in a secret store: a GitHub Actions
secret, a GitLab masked CI/CD variable, or a Gitea Actions secret. Never commit
one to `.lgtmaybe.yml` or any other file in the repository. lgtmaybe does not
log or display key values.

---

<!-- Source: https://lgtmaybe.coles.codes/explanation/data-and-privacy/ -->

# Data and Privacy

This page explains what lgtmaybe sends to a model
[provider](../reference/glossary.md#provider), what it
[redacts](../reference/glossary.md#redaction) first, how local mode differs, and
how credentials are handled.

## What Is Sent to the LLM Provider

Under the default `fast` [preset](../reference/glossary.md#preset), lgtmaybe
makes five core review calls per diff [batch](../reference/glossary.md#batch).
Under `full`, it makes one per built-in category. A matching committed spec adds
a separate spec-review call, and a [reflection](../reference/glossary.md#reflection)
pass follows. These calls can contain:

- **The PR diff**: the unified diff of changed files, after generated files,
  lockfiles, minified assets, and vendored code have been skipped. File paths
  appear in the diff headers. Each batch also lists the PR's changed files that
  its own diff does not show.
- **Surrounding context lines**: unchanged lines around each changed
  [hunk](../reference/glossary.md#hunk), read from the head revision (the PR's
  latest commit) of the **changed files only**. They give the model the
  enclosing function and definitions, which cuts false positives.
    - Before each hunk, lgtmaybe adds up to `context_lines` lines (default 20,
      `0` disables it). It extends that up to the enclosing function or class
      signature where that can be found.
    - After each hunk, it adds about a quarter as many.
    - The amount shrinks as the diff grows, and the text is redacted like the
      diff.
    - On GitHub it is fetched read-only through the API. Pull request code is
      never checked out or executed.
- **The PR's stated intent**: the PR title, description, and the first line of
  each commit message. On the CLI, it is the commit subjects from your local
  `git log`. It feeds the intent check ("does the PR do what it says?"). It is
  redacted like the diff and wrapped as untrusted data. It is sent on only one
  review call: the correctness call under `fast`, or the dedicated intent
  [lens](../reference/glossary.md#lens) under `full`. The change overview's
  calls also send it (see below).
- **A system prompt**: the fixed instructions that tell the model to return
  structured JSON findings.
- **A project paragraph**, if the `project` block is set: its stage guidance,
  `domain` and `notes`, as written in `.lgtmaybe.yml`. Delimiter tokens in it
  are neutralised (made harmless, see
  [Prompt-Injection Defence](#prompt-injection-defence)). Don't put anything in
  `notes` you wouldn't send to the model provider.
- **Configured instructions and reference files**, if `directory_rules` is set.
  Reference files come from the trusted base-branch workspace, are bounded, and
  are redacted before model calls.
- **Static-analysis hints**, unless `static_analysis` is turned off
  ([static-analysis fusion](../reference/glossary.md#static-analysis-fusion)):
  redacted findings from tools run locally over the changed files. The tools
  run in a sandbox with no network, so the file text never leaves the machine
  through them. Only the redacted hints reach the model. A hint about a
  lockfile names the package, version and advisory; the lockfile text itself
  is never sent.
- **Matching specification text**, when a repository has a supported spec
  workflow and the change matches a committed spec. The
  [spec lens](../reference/glossary.md#spec-lens) sends a bounded, redacted
  selection from that spec.
- **Additional file context**, when a review or reflection needs to check a
  finding against another file. Retrieval is read-only, bounded, and redacted.
  `mid_review_retrieval` is opt-in.

With `triage_model` set, one extra call sends the same redacted per-file diffs
to the triage model, on the same provider. The triage model is a cheaper model
that skips plainly non-substantive files and ranks the rest by risk.

Review calls do not send:

- PR comments or review threads
- Commit message bodies (only the first line of each message)
- The repository name, PR number, or commit SHAs
- Unrequested repository files or the whole repository
- Committer identity or email addresses
- Any other data from the repository's git history

The [change overview](../reference/glossary.md#change-overview) (`/diagram`,
`auto_diagram`) makes up to three calls: description,
[High Impact Areas](../reference/glossary.md#high-impact-areas), and diagrams.
They use the redacted diff and, when present, the redacted stated intent. The
High Impact Areas call also sends the paths of changed files that match its risk
patterns, which are already in the diff. No new data flows; these calls only ask
for a different output. The standalone `/describe` comment sends the same inputs
again, and `/ask` sends your question with the redacted diff.

The overview comment includes an "Open full screen"
[mermaid.live](https://mermaid.live) link per diagram. The link's URL fragment
(the part after `#`) embeds that diagram's source. That source is already in the
posted comment and was built from redacted model output. Browsers decode the
fragment client-side and never send it to a server. Nothing is fetched unless a
reader clicks the link.

## Secret Redaction Before Egress

Before the diff is sent to any provider, lgtmaybe scans it for patterns that
look like secrets. It replaces the matched values with `[REDACTED]`. The same
scrub applies to:

- the context lines read from changed files;
- the stated-intent text (PR title, description, commit subjects);
- static-analysis hints;
- spec text;
- any fetched file context.

Recognised formats include:

- **Cloud and provider keys**: AWS access key IDs (`AKIA…`), OpenAI keys
  (`sk-…`), Stripe secret keys (`sk_live_…` / `sk_test_…`), and Google API keys
  (`AIza…`).
- **Source-control, chat and registry tokens**: GitHub classic tokens (`ghp_`,
  `gho_`, …), GitHub fine-grained PATs (`github_pat_…`), Slack tokens
  (`xoxb-…`), npm tokens (`npm_…`), and PyPI tokens (`pypi-…`).
- **JSON Web Tokens**: `eyJ….eyJ….…` and five-part encrypted JWEs, as whole
  tokens, since the payload can carry claims and PII.
- **Private keys**: PEM `-----BEGIN … PRIVATE KEY-----` blocks, encrypted ones
  included.
- **Generic credentials**:
    - `api_key` / `secret_key` / `access_token` / `token` assignments with a
      value of 16 or more characters;
    - quoted `password` / `passwd` / `passphrase` / `pwd` literals (the key may
      be quoted too, as in JSON);
    - `Authorization: Bearer/Basic …` headers;
    - passwords in connection-string URLs (`scheme://user:secret@host`);
    - Azure storage or Cosmos connection-string keys (`AccountKey=…` /
      `SharedAccessKey=…`).

For credential assignments only the value is replaced. The key name or URL
host stays readable, so the reviewer can still reason about the change.

Redaction is the **first** pipeline stage, before the diff is compressed or the
prompt is built, so redacted values never reach the LLM.

Redaction is a best-effort defence. Do not commit real secrets and rely on it
alone.

## Model Replies in the Log

When a model's reply can't be parsed into findings, lgtmaybe logs why. At the
default log level it records only:

- the kind of parse failure (`prose`, `malformed_json`, `not_findings`,
  `schema`, `truncated`, `empty`);
- the reply's length in characters;
- a short hash that tells you whether two runs failed on the same reply.

It never logs the content.

Set `LGTMAYBE_LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG` and the log line also carries a capped excerpt
of the reply (the first 2,000 and last 500 characters, with the gap marked).
This lets you diagnose a model that stops following the output schema without
re-running the review. The excerpt:

- passes through the same secret redaction described above. It is redacted
  **before** it is cut, so a truncated match can't slip past the redactor;
- is written to **stderr** with the other structured JSON log lines. It never
  goes to stdout (the machine-readable channel) and never to the PR;
- is model output, which can quote the diff back. That is why it is off unless
  you ask for it.

## The Repair Re-ask

When a review call's reply can't be parsed into findings, lgtmaybe sends that
reply back to the **same provider** once. It sends the output schema with it and
asks the model to re-express the reply in the required shape. This is
`repair_unparseable`, on by default.

This adds no new data. The reply is the model's own output about a diff it has
already seen. The repair call carries **no diff, no context lines, and no PR
metadata**: only the reply itself, capped and wrapped as untrusted data. It
happens at most once per failed call and never recursively.

## The Schema-less Re-run

When that reformat also fails *and* the original call carried the provider's
JSON schema, lgtmaybe re-runs that one lens once without the schema
(`retry_without_schema`, on by default). The prompt asks for JSON regardless.
Some providers force the output to fit the schema (constrained decoding). A
model whose constrained decoding produced something unreadable often answers
fine without it.

Unlike the repair, this **does re-send the diff**. It is the same request, minus
one parameter, to the same provider. So no new data leaves the process, but it
is a second full send rather than a small one. It runs at most once per lens
per batch, only after the cheaper repair has failed, and only where a schema
was sent. Set `retry_without_schema: false` to turn it off.

## Prompt-Injection Defence

lgtmaybe treats PR diff content as untrusted input throughout the pipeline. It
defends against [prompt injection](../reference/glossary.md#prompt-injection) in
depth (OWASP LLM01):

1. The diff is wrapped in explicit `DIFF_START`/`DIFF_END` delimiters and
   labelled as untrusted data. The stated-intent text gets its own
   `INTENT_START`/`INTENT_END` block with the same labelling. Every other
   untrusted block (static-analysis hints, spec text, path signals, fetched
   context) has its own delimiter family.
2. lgtmaybe **neutralises** forged delimiter markers smuggled into the diff or
   the intent text before wrapping. It does this for both marker families in
   both blocks. So a malicious PR can't close a data block early, append its own
   instructions, or fake an intent block from inside the diff.
3. The system prompt tells the model to ignore any instructions embedded in the
   diff or the intent text that try to change reviewer behaviour.
4. The model's response must validate against a strict JSON schema
   (`extra="forbid"`). lgtmaybe rejects drifted or injected fields rather than
   acting on them.

lgtmaybe does not execute any code from the PR.

## Ollama: Local or Self-Hosted

With `--provider ollama`, the diff and all other data go only to the ollama
server you name with `--api-base` (default `http://localhost:11434`). If that
server is on your machine, no data leaves it. If it is a remote host (a
Tailscale peer, a self-hosted VM), data goes only to that host. The same holds
for an `openai-compatible` server you run yourself.

lgtmaybe does not operate ollama. See ollama's own documentation for its data
handling.

## Hosted Providers: Data Handling

With any hosted provider, the redacted diff and the other inputs above are sent
over HTTPS to that provider's inference endpoint. Review each provider's data
handling policy, for example:

- **AWS Bedrock**: [AWS Bedrock data protection](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/data-protection.html)
- **Google Vertex AI**: [Vertex AI data governance](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/general/data-governance)
- **Azure OpenAI**: [Data, privacy, and security for Azure OpenAI](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/legal/cognitive-services/openai/data-privacy)
- **OpenAI**: [OpenAI API data privacy](https://openai.com/policies/api-data-privacy)
- **Anthropic**: [Anthropic privacy policy](https://www.anthropic.com/legal/privacy)
- **OpenRouter**: [OpenRouter privacy policy](https://openrouter.ai/privacy)

For z.ai and hosted `openai-compatible` endpoints such as DeepSeek, check that
provider's own policy.

## Credentials

lgtmaybe does not log or persist API keys. API-key providers receive the key
only to authenticate model calls. For Bedrock, Vertex, and keyless Azure,
lgtmaybe uses short-lived
[ambient credentials](../reference/glossary.md#ambient-credentials) and does not
write them to disk. See [Auth Model](./auth-model.md) for details.

## GitHub Token

lgtmaybe uses `GITHUB_TOKEN` to:

1. Read the PR diff and metadata through the GitHub REST API.
2. Post the review (inline comments and summary) back to the PR.

The token is never sent to an LLM provider. It needs only `contents: read` and
`pull-requests: write`. GitLab and Gitea use their own tokens, listed in
[Code-Host Auth](./auth-model.md#code-host-auth).

## Fork Pull Requests

On GitHub, lgtmaybe uses the `pull_request_target` trigger. It runs in the
context of the **base branch** (the branch the PR merges into). Code from the
fork is never checked out or executed, and the diff is fetched only through the
host's API. A malicious PR therefore can't reach the repository's secrets.

lgtmaybe never checks out or executes change-request code on any host, so a
change has nothing of its own to run inside the review. That does not protect
the pipeline definition. These all run the CI configuration from the change
itself:

- a GitLab merge request pipeline;
- a Gitea `pull_request` run;
- an Azure Pipelines pull request build.

So anyone who can push a branch can rewrite the job that holds the secrets.
Gitea 1.21 and later supports `pull_request_target`, which the supplied Gitea
workflow uses; GitLab and Azure DevOps have no equivalent. Each guide's security
section covers who can change the pipeline and how to keep the secrets out of
their reach:
[GitLab](../how-to/review-on-gitlab.md#security-who-can-change-the-pipeline),
[Gitea](../how-to/review-on-gitea.md#security-who-can-change-the-workflow) and
[Azure DevOps](../how-to/review-on-azure-devops.md#security-who-can-change-the-pipeline).

---

<!-- Source: https://lgtmaybe.coles.codes/explanation/trust-and-cost/ -->

# Trust and Cost

You decide **who can trigger a review**. Hosted models charge for each run, so
that choice affects cost. The setup steps are in
[Use as a GitHub Action](../how-to/use-as-github-action.md).

## Who Do You Want Reviews to Run For?

There is no single right answer. It depends on your repo and provider:

- **Everyone**, including strangers opening fork PRs. Good for a welcoming
  open-source project where every contributor should get feedback.
- **Trusted contributors**: members and collaborators, the people who already
  have a relationship with the repo. This is the default.
- **Admins and owners only**: the tightest setting, handy while you try
  lgtmaybe out.

The example workflows ship with the trusted-contributors setting, and widening
or narrowing it is a one-line change.

## The Cost Angle

This choice matters only because hosted providers bill per run:

- **ollama** runs the model on your own hardware, so there is no per-run cost.
  Trigger it for whoever you like. The same goes for an `openai-compatible`
  server you host yourself.
- **Hosted providers** (OpenAI, Anthropic, OpenRouter, z.ai, Bedrock, Vertex,
  Azure, and hosted `openai-compatible` endpoints such as DeepSeek) charge for
  the tokens each review uses.

So on a hosted provider with a public repo, "everyone" means anyone can start a
paid run. That is fine for plenty of projects, as long as you choose it on
purpose. The default keeps reviews to people you already trust, and you can open
it up whenever you want.

Built-in limits keep any single run bounded, whoever starts it:

- `max_files` (default 50) and `max_file_diff_lines` (default 2000) limit how
  much of the diff is reviewed. See [What Gets Reviewed](what-gets-reviewed.md).
- `max_input_tokens` (default 100k) limits how much one call sends. A larger
  diff is split into more [batches](../reference/glossary.md#batch), not
  dropped.
- `max_review_seconds` (default 3600) stops dispatching new calls once a run
  has taken an hour.
- `max_review_tokens` (off by default) stops dispatching new calls once a run
  has spent a token budget you set.

When a run hits a limit, it degrades rather than fails. Take a review call that
outruns its wall clock, or writes until it hits the `max_tokens` ceiling. That
call is not lost: lgtmaybe splits the batch in half, reviews the pieces, and
keeps anything the model had already written. That costs up to twice the calls
for the affected batch and is bounded to one split.

A partial review always says so. The summary carries a "results may be
incomplete" notice, and a [lens](../reference/glossary.md#lens) that was cut
short is never presented as a clean bill of health. lgtmaybe will not answer 👍
LGTM for code no model finished reading.

To measure what a run actually spends and bring it down (triage, static
analysis, prompt caching, and the `max_review_tokens` ceiling), see
[Reduce Review Cost](../how-to/reduce-review-cost.md).

## How the Choice Is Expressed

The example workflows gate the `review` job on the triggering user's
[author association](https://docs.github.com/en/graphql/reference/enums#commentauthorassociation),
GitHub's classification of a user's relationship to the repo. By default the
job runs when that association is `OWNER`, `MEMBER`, or `COLLABORATOR`:

```yaml
if: >-
  (github.event_name == 'pull_request_target' &&
   contains(fromJson('["OWNER", "MEMBER", "COLLABORATOR"]'), github.event.pull_request.author_association)) ||
  (github.event.issue.pull_request &&
   contains(fromJson('["OWNER", "MEMBER", "COLLABORATOR"]'), github.event.comment.author_association) &&
   (contains(github.event.comment.body, '/review') ||
    contains(github.event.comment.body, '/improve') ||
    contains(github.event.comment.body, '/ask') ||
    contains(github.event.comment.body, '/describe') ||
    contains(github.event.comment.body, '/diagram')))
```

A maintainer can still review an outside contributor's PR at any time by
commenting `/review` on it, because the maintainer's own association passes the
gate. To change the policy, edit the list:

- **Open it to everyone**: drop the author-association checks so any PR or
  `/review` comment runs a review.
- **Welcome returning contributors**: add `CONTRIBUTOR`, which covers anyone
  who has committed to the repo before.
- **Tighten to admins**: keep only `OWNER` (and `MEMBER` for your org).

The gate lives in your workflow YAML, not in the action's code, so the policy
for automatic PR reviews is entirely yours.

Slash commands have one floor the YAML cannot lower. lgtmaybe runs a command
only when the commenter has write access to the repository. It ignores anyone
else's with a log line and no model call. So opening the comment arm (the
`issue_comment` half of the `if:`) to everyone, or adding `CONTRIBUTOR`, changes
who triggers a run, not who can spend the model through one.

The slash-command half of the comment arm saves runner time rather than
tokens. `issue_comment` fires on every comment on every pull request. Without
the check, a comment with no slash command still claims a runner, pulls the
container and boots Python before lgtmaybe exits. Filtering in the `if:` costs
nothing. On a busy runner pool it keeps reviews from queueing behind ordinary
comment threads.

The check is deliberately looser than lgtmaybe's own parser: a case-insensitive
substring match, not a prefix match. A guard stricter than the parser would
silently disable a command that used to work. Replies inside a finding's review
thread don't trigger a run at all; the next
[incremental review](../reference/glossary.md#incremental-review) checks a
pushed fix.

## If You Want Extra Guardrails

Optional, for repos that want more:

- Require approval for fork-PR workflow runs in
  **Settings → Actions → General → Fork pull request workflows**.
- Put the provider key behind a protected `environment`.
- Set a spending limit in your provider console.

## Reviews Are Safe to Run for Anyone

Whoever triggers a review, a malicious PR can't use it to do harm. On GitHub,
lgtmaybe triggers on `pull_request_target` (so it has the secrets it needs) but
never checks out or executes PR code. It fetches the diff through the host's
API and treats it as untrusted input. That second part is what does the work,
and it holds the same way on Gitea. It also holds on GitLab, which has no
`pull_request_target` of its own. So opening the gate wide is a
cost decision, not a security one. The full boundary (secret
[redaction](../reference/glossary.md#redaction), prompt-injection defence, and
fork safety) is in [Data and Privacy](data-and-privacy.md).
